The Retiree’s Portfolio

Active Selection versus Indexing over Thirty Years

The Index Holds: Retirement Portfolios Built from Top-Ranked Vanguard Funds, 1995–2026

Preface

This book examines a single question across thirty years of market history. How does a retirement fare when the retiree holds whichever Vanguard funds have performed best recently, re-selecting them each January, while drawing a fixed and rising income? And does it fare better than holding the market through two index funds and never choosing at all?

The question is asked not of one retirement but of every year in which a retirement could have begun since 1995. The same withdrawal rule is then run over the long market histories, from 1872, to reach the start years the study's own thirty years cannot: the crash of 1929 and the inflation that followed the mid-1960s.

A credible answer depends on details that are easy to get wrong and difficult to detect once they are wrong:

  • which funds were genuinely available on the day a choice was made;
  • which were closed to new investors;
  • which later merged or were liquidated;
  • how each fund's early price history was recorded;
  • when withdrawals are taken;
  • where the money is held until it is spent.

Each of these details altered the answer at some stage of the work, and several reversed it. The study proceeded through a sequence of numbered tests, each listed in appendix B, and a series of documented corrections.

The book has eight parts, in the order a portfolio is built. Part I sets the question. Part II asks what safe money alone can do — cash, then bonds; Part III what the S&P 500 adds; Part IV how a mix of the two behaves, over the study's years and over the long market histories, and whether moving the split from year to year helps. Part V sets out the method of choosing funds, Part VI the results, and Part VII what the results support and the errors corrected along the way. Part VIII is a short preview of the same markets seen by a saver rather than a retiree. "How to read this book" describes each part.

It is written for readers who wish to understand what the figures mean and how far they can be relied upon, not only what they are. The answer in brief, which follows, gives the result at once; the rest of the book shows how it was reached, one piece at a time, and how far it holds.

The answer in brief

Which matters more to a retiree: the most money at the end, or the highest lowest point along the way — the point at which a retiree might have given up on the plan or gone back to work? This summary gives both, and its comparisons take the lowest point first.

The setting: a retiree starting in any year from 1995 to 2006 with $1 million, 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, following the withdrawal rule of chapter 1 for twenty years. Both measures are shown as the median and the worst of the 12 retirements. Beside each worst low point, "N yr M mo in" is how far into that retirement it fell, counted in calendar months from January of the start year (see "Terms used throughout" below).

Cash and bonds held alone, with no stocks at all (chapters 2 and 3), are shown for comparison. Cash held alone ended every retirement at its lowest value, far below the $1M it started with, and ran out in the longer ones. Bonds alone grew for the early retirees — 5 of the 12, those begun 1995 to 1998 and 2000, ended above the $1M they started with — but for 6 of the 12 (those begun 1999 and 2002 to 2006) the lowest value was the ending itself, and Total Bond Market's 13.2% fall in 2022 deepened it for those that ended from 2022 on.

SPY is the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500. It is not a Vanguard fund; it serves only as a benchmark for holding the stock market alone, with no bonds.

The two low-point columns say how far each retiree had to sit through a fall, and so whether the plan could be kept; the comparisons below take them first. Over twenty years:

  • The menu each January held a higher floor than the plain index, and ended lower. Its worst low point was $515k against the plain index's $492k (both the 2000 retirement, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), its median low point $755k against $674k, and its low point was the higher in 9 of 12 retirements. The cost came at the end: a worst ending of $692k against $835k, and a median ending of $1.78M against $2.10M. It ended lower in 10 of the 12 retirements, and in 7 of those its low point had been the higher: the shortfall came after the low point, not at it.
  • The menu's edge at the low point came from its bond picks, mostly long-term bond funds, not from its stock picks, and that bond bet reversed in 2022 (chapter 16).
  • The list frozen at retirement fell deeper at the worst than the menu at every split, and than the plain index at 70/30 only; it ended higher than the menu. Its worst low point, $476k (the 2000 retirement, 9 yr 2 mo in), was below the plain index's $492k and the menu's $515k; its median low point, $721k, was above the plain index's $674k, though below the menu's $755k; and at 60/40 and 50/50 its worst low point was above the plain index's, though still below the menu's. Its worst ending, $943k, was above both (the plain index $835k, the menu $692k); its median, $2.07M, was below the plain index's $2.10M, yet it finished ahead of the plain index in 7 of 12 retirements.
  • Picking once and keeping had the deepest worst low point of the four mixes of stock and bond funds, $352k (the 2000 retirement, 9 yr 2 mo in), for the highest median, $2.83M, and the lowest worst ending of the 70/30 portfolios, $408k. That reflects a few fortunate choices at retirement, not a repeatable method.

70/30 is one sample, not a recommendation. Every method was run at three splits: 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, 60% and 40%, and 50% and 50%. The book uses 70/30 as its worked example because it is a common split for a retiree; the other two are reported in chapters 9, 10, 11, 12, 18, 19, 20, 22 and 25, and appendix G gives the detailed tables at all three. What does moving money from stock funds to bond funds buy, and what does it cost? Each row, read from left to right, answers:

  • More in bonds raised every low point and every worst ending, and lowered every median, for every method.
  • The menu each January held a higher floor than the plain index at every split, and ended lower at every split. Its worst low point was $515k, $616k and $725k against the plain index's $492k, $573k and $662k — all six in the 2000 retirement, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in — and its median low point was the higher too; its worst and its median endings were the lower.

Which split suits a retiree is a question of how deep a fall they can sit through, not something this backtest can answer for them.

At the floor it held: the menu's worst low point, $515k, was above the plain index's $492k, and the frozen list's, $476k, below it — all three in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in — while picking once's, $232k, the deepest of the four, was the ending of that retirement itself, 24 yr 11 mo in. The medians rank differently. The menu's top two edged the plain index at the median, $1.76M against $1.70M, yet its worst ending, $651k, was below the plain index's $892k, and it ended ahead in only 2 of 7 retirements; picking once again had the highest median, $3.33M, and the lowest worst ending of the 70/30 portfolios. So few retirements, overlapping by up to twenty-four years, cannot settle the ranking either way.

Beyond the study's thirty years (chapters 10 to 12). Were the study's twelve retirements the hardest a retiree could have met? The long market histories say not; chapter 12 then tests a rule that moves the split.

  • The long histories. With fixed mixes of the S&P 500 and a 10-year Treasury, the hardest twenty-year retirements at 70/30 under the study's rule began in 1928, 1929 and 1930, and 1 of 79 ran out; with withdrawals rising with inflation, the hardest thirty-year retirements began in 1965 and 1966.
  • The hard stop over the study's twelve retirements. Chapter 12 moves the split each January, and to 20% stocks and 80% bonds whenever the S&P 500 is 20% below its high. On the two index funds day by day, that hard stop held a far higher floor than the plain index at 70/30 (as Part VI simulates it, with its Treasury-bill account): a worst low point of $755k against $492k (both the 2000 retirement, 9 yr 2 mo in), a median low point of $905k against $674k, and a worst ending of $1.09M against $835k, at the cost of a lower median ending, $1.81M against $2.10M. Against the plain index at 50/50 there was no such cost: it led on all four measures (chapter 12), with $755k against $662k at the worst low point, $905k against $771k at the median low point, $1.09M against $991k at the worst ending and $1.81M against $1.63M at the median ending. Set against the same two funds held at a fixed 70/30 or 50/50 and simulated as the rule is, without a Treasury-bill account, each of these comparisons goes the same way (chapter 12). The result has its limits: no fees, taxes or trading costs and no Treasury-bill account; settings declared in advance and never varied.
  • The hard stop over the long history. Month by month from 1872, its median ending was close to a fixed 50/50's only over twenty and twenty-five years, and its floor depended on the withdrawal rule. Over twenty years its worst low point was above a fixed 50/50's under the study's rule; with withdrawals rising with inflation it was $232k (the 1903 retirement, 19 yr 11 mo in), below that of every fixed mix of stocks and bonds, from 70/30 to 50/50 — a fixed 50/50's was $490k. That $232k is the hard stop's, not picking once's twenty-five-year low point above, which happens to round to the same sum. From thirty years on the hard stop ran out more often than every fixed mix under both withdrawal rules, though over fifty years under the study's rule only narrowly: in 36 of 102, against 35 for a fixed 50/50.

Saving instead of spending (chapter 27). On the yearly history from 1928, $1M left alone in stocks fell below the $1M at some year end in 36 of 79 twenty-year accounts, the deepest to $352k (the account begun in 1929, in December 1932, 3 yr 11 mo in; a different portfolio from picking once's $352k above, which rounds to the same sum), yet left for twenty to forty years it never ended below where it started. $10,000 a year saved into stocks, rising with inflation, was worth at worst 45.4% of the deposits made so far (the saver begun in 1928, in December 1931, 3 yr 11 mo in), yet over twenty years it earned a median of 11.4% a year on the deposits, against 4.1% in bonds alone and 3.6% in cash alone.

Chapter 25 sets out the complete comparison. The chapters before it build to it one piece at a time: cash, then bonds, then stocks, the mix, the century, the moving split, and then the funds.

All the figures above are in nominal dollars and before taxes and trading costs, for a retiree who follows the rule without deviating. Chapter 16 lists every assumption behind the study's own figures, and chapters 10 to 12 and 27 the assumptions behind the long histories.

Three principles apply throughout:

  • Every table and chart is generated, not transcribed. They are produced directly from the backtest results, and the figures quoted in the text are drawn from the same results.
  • From the point each is introduced, every results table on the study's own years carries two benchmarks: SPY (the S&P 500 alone, with no bonds; chapter 6) and the plain index (two Vanguard index funds, in the same stock/bond proportions as the portfolio it is compared with; chapter 8). The long histories of chapters 10-12 and 27 begin decades before either existed, so their tables carry neither, apart from the checks against the study's own twelve retirements in chapters 10 and 12, and chapter 27's daily rows, whose fixed mixes are the plain index's own two funds. Charts show the benchmarks where they bear on the comparison, and each caption says which lines are drawn.
  • Every result is accompanied by its limitations. A backtest of thirty years in a single fund family is evidence, not a forecast.

Nothing in this book constitutes investment advice.

How to read this book

Why does a book about choosing funds begin with cash? Because each piece of a retirement portfolio is judged against the simpler one before it, the book builds the portfolio one piece at a time, from the safest money to the choice of individual funds.

  • Part I, the question: the retiree and the withdrawal rule.
  • Part II, safe money: cash, then bonds from short to long term — what each does to a retirement on its own.
  • Part III, the S&P 500: what the index is, a century of its history, and what holding it for decades has paid.
  • Part IV, mixing stocks and bonds: why a mix works, the plain index (two Vanguard index funds) that serves as the yardstick, whether to restore the mix every year (chapters 7 to 9), and then three chapters on the long market histories:
    • chapter 10, the same retirement rule over the long market histories — stocks alone, bonds alone, cash alone and fixed mixes of the S&P 500 and a 10-year Treasury — over 20 to 50 years, for retirements begun from 1928 on the yearly data;
    • chapter 11, the same rule month by month, for retirements begun from 1872 on the monthly data, and what retirements of forty and fifty years show;
    • chapter 12, a walk-forward rule that moves the split each January, and to 20% stocks and 80% bonds whenever the S&P 500 is 20% below its high, set beside the fixed splits; it closes with every retirement that ran out in the three chapters and what the markets did around them.
  • Part V, choosing funds — the method: the funds a retiree could actually buy at each date, the prices, the ranking rule, the simulation and its assumptions, and the checks.
  • Part VI, choosing funds — the results, in this order:
    • picked once and kept: the top funds chosen at retirement and never changed;
    • the list frozen at retirement: the funds offered on the first day of retirement, re-ranked within that list each January;
    • the menu rebuilt every year, the study's principal method;
    • the 1999 list, as a comparison;
    • followed by rebalancing frequency, five individual retirements and how long the money lasts.
  • Part VII assesses what the results support and records the errors corrected during the study.
  • Part VIII, before retirement, is a short preview (chapter 27): the same markets and portfolios with money saved instead of withdrawn — $1M left alone, and $10,000 a year rising with inflation.
  • The appendices contain the glossary, the register of tests, the sources, the reproduction procedure, superseded analyses, every fund's quarterly and annual returns, and, in appendix G, the detailed tables behind each chapter.

Readers new to investing should start at Part I. Readers who know the basics can start at Part IV, and readers with time for a single chapter should read chapter 20: what a retiree from 1995 onwards could actually have achieved with the funds available each year.

Charts:

  • In Parts I to IV each caption names every line drawn; the thick lines there are the funds or series being compared.
  • In Part VI's comparisons of what was left, thick lines are the fund-selection methods, the thin solid line is the plain index, and the pink line is SPY.
  • On charts that show many retirements at once, each thin line is one retirement and the thick line is their median at each point in time — the typical path, not that of any single retiree.
  • A thin grey line marks the $1M each retiree started with (on charts of yearly returns, it marks zero).

Every legend shows a sample of each line as drawn. Each caption explains any line particular to its chart (in Figure 1.1, for example, the thick amber line is the running total withdrawn).

Terms used throughout:

  • The top two / three / four — the two (three, four) best-ranked stock funds plus as many of the best-ranked bond funds, in equal amounts within the stock part and within the bond part.
  • 70/30, 60/40, 50/50 — the split between stock funds and bond funds: 70/30 is 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds. All three were run for every method; most tables show 70/30 as the worked example, and the other two appear wherever they change the comparison. The bond part is always invested in bond funds, never held as cash; the only cash is the Treasury-bill account that holds the coming year's spending (chapter 1).
  • Complete retirement — in the fund study, a 20- or 25-year retirement whose end lies inside the data (20 years: starts 1995-2006; 25 years: starts 1995-2001). Chapters 10-12 and 27 apply the same idea to the long histories: every retirement of 20 to 50 years (in chapter 27, every savings account of 10 to 40 years) whose end lies inside those data — for example 79 twenty-year retirements begun 1928-2006 on the yearly data.
  • Ending balance / what was left — what is in the funds at the end of the retirement, after that year's withdrawal. Every retiree starts with $1M; an ending balance of $3M means the funds grew faster than the withdrawals drew them down.
  • Median / worst — the middle and the lowest outcome over the complete retirements. With 12 retirements the median is the average of the 6th and 7th, so no single retiree had it; with 7 (25 years) it is the 4th. "Worst" alone is the worst ending. The "lowest value at any point" (or "low point") is the lowest one retirement's balance fell along the way; the worst low point is the lowest of the 12 low points (of the 7 at 25 years), and the median low point is their median. In chapters 10-12 and 27 the same measures are taken over those chapters' own retirements, and where their data are yearly or monthly the low points are read at year ends or from monthly averages, so they read shallower than daily prices would show.
  • N yr M mo in — beside a worst low point, how far into that retirement it fell: the calendar months from January of the start year to the month of the lowest value, written in full ("9 yr 2 mo in", "0 yr 11 mo in").
  • Ran out — a year-end withdrawal larger than what was left; the retirement ends at $0.
  • The plain index — Vanguard's 500 Index Fund (VFIAX) for the stock part and its Total Bond Market Index Fund (VBTLX) for the bond part, in the same stock/bond proportions as the portfolio it is compared with (70/30, 60/40 or 50/50), restored each January (chapter 8).
  • Picked once and kept — the top-ranked funds on the day of retirement, never changed (chapter 18).
  • The list frozen at retirement — the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement (for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994), frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January (chapter 19).
  • The menu each January (the menu rebuilt every year) — the funds Vanguard offered that January, re-ranked and the top funds held; the study's principal method (chapter 20).
  • The 1999 list — the menu as it stood on 31 December 1999, re-ranked within it each January; usable only for retirements from 2000 (chapter 21).
  • The walk-forward rule (chapter 12) — a rule whose every decision uses only what had already happened: each January the split is moved by the S&P 500's lead over bonds. Its hard stop moves to 20% stocks and 80% bonds (or 40/60) whenever the S&P 500 is 20% or more below its highest level so far, and holds until a January check finds it less than 20% below.

Part I: The question

Part I sets the terms: the retiree and the withdrawal rule that every portfolio in the book must carry. The chapters that follow put the same test to one portfolio after another — cash, bonds, the stock market, a mix of the two, and funds chosen by ranking: whether it can carry that rule, and how low it falls on the way.

Chapter 1. The retiree and the rule

What, exactly, must every portfolio in this book pay? This chapter fixes the retiree and the withdrawal rule that every simulation follows: an income that rises every year and is never cut.

The starting capital

The retiree invests $1,000,000 at the close of the first trading day of the year retirement begins (1 January is always a market holiday). Spending for the first year is assumed to be provided for separately, so the full amount is invested.

The withdrawals

At the end of the first year the retiree withdraws 4% of the initial capital, $40,000. Each subsequent withdrawal is 3% larger than the one before, regardless of market conditions. The amount is never reduced.

year withdrawal
1 $40,000
11 $53,757
21 $72,244
30 $94,263

Over a 20-year retirement the withdrawals total $1.07M, more than the original capital.

Does a 3% rise keep pace with prices? It is fixed; it is not an adjustment for inflation, and it does not change with what prices do. Consumer prices rose about 2.5% a year on average from 1995 to 2025, each year measured from December to December, so over the period as a whole the income rose a little faster than prices, though prices rose faster than 3% in 8 of 31 years. Every dollar figure in the book is in nominal dollars; chapters 5 and 6 also give returns after inflation.

Where the spending money is held

Each withdrawal passes through a Treasury-bill account before it is spent:

  • At the last close of the year, the withdrawal is realised and transferred to the account.
  • Each month, one twelfth is paid to the retiree.
  • While it is held, the balance earns the 3-month Treasury yield.
  • At the next year end, any interest remaining reduces the sale made at that year end.

The capital invested in funds is therefore always capital not yet required for spending.

Rebalancing

The portfolio is rebalanced each January. The stock allocation is divided equally among the selected stock funds and the bond allocation equally among the selected bond funds, restoring the target allocation — for example 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds. The study ran every method at three splits, 70/30, 60/40 and 50/50; 70/30 is the worked example used through most of the book, and the others are reported beside it where they differ.

Rebalancing sells what has risen and buys what has fallen. Chapter 9 asks whether to rebalance at all, and chapter 22 examines rebalancing every six or every three months instead.

A worked example

A worked example (selected years) is set out in appendix G.1. It follows a retirement beginning in January 2000 with the two highest-ranked stock funds and the two highest-ranked bond funds on the list of that day — the 1999 list, which for a 2000 retiree is also the list frozen at retirement (chapters 21 and 19; both are defined under "Terms used throughout" in "How to read this book") — re-ranked within it every January. It illustrates the mechanics only; the study's principal method, the menu rebuilt every year, is the subject of chapter 20. For each year shown, the worked example gives:

  • the amount due;
  • the interest left in the Treasury-bill account at the year end, which reduces the sale;
  • the amount sold;
  • the balance remaining.

Where should the $1M be held to pay that income? Part II begins with the answer that looks safest: cash, whose value never falls.

Part II: Safe money

Before stocks, the safest places a retiree can keep money: cash, then bonds. Part II follows the $1M, and the rising income it must pay, when none of it is ever exposed to the stock market. The result is the floor against which everything later is measured.

Chapter 2. Cash

Cash never falls in value. Can it pay an income that rises every year, for twenty years and beyond? For a retiree drawing that income, the choice that looks safest is the riskiest of all: it runs out.

What cash means here

"Cash" is three-month United States Treasury bills, among the shortest and safest loans a saver can make. A money-market fund holds much the same thing. Here the cash account simply earns the Treasury-bill rate of the day, with no fees — a generous version of cash.

The rate has moved a long way:

  • In 1995 it averaged 5.7%.
  • In 2000 it averaged 6.0%.
  • From 2009 to 2015 it averaged 0.08% — for seven years cash earned almost nothing.
  • From 2016 to 2019 it rose again, to yearly averages between 0.3% and 2.1%.
  • In 2020 and 2021 it fell back to almost nothing: yearly averages of 0.04% to 0.36%.
  • In 2023 it averaged 5.3%.

A retirement held in cash

The same retiree as in chapter 1 — $1M, $40,000 in the first year, 3% more every year — with everything in cash, and in the safest bond funds (chapter 3 covers bonds in full). Did cash last the twenty years — and how much did it leave to pay for the years after them? The cash row's median and worst columns answer:

held alone, 20 years, retirements 1995-2006 median left best worst lowest value at any point: median / worst own worst fall, nothing withdrawn 10-year return a year: median / best / worst
Cash (3-month Treasury bills) $189k $491k $120k $189k / $120k (19 yr 11 mo in) 0% 1.6% / 4.0% / 0.3%
Short-Term Treasury $528k $972k $280k $528k / $280k (19 yr 11 mo in) 7% 2.8% / 6.0% / 0.7%
Short-Term Federal $587k $1.05M $331k $587k / $331k (19 yr 11 mo in) 7% 3.2% / 6.2% / 0.8%
Short-Term Investment-Grade $663k $1.10M $437k $663k / $437k (19 yr 11 mo in) 9% 3.6% / 6.2% / 1.5%

Ten-year return a year: the 22 ten-year periods beginning 1995-2016, with nothing withdrawn. The fund's own worst fall: its largest drop from a high, on daily closes with nothing withdrawn, over 1995-2025.

The median after twenty years was $189k left of the $1M — the average of the 6th and 7th of the 12 endings, $156k and $222k, so no single retiree had it — and even the worst still held $120k. In the cash row the lowest value at any point is the ending itself, at the median and at the worst: the balance was at its lowest when the twenty years ended. Every cash retirement lasted the twenty years. The failure came after them:

  • Every retirement begun from 1995 to 2004 and held in cash then ran out of money — the earliest start, the 1995 retiree in 2021, its 27th year; the latest, the 2004 retiree in 2025, its 22nd year.
  • No retirement held in a bond fund had run out by 9 October 2026. But 4 held in Short-Term Treasury, those begun 1996 to 1999, held less on that date than the withdrawal due at the end of 2026: the 1996 retiree had $13k left against $97k due.

Why cash fails

The first withdrawal is 4% of the starting capital, and each one is 3% larger than the last. The Treasury-bill rate averaged below 4% in 20 of the 31 years from 1995 to 2025, and almost nothing from 2009 to 2015. Once the withdrawals exceeded the interest, the capital shrank, and the shrinking capital earned even less.

The lesson is not that cash is dangerous in a crash. It is that a fixed, rising income needs the capital to grow, and cash does not grow fast enough. Does lending for longer, at a higher rate, close the gap? Chapter 3 follows bonds from the shortest term to the longest.

Chapter 3. Bonds, from short to long

A bond is a loan with a fixed term, and the longer the term, the more it usually pays. What does the extra pay cost? This chapter walks along the term — from bonds that mature in a year or two to bonds that mature in twenty or thirty — and sets what the extra years paid beside what they risked.

The trade-off

  • Short-term bonds pay a little more than cash and barely move when interest rates change.
  • Intermediate-term bonds pay more and move more.
  • Long-term bonds pay the most, and their prices swing hardest: when rates rise their prices fall, and when rates fall their prices rise.

Vanguard offers each step in two kinds: Treasury bonds, backed by the United States government, and investment-grade bonds, lent to companies with good credit for a little more interest. At the short end there is a third, Short-Term Federal, which lends mainly to United States government agencies. Its prospectuses of 1999 to 2002 said that most of those bonds were not backed by the full faith and credit of the government, and those of 2003 and 2004 that many were not. The GNMA fund holds government-guaranteed mortgages. Total Bond Market holds all of these in one fund; chapter 8 uses it as the bond part of the book's simplest mix of stocks and bonds.

A retirement held in each

Each fund held alone, with the same $1M and the same rising withdrawal. Which column rewards the longest bonds, and which warns against them?

The columns are as in chapter 2's table. The own worst fall warns: Long-Term Treasury fell 46% from a high and Long-Term Investment-Grade 36%, the two deepest falls in this table and chapter 2's, against 7% for Short-Term Treasury. The median left rewards: broadly, the longer the bonds, the more was left:

  • Short-Term Treasury: a median of $528k after twenty years (chapter 2's table).
  • Total Bond Market: $906k.
  • Long-Term Treasury: $1.77M; Long-Term Investment-Grade: $1.78M.

The order is not strict:

  • The middle of the range is uneven. GNMA ($925k) and Total Bond Market ($906k) left less than Intermediate-Term Treasury ($972k) and Intermediate-Term Investment-Grade ($1.20M).
  • Over ten years, length could hurt. Long-Term Treasury had the worst ten-year return of any safe fund in the table, -0.7% a year, below cash's worst of +0.3%.
  • The worst retirement does not follow the term. Long-Term Treasury's worst ending, $743k, was below Intermediate-Term Investment-Grade's, $760k.

Why long bonds did so well — and why that may not repeat

Long-bond prices move against long-term interest rates, not the Treasury-bill rate, and for most of these thirty years those rates fell. The 10-year Treasury yield fell from 7.8% at the end of 1994 to 0.9% at the end of 2020. Every fall in rates lifted the price of the long bonds already held. A long bond fund was, in effect, a bet that rates would keep falling, and the bet kept paying.

When rates rose, the bet reversed: the 10-year yield was back to 3.9% by the end of 2022. In 2022 alone Long-Term Treasury lost 29.5% and Long-Term Investment-Grade 25.5%, against 13.2% for Total Bond Market. The "own worst fall" column in the table shows the same risk: the long funds' own worst falls are deep for funds called bonds.

What did that bet mean for a retiree living on it? Figure 3.2 follows one retirement, begun in 1995, in four of the holdings, with the withdrawals of chapter 1 taken out.

What Part II shows

  • Cash cannot carry a rising income. Left alone, $1M in cash grew to $2.21M by 9 October 2026 (Figure 27.1, nothing withdrawn). With the withdrawals of chapter 1 taken out ($1.07M over the first twenty years alone), every cash retirement lasted the twenty years, and every one begun from 1995 to 2004 then ran out, in its 22nd to 27th year (chapter 2; the retiree of 1995 in Figure 3.2).
  • Longer bonds can, in a period of falling rates. Short-term bonds barely did: 4 Short-Term Treasury retirements held less on 9 October 2026 than the withdrawal due at the end of 2026. Broadly, at the median, the longer the bonds, the better they did, at the price of deep falls when rates turned.
  • How bonds alone compare with a mix that adds stocks is taken up in chapter 8, once the mix has been defined.

Safe money alone either runs out or leans on falling interest rates. What does the stock market add, and at what cost? Part III turns to it, beginning with the index that stands for the market: the S&P 500.

Part III: The S&P 500

Before asking what stocks can do for a retiree, Part III asks what "the stock market" is. It introduces the market through its best-known index — what it is, how it has behaved over a century, and what holding it for ten to fifty years has paid.

Chapter 4. What the S&P 500 is

"The market" usually means the S&P 500. Is it simply the 500 largest American companies? This chapter explains what the index actually holds, who decides what goes in, and why a handful of companies can steer it.

From 233 stocks to 500

  • 1923: the Standard Statistics Company built its first stock index: 233 U.S. companies, calculated weekly.
  • 1926: it became a 90-stock composite, calculated daily.
  • 4 March 1957: the S&P 500 was launched — 425 industrial companies, 25 railroads and 50 utilities, weighted by market value and, thanks to an early electronic calculator, computed every hour.

Index values before 1957 are reconstructed: the series runs back to January 1928, scaled so that its 1941-43 average equals 10. Chapter 5's history before 1957 is therefore the history of the earlier, smaller composite.

Today the index is run by S&P Dow Jones Indices, formed in 2012. On 30 September 2026 it held 503 stocks — more than 500 because a few companies are in it with two classes of shares — worth US$68.4 trillion together, about 80% of the value of U.S. shares available to the public.

Who decides what goes in

The index is not simply "the 500 largest companies". Membership is decided by an Index Committee of S&P Dow Jones Indices staff, which meets monthly and keeps its discussions confidential. It chooses among the companies that meet the published rules, "taking sector representation into account".

To be added today, a company must be:

  • American: domiciled in the U.S., filing U.S. annual and quarterly reports, listed on a major U.S. exchange.
  • Large: worth at least US$22.7 billion (since July 2025). The bar moves with the market — it was $5.0 billion in 2007, cut to $3.0 billion in the 2008 crisis, raised step by step since, and cut once more after the 2022 fall.
  • Widely held and traded: enough shares in public hands and enough trading in them.
  • Profitable: positive earnings in the latest quarter and over the last four quarters combined.
  • Seasoned: a new listing must trade for at least twelve months first.

The rules apply to joining, not to staying: a member that later fails them is removed only when the committee judges that conditions warrant it. Changes are made as needed rather than on a schedule — from 1995 to mid-2021 there were 715 additions and 711 deletions, about 27 of each a year.

Weighted by size

Each company counts in proportion to its market value — its share price times the shares available to the public. Since 2005 only the shares that actually trade count; blocks held by founders, executives or governments are left out. S&P announced that change in March 2004 and phased it in over eighteen months.

Weighting by size means the largest companies dominate. In June 2024 the average member was worth US$96 billion, but the weighted average — the size of company a dollar in the index is actually invested in — was nearly US$1 trillion.

A handful of companies can steer it

How much of the index rides on its ten largest holdings, and has that share held steady? The share they held, a company's share classes counted separately:

date ten largest, share of the index the largest single company
30 April 2015 17.4% 3.9%
31 December 2020 27.4% 6.7%
31 December 2024 37.3% 7.6%
30 September 2026 39.1% 8.4%

S&P Dow Jones Indices reports that by mid-2025 the ten largest made up almost 40% of the index, "a level of concentration not seen since the mid-1960s". In June 1965 the ten largest — led by AT&T, General Motors and Standard Oil of New Jersey — held about 38%, adding up the weights in S&P Dow Jones Indices' table (the same article's text says "almost half"). Sixty years later those ten held a quarter of a percent each on average, and three had been through bankruptcy. None of the 2025 leaders was in the index in 1965.

The sectors move

What the index holds has changed with the economy:

year end the five largest companies
1970 IBM, AT&T, General Motors, Standard Oil (N.J.), Eastman Kodak
1980 IBM, AT&T, Exxon, Standard Oil (Indiana), Schlumberger
1990 IBM, Exxon, General Electric, Philip Morris, Royal Dutch Petroleum
2000 General Electric, Exxon Mobil, Pfizer, Cisco, Citigroup
2010 Exxon Mobil, Apple, Microsoft, General Electric, Chevron
2020 Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Facebook
February 2025 Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet
  • Energy in 1980: three of the five largest companies — Exxon, Standard Oil (Indiana) and Schlumberger — were energy companies.
  • Technology in 2000: information technology was 33.6% of the index in August 2000, at the height of the dot-com boom — and 33.0% again in March 2026.
  • Financial companies in the 2000s: they reached a record 22.4% of the index in September 2006, according to Morningstar, shortly before the 2008 crisis.

The sector labels themselves have changed: the standard classification began in 1999, real estate was separated from financials in 2016, and in 2018 several internet and media companies moved into a widened Communication Services sector.

Dividends

The index's headline figure counts price changes only. Dividends matter far more than that suggests. By S&P Dow Jones Indices' calculation:

  • About 31% of the average monthly total return from 1926 to February 2025 came from dividends — about half in the 1940s (53%) and the 1970s (50%), as little as 14% in the 1990s, and about 68% of the average monthly return in the 2000s, a decade whose total return, compounded, was negative (chapter 5).
  • Compounded, the gap is far larger: from 1 January 1930 to February 2025 the index grew to 278 times its starting level on price alone, and to 9,584 times with dividends reinvested — about 34 times as much.

Every return in this book includes dividends, reinvested, unless it is marked "price only".

What this means for a retiree

Owning "the market" through the S&P 500 means owning what the committee admits, in proportions set by market value. That has worked well over long periods, but it is not neutral: when a few companies or one sector grow large, the index's path follows theirs — energy around 1980, technology in 2000, and the largest technology companies again today.

How has an index built this way rewarded those who held it, through crashes, inflation and booms? Chapter 5 follows it year by year from 1928, and decade by decade from 1930.

Chapter 5. A century of the S&P 500

A long-run average says little about the decade a retiree actually lives through. How different were the decades, and how deep were the falls between them? This chapter walks through them, using annual total returns — price change plus reinvested dividends — since 1928.

Decade by decade

The S&P 500 column gives the return in dollars, the last column what was left after rising prices. In which decade did stocks gain in dollars and still lose to inflation — and in which the reverse?

decade S&P 500, a year 3-month T-bills 10-year Treasury inflation S&P 500 after inflation
1930s -0.9% +1.0% +4.0% -2.0% +1.1%
1940s +8.5% +0.5% +2.5% +5.4% +3.0%
1950s +19.5% +2.0% +0.8% +2.2% +16.9%
1960s +7.7% +4.0% +2.4% +2.5% +5.1%
1970s +5.9% +6.3% +5.4% +7.4% -1.3%
1980s +17.3% +9.0% +12.0% +5.1% +11.7%
1990s +18.0% +5.0% +7.4% +2.9% +14.7%
2000s -1.0% +2.7% +6.3% +2.5% -3.4%
2010s +13.4% +0.6% +4.1% +1.8% +11.5%
2020s (to 2025) +14.9% +2.8% -0.6% +4.0% +10.5%
  • The 1930s: the Depression. The table starts in 1930, so the boom of 1928 and the crash of 1929 are not in it. In dollars stocks returned -0.9% a year; consumer prices fell faster (inflation -2.0% a year), so after inflation stocks returned +1.1% a year. 10-year Treasuries, at +4.0% a year, did better than stocks.
  • The 1950s: the best decade in the table, and the decade in which the 500-stock index itself was launched.
  • The 1970s: stocks rose in name, but inflation took all of it and more — the column on the right shows what was left after rising prices.
  • The 1980s and 1990s: two strong decades in a row, with falling inflation and falling interest rates.
  • The 2000s: the "lost decade", two crashes in ten years, ending with less than it began.
  • The 2010s and 2020s: recovery, and a long run of strong returns.

The worst and the best years

Since 1928 the S&P 500 lost money in 26 of 98 calendar years. The five worst were 1931 (-44%), 2008 (-37%), 1937 (-35%), 1974 (-26%), 1930 (-25%); the three best were 1954 (+53%), 1933 (+50%), 1935 (+47%).

The great falls

The worst years above were parts of longer falls. Which matters more to a retiree drawing an income: how far a fall went, or how long the wait for the recovery lasted? First the depth, measured from peak to trough:

fall from to size
The crash of 1929 September 1929 June 1932 about 86%, price only (computed from levels published by Yardeni Research)
1937-38 March 1937 March 1938 54.5%, price only (Yardeni Research)
Inflation and the oil shock January 1973 October 1974 44.9%, with dividends
Black Monday 25 August 1987 4 December 1987 32.6%, with dividends; about 20% on 19 October alone, price only (Federal Reserve)
The dot-com bust 1 September 2000 9 October 2002 47.4%, with dividends
The financial crisis October 2007 March 2009 57%, price only (Federal Reserve); 55.3% with dividends
COVID 19 February 2020 23 March 2020 33.9% in 33 days, price only (Yardeni Research)
Rates and inflation 3 January 2022 12 October 2022 25.4%, price only (Yardeni Research)

Every one of these was eventually recovered, but the waits differed enormously. Where a source dates the recovery:

  • 1929: the Dow Jones Industrial Average did not regain its September 1929 high until November 1954, 25 years later, price only (Federal Reserve). The sources give the Dow's recovery date, not the S&P 500's.
  • 1973-74: the S&P 500 regained its peak on 9 July 1976, with dividends.
  • 1987: on 15 May 1989, with dividends — less than two years.
  • 2000-02: on 23 October 2006, with dividends.
  • 2007-09: on 2 April 2012, with dividends.
  • 2020: on 18 August 2020, six months after the peak, price only.
  • 2022: no new record close for 513 trading days, until 19 January 2024, price only.

For a retiree drawing an income, the length of the wait matters as much as the depth of the fall. Chapter 6 measures every stretch of ten to fifty years since 1928, and whether the falls were made up over the twenty or thirty years a retirement lasts.

Chapter 6. Holding the S&P 500 for decades

A retiree does not live through one year but through twenty or thirty. Does holding the S&P 500 that long remove its risk? This chapter looks at every stretch of 10 to 50 years since 1928, and then at the retirements this book follows. Its figures are before inflation unless stated.

Every stretch since 1928

The table shows, for each holding period, the typical, the best and the worst annual return over every possible start year, with dividends reinvested, nothing withdrawn, and before inflation. Chapter 7 repeats these columns beside a mix of stocks and bonds, 10-year Treasuries alone and 3-month T-bills. For someone who cannot choose the year to begin, which of the three figures in each row matters most?

held for S&P 500, return a year before inflation: median / best / worst holding periods
10 years 11.0% / 20.1% / -1.7% 89
20 years 10.9% / 17.7% / 2.4% 79
25 years 10.3% / 17.1% / 5.2% 74
30 years 10.8% / 13.6% / 8.0% 69
40 years 11.2% / 12.5% / 8.5% 59
50 years 10.8% / 13.6% / 7.4% 49

The worst: a retiree learns where a start year stood in history only afterwards.

  • Over ten years the S&P 500 lost money 5 of 89 times — but these form only two episodes: the periods starting in 1928-1930 and 1999-2000. The worst decade began in 1929.
  • Over twenty years it never lost money, but the worst stretch, from 1929, earned only 2.4% a year.
  • From ten to forty years, the longer the holding period, the narrower the range: even the worst thirty-year stretch earned 8.0% a year, and over forty years the best was 12.5% and the worst 8.5%.
  • At fifty years the range widens again, to 13.6% and 7.4%. Only one fifty-year period fits in the 98 years without sharing a year, and the 49 in the table overlap heavily, so single decades decide the extremes: the best, from 1950, took in the 1990s as well as the 1950s; the worst, from 1929, took in the 1970s as well as the Depression.

The periods overlap: two ten-year periods that start a year apart share nine of their years. The 98 years from 1928 to 2025 hold only 9 ten-year periods and 4 twenty-year periods that share no year, so the counts above describe a handful of independent experiences, not dozens.

After inflation

Does the protection that time gives survive inflation? The same periods, with each year's return reduced by that year's rise in consumer prices; the last column counts the periods that lost money after inflation:

held for S&P 500, return a year after inflation: median / best / worst periods that lost money after inflation
10 years 6.7% / 17.9% / -3.8% 11 of 89
20 years 7.0% / 13.2% / 0.6% 0 of 79
25 years 7.0% / 11.7% / 2.8% 0 of 74
30 years 7.3% / 10.1% / 4.3% 0 of 69
40 years 6.8% / 9.2% / 4.2% 0 of 59
50 years 6.4% / 9.2% / 4.5% 0 of 49
  • Over ten years the S&P 500 lost money after inflation in 11 of 89 periods: those starting in 1937, 1965-1966, 1968-1970, 1972-1973 and 1999-2001. The worst began in 1999, at -3.8% a year.
  • Over twenty years it never lost money after inflation, but the worst stretch, from 1929, earned 0.6% a year.
  • Over thirty years the worst was 4.3% a year, starting in 1965, against 8.0% from 1929 before inflation. After inflation the thirty years from 1929 were helped by the falling prices of the 1930s, while those from 1965 ran through the inflation of the 1970s.

The same index in a retirement

The retirements of this book began between 1995 and 2006, a period that included both the 2000-02 and the 2008-09 falls. The same index can be held through SPY, an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500. Held entirely in SPY, with the withdrawal rule of chapter 1, the 12 complete twenty-year retirements had a median ending and a lowest value on the way that tell different stories:

  • Median of the 12 after twenty years: $2.42M left of the $1M.
  • Worst ending: $385k, for the retiree of 2000.
  • Lowest value at any point: a median of $515k across the 12 retirements. The worst was $290k, for the retiree of 2000, on 9 March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in; the balance had fallen 72.6% from its high, withdrawals included.
  • The market's own fall: SPY itself, with dividends and nothing withdrawn, fell 55.2% from 9 October 2007 to 9 March 2009 — slightly less than the index's own fall with dividends in chapter 5's table. SPY is a fund that tracks the index; a gap of this size can come from how the fund holds and pays dividends, its fee and small differences in the price data.

The medians say stocks win over twenty years; the retiree of 2000 shows why that is not enough. Withdrawals taken while prices are low sell more shares than they would at the high, and those shares are not there for the recovery. Part IV holds bonds beside the stocks, and measures what they buy at the low point and what they cost at the median.

Part IV: Mixing stocks and bonds

Parts II and III held cash, bonds and stocks each alone. Stocks left the most at the median, but with falls that are hard to live through while drawing an income. How much of that median can a retiree keep while softening the falls? Part IV puts stocks and bonds together. Chapter 7 shows why a mix works. Chapter 8 builds the plain two-fund mix that serves as this book's yardstick and sets it beside stocks alone and bonds alone. Chapter 9 asks whether the mix should be restored every year. Chapter 10 follows the same retirement rule over a century of yearly market history, from 1928, for the plain mixes that can be followed that far back; chapter 11 follows it over a monthly history from 1872, and over retirements of forty and fifty years. Chapter 12 tests whether a rule that moves the split as the market moves did better than a fixed split.

Chapter 7. Why a mix

What does a retiree give up by holding bonds beside stocks, and what does it buy? Over ten and twenty years, with nothing withdrawn, a mix of stocks and bonds gave up some of the stock market's best outcomes to avoid most of its worst. Over longer periods, with nothing withdrawn, it simply earned less; with withdrawals, over twenty to thirty years, the worst retirement fared better with it, by its lowest point or by how many ran out (chapter 11 follows retirements of forty and fifty years, where that edge was gone). This chapter measures the trade over a century.

A century of mixes

The table below repeats the long-run record of chapter 6, now with a mix: 70% in the S&P 500 and 30% in 10-year Treasury bonds, restored to 70/30 at the start of every year. Like chapter 6, it uses yearly index returns from 1928 to 2025, before inflation, with no fund costs and nothing withdrawn; chapter 8 turns to real funds, priced daily, net of their costs.

Read the worst figure, the last in each cell, in the S&P 500 column and the mix's beside it. At which lengths was the mix's worst stretch better than the S&P 500's, and from which length did that stop?

held for (return a year before inflation: median / best / worst) S&P 500 70% S&P 500 + 30% 10-year Treasuries, restored yearly 10-year Treasuries 3-month T-bills holding periods
10 years 11.0% / 20.1% / -1.7% 8.9% / 16.5% / 1.1% 3.9% / 13.7% / 0.1% 2.7% / 9.2% / 0.2% 89
20 years 10.9% / 17.7% / 2.4% 9.4% / 15.5% / 3.3% 4.3% / 10.7% / 1.6% 3.4% / 7.8% / 0.5% 79
25 years 10.3% / 17.1% / 5.2% 9.5% / 14.7% / 5.2% 5.0% / 9.6% / 1.9% 3.7% / 7.3% / 0.8% 74
30 years 10.8% / 13.6% / 8.0% 9.4% / 12.4% / 7.0% 5.5% / 9.2% / 1.9% 4.1% / 6.8% / 1.1% 69
40 years 11.2% / 12.5% / 8.5% 9.8% / 11.2% / 7.2% 6.0% / 7.9% / 2.4% 4.8% / 6.2% / 1.7% 59
50 years 10.8% / 13.6% / 7.4% 9.5% / 11.5% / 6.6% 6.0% / 7.0% / 2.9% 4.8% / 5.5% / 2.5% 49
  • Over ten years, the mix's worst decade still earned 1.1% a year, while the S&P 500 alone lost money over 5 of 89 of its ten-year stretches.
  • Over twenty years, the mix's worst was better than the S&P 500's (3.3% against 2.4% a year), and the price was a lower typical return (9.4% against 10.9%).
  • Over twenty-five years, the worst stretches were about the same: 5.2% a year for the S&P 500 alone and 5.2% for the mix.
  • Over thirty years and more, even the worst stretch for stocks alone beat the mix's worst (8.0% against 7.0% a year over thirty years). With nothing withdrawn, the stock market's worst decades were made up given enough time, and the bonds only lowered the return. A retiree does withdraw, and then, over twenty to thirty years, the worst retirement fared better with the mix, by its lowest point or by how many ran out: chapter 8 shows it with real funds, and chapter 10 over a century of start years — over thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation, for example, stocks alone ran out in 2 of 69 retirements and the 70/30 mix in none. Over forty and fifty years chapter 11 finds that edge gone: in 7 of the 8 comparisons of those lengths, in both data sets and under both withdrawal rules, stocks alone ran out no more often than the 70/30 mix, and in 3 of them less often.
  • Bonds alone and bills alone earned far less at the median and at best over every horizon. Only their worst ten years beat the S&P 500's worst, which lost money.
  • More bonds moved the trade further. At 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds, and at 50/50, the worst ten years earned 1.8% and 2.4% a year (1.1% at 70/30), the worst thirty years 6.6% and 6.1% (7.0%), and the median was lower over every length in the table.

Why the mix helps a retiree in particular

A retiree sells every year to pay the income. In this book each withdrawal is taken from every fund in proportion to what it holds, so stocks and bonds are sold alike. The mix differs in two ways:

  • The balance falls less in a stock-market fall, so each withdrawal taken near the low is a smaller share of what is left, and fewer stock shares are sold cheaply.
  • The split is restored each January. After a fall in stocks the bond part is above its share and the stock part below it, so restoring the split sells bonds and buys stocks after they have fallen; after a strong year for stocks it does the reverse. It does not simply help: in the study's own retirements the yearly reset raised the worst ending but lowered the worst low point, at every split (chapter 9).

Does the same hold for real funds, priced daily and net of their costs, in the retirements this book follows? Chapter 8 builds the simplest such mix and sets it beside the S&P 500 alone.

Chapter 8. The plain index

What could a retiree have had without choosing any fund at all? The plain index is the simplest mix a retiree could hold, and the yardstick for everything that follows. This chapter defines it and shows how it fared beside the S&P 500 alone and beside the bond funds of chapter 3, each held alone.

What it holds

The plain index consists of two Vanguard index funds, held at a fixed split and restored to that split each January:

  • 500 Index (VFIAX) for stocks — a Vanguard fund that tracks the S&P 500 of Part III;
  • Total Bond Market Index (VBTLX) for bonds — the fund of chapter 3 that holds bonds of every kind and term in one.

At 70/30 it holds 70% VFIAX and 30% VBTLX. Before 2004 the older share classes of the same funds (VFINX, VBMFX) are used, because the early price records of the Admiral classes are unreliable (chapter 14). It represents the passive alternative: the outcome available without choosing any fund.

The plain index holds Vanguard's 500 Index fund, not SPY, the exchange-traded fund the book uses for its all-stock comparison. The two track the same index and ended close together: held alone, the 500 Index fund left a median of $2.46M and a worst of $397k over the retirements below, against $2.42M and $385k for SPY.

How it fared

Over the 12 complete 20-year retirements (start years 1995-2006), with 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds (chapter 9 gives the plain index at 60/40 and 50/50 as well), what did SPY's higher median cost at the worst moment? The two low-point columns answer it:

20 years, retirements 1995-2006; plain index at 70/30 median ending worst ending lowest value at any point: median lowest value at any point: worst biggest fall, withdrawals included, worst fall of the investment itself, nothing withdrawn, worst
SPY (the S&P 500 alone) $2.42M $385k $515k $290k (9 yr 2 mo in) 72.6% 55.2%
Plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January) $2.10M $835k $674k $492k (9 yr 2 mo in) 53.5% 39.8%
  • The plain index's low point was far higher at worst and higher at the median, and its worst ending more than twice SPY's: the 2000 retiree, the worst retirement for both, was protected by the bonds.
  • The price was the median: SPY's was higher; stocks earned more over these twenty-year stretches.
  • Over twenty-five years the gap was wider still. Only the 7 retirements begun 1995-2001 have run that long. At 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, the plain index's worst ending was $892k and SPY's $244k, both for the retiree of 2000; the medians were $1.70M and $1.80M — lower than the twelve-start medians above because these seven start years include the hardest ones, 1999-2001. Over the same seven start years the twenty-year medians were lower still, $1.52M for the plain index and $1.43M for SPY: over these seven, the plain index led SPY at twenty years and trailed it at twenty-five.
  • The "biggest fall" is the fall in the retiree's own balance, so it includes every withdrawal taken between the high and the low; the last column is the fall of the investment itself, with nothing withdrawn.

The plain index against the bond funds of chapter 3

Chapter 3 held each bond fund alone. Did the plain index's stocks, at 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, cost it at the worst? In its worst retirements they did:

  • Long-Term Investment-Grade's lowest value at any point in any retirement was higher: $830k (the 2006 retiree, October 2008), against the plain index's $492k (the 2000 retiree, March 2009). Its worst ending was higher too: $1.03M against $835k.
  • Long-Term Investment-Grade ended ahead of the plain index in 5 of 12 retirements, those begun 1998 to 2002. The 2000 retiree was left $2.32M against $835k.
  • Long-Term Treasury did the same in 4 of 12, those begun 1998 to 2001.
  • For the 2000 retiree, 6 of the 9 bond funds held alone ended ahead of the plain index's $835k — every one except the three short-term funds. Beyond the two long funds, Total Bond Market left $1.08M, GNMA $1.08M, Intermediate-Term Treasury $1.21M and Intermediate-Term Investment-Grade $1.41M.

The price of holding a bond fund alone was the median: every one left less than the plain index, $1.78M for the best, Long-Term Investment-Grade (just ahead of Long-Term Treasury's $1.77M), against $2.10M.

Two things set apart the start years in which the long bond funds led:

  • The stock share. With 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, the plain index met the stock-market falls of 2000-2002 early in these retirements and the fall of 2008-2009 midway, and each year's withdrawal was sold from a fallen balance. The bond funds held alone fell far less in both.
  • Falling interest rates, which lifted the prices of long bonds most. These retirements ended by 2021, before rates rose in 2022.

Two yardsticks

Every method later in the book is compared with both SPY and the plain index. Neither is simply the harder one to beat:

  • SPY has the lower worst ending and low point, and the higher median ($2.42M against $2.10M). Against SPY, any portfolio holding bonds will generally fall less in a severe decline and earn less in a long rise, so the comparison mostly measures the stock / bond split.
  • The plain index is the like-for-like test. It holds the same stock/bond proportions as the methods, so beating it requires the choice of funds itself to add value. It is the harder yardstick on the worst retirement.

The plain index is restored to its split every January. Is that trading worth doing, or would a retiree who bought the two funds once and left them alone have fared as well? Chapter 9 compares the two.

Chapter 9. To rebalance or not

Once a year the plain index is restored to its split: after a good year for stocks some are sold and bonds bought, after a bad year the reverse. What would change if the retiree never traded at all? This chapter asks what happens if the retiree does nothing instead, and simply lets the split drift while the withdrawals are taken from every fund in proportion.

The two choices

  • Rebalanced each January: the split goes back to 70/30 (or 60/40, 50/50) at the first close of every year.
  • Left to drift: the funds are bought once; nothing is ever traded again except the withdrawals, which come out of both funds in proportion to what each holds.

What happened

The table pairs each split rebalanced each January with the same split left to drift. Within each pair, does drifting move the worst ending and the worst lowest value the same way?

20 years, retirements 1995-2006 median ending worst ending lowest value at any point: median lowest value at any point: worst biggest fall, withdrawals included, worst
SPY (all stocks, nothing to rebalance) $2.42M $385k $515k $290k (9 yr 2 mo in) 72.6%
plain index, 70% stocks / 30% bonds, rebalanced each January $2.10M $835k $674k $492k (9 yr 2 mo in) 53.5%
plain index, 70% stocks / 30% bonds, left to drift $2.05M $762k $681k $544k (9 yr 2 mo in) 49.8%
plain index, 60% stocks / 40% bonds, rebalanced each January $1.91M $932k $721k $573k (9 yr 2 mo in) 45.9%
plain index, 60% stocks / 40% bonds, left to drift $1.91M $841k $729k $635k (9 yr 2 mo in) 42.5%
plain index, 50% stocks / 50% bonds, rebalanced each January $1.63M $991k $771k $662k (9 yr 2 mo in) 37.7%
plain index, 50% stocks / 50% bonds, left to drift $1.73M $866k $778k $727k (9 yr 2 mo in) 36.9%

It does not. At every split, leaving the mix to drift gave a higher lowest value at any point, at worst and at the median, but a lower worst ending: the two measures went opposite ways. Which matters more, the worst moment or the worst ending?

By the measure this book puts first, the floor, drift did better at every split. Its worst low point, at every split drifting or rebalanced the 2000 retirement's on 9 March 2009 (9 yr 2 mo in), was $544k against $492k rebalanced at 70/30, $635k against $573k at 60/40 and $727k against $662k at 50/50, and its median low point was higher too ($681k against $674k at 70/30, $729k against $721k at 60/40, $778k against $771k at 50/50). The cost was the worst ending, lower at every split: $762k against $835k at 70/30, $841k against $932k at 60/40 and $866k against $991k at 50/50.

Paired by start year, the drifting portfolio ended with more in 4 of 12 retirements at 70/30, 4 of 12 at 60/40 and 4 of 12 at 50/50 — in each case those that began in 2003-2006. Drift raised the stock share by the end of every retirement, and most in these, the only ones that began after the 2000-02 fall: their stock share drifted up through the long rise after 2009 and, at 70/30, the split had drifted to between 89/11 and 91/9 by the end of their twenty years, against the 70/30 restored each January. The higher drifting median at 50/50 in the table comes from those same start years, not from a general advantage.

Why the two measures disagree

At 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds:

  • For the retirements that began in 1999-2002, the drifting portfolio held fewer stocks after the 2000-02 fall and again late in the 2008-09 fall, because nothing was bought back: its split had drifted to between 54/46 and 63/37 at the start of 2003, and to between 50/50 and 60/40 at the start of 2009, against the 70/30 restored each January. Its low point, on 9 March 2009, was higher in every one of them — for the 2000 retiree, the worst retirement, $544k against $492k.
  • For those that began in 1995-1998, it went the other way, and not for a single reason. The drifting portfolio's low point was the same for 1995 and 1996, which reached it in the first days of the retirement, and lower for 1997 and 1998; its biggest fall was larger for all four. No stocks were sold during the rise of the late 1990s, so all four met the 2000-02 fall with more in stocks: their split had drifted to between 77/23 and 85/15 by 1 September 2000, against 70/30 rebalanced.
    • 1995: the drifting portfolio regained its 2000 high, but went into the 2008 fall at 81/19, against 72/28 rebalanced, at the peak of 9 October 2007. Its biggest fall, from that peak to 9 March 2009, was 46.4% against 42.8%.
    • 1996-1998: the drifting portfolio never regained its high of 1 September 2000 before the 2008 fall, so its biggest fall ran from that day to 9 March 2009 (1997: 46.8% against 44.3%).
    • 1997 and 1998: ahead of the rebalanced portfolio on 1 September 2000, the drifting portfolios began 2003 behind it and with fewer stocks (67/33 and 63/37, against the 70/30 restored), stayed behind through the rise to 2007 and the fall that followed, and reached lower low points (1997: $931k against $968k rebalanced, on 9 March 2009).
  • Rebalancing buys stocks after a fall, which deepens the next fall but takes part in the recovery; at 70/30 the rebalanced portfolio ended with more in 8 of 12 retirements.

Start year by start year, the drifting low point was not always the higher one. It was higher in 7 of 12 retirements at 70/30, 7 of 12 at 60/40 and 7 of 12 at 50/50. It was the same for 1995 and 1996 at 70/30 and 60/40, and for 1995, 1996 and 1997 at 50/50: each of these reached its low point in the first days of the retirement, before the two portfolios could differ. It was lower for 1997, 1998 and 2003 at 70/30 and 60/40, and for 1998 and 2003 at 50/50. At 70/30 each of these met a fall after a rise, with more in stocks than the rebalanced portfolio: 1997 and 1998 the fall that began on 1 September 2000, and 2003, begun after that fall, the fall of 2008-09, which its drifting portfolio entered at 78/22 at the peak of 9 October 2007, against 72/28 rebalanced.

The worst low point of every split, drifting or rebalanced, was set in March 2009, so none of them measures a deep fall late in a drifting retirement, when its stock share is highest. The retirements begun 2003-2006, whose drifting split rose highest, did meet two shorter falls late. At 70/30 they entered the fall of 2020 at between 82/18 and 86/14 (at the high of 19 February 2020) and that of 2022 at between 87/13 and 89/11 (at the start of the year), and fell 28.0% to 29.1% and 23.2% to 23.5%, against 24.2% and 21.6% rebalanced; their lowest values in those two years stayed well above their low points of March 2009.

Over these twelve retirements, then, the floor favoured drift at every split. The book nevertheless keeps rebalancing each January as its rule for every portfolio unless a chapter says otherwise, for a reason this floor does not measure: left alone, the split does not stay where the retiree set it. By the end of its twenty years the drifting 70/30 portfolio held between 74/26 and 91/9, depending on the start year, and the drifting 50/50 between 56/44 and 81/19: in all 12 retirements, more in stocks than the split chosen. Its higher floor came from the order of the falls: the hardest retirements, begun 1999-2002, had drifted toward bonds in the 2000-02 fall and met the 2008-09 fall with fewer stocks. Chapters 18 and 19 repeat this comparison for the chosen funds, and chapter 22 rebalances more often than once a year.

These are retirements of one stretch of market history. Chapter 10 takes the same rule back over a century, to the crash of 1929 and the inflation of the 1970s, which the study's retirees never met.

Chapter 10. A century of retirements

How would the plain mixes have fared for a retiree who began just before the crash of 1929, or at the start of the long inflation of the mid-1960s? The study's own retirements begin in 1995, and only 12 of them have yet run twenty years, so they cannot say. This chapter applies the same retirement rule to the yearly market history of chapters 5 to 7 (chapter 11 applies it to a monthly history that reaches further back), for the plain mixes of stocks and bonds that can be built from them, and so follows 79 complete twenty-year retirements in the yearly data, begun every year from 1928 to 2006, instead of 12.

What is tested

The rule is the study's own (chapter 1):

  • $1M at the start of the first year, divided between stocks and bonds;
  • $40,000 withdrawn at the end of the first year, each later withdrawal 3% larger than the one before, never cut;
  • the split restored each January.

Each withdrawal is taken at the year end from the whole portfolio, stocks and bonds in proportion. Six portfolios are followed: the S&P 500 alone; 70% stocks and 30% bonds; 60/40; 50/50; a 10-year Treasury bond alone; and 3-month Treasury bills alone. Each is followed for 20, 25, 30, 40 and 50 years from every start year the data allow: 79 twenty-year retirements (begun 1928-2006), 74 of twenty-five years (begun to 2001), 69 of thirty years (begun to 1996), 59 of forty (begun to 1986) and 49 of fifty (begun to 1976).

The rule is also run a second way, with each withdrawal rising by that year's inflation (the change in consumer prices from December to December) instead of by 3%. Over this history inflation was far from steady: consumer prices fell 24% from 1930 to 1932 and rose 7.0% a year from 1966 to 1981. The two rules differ most in those years.

The long histories reach the start years the study cannot. At 70/30 under the study's rule, the three hardest twenty-year retirements began in 1928, 1929 and 1930, just before and during the crash; with withdrawals rising with inflation, the two hardest thirty-year retirements began in 1965 and 1966.

The data, and what they are not

Two long histories are used, here and in chapters 11 and 12, both listed in appendix C:

  • Yearly, 1928-2025: the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested, a 10-year Treasury bond, 3-month Treasury bills and consumer-price inflation — the series of chapters 5 to 7.
  • Monthly, January 1871 to August 2023: the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested, built from monthly-average prices, a 10-year Treasury bond built from its yield, and a consumer price index (the file's own heading; it does not document how the index was compiled for its early years, appendix C). Chapter 11's retirements use its complete years, 1872-2022; chapter 12's rule reads it from January 1871. It has no Treasury-bill series, so no cash portfolio.

What they are not:

  • The bonds are a 10-year Treasury, not Total Bond Market. A government bond of a single term behaves differently from a fund holding bonds of every kind and term, and nothing in this chapter says how Total Bond Market would have fared before it existed.
  • There are no fees and no trading costs. The funds in the rest of the book are priced net of their costs.
  • There is no Treasury-bill account. The study holds each withdrawal in Treasury bills for the year it is spent (chapter 1); here it is simply taken out at the year end, and the interest the account would earn is ignored.
  • Low points are seen only at year ends in the yearly data, and only as monthly averages in the monthly data, so the lowest values read higher than they were: a fall and recovery within a year does not show.
  • Only the plain mixes go back this far. Choosing funds needs the funds' own prices, which begin decades later.
  • Neither benchmark covers these years. SPY's prices begin in 1993, and those of Total Bond Market, the plain index's bond fund, in December 1986: decades after the first start years here. The results tables below therefore carry neither SPY nor the plain index; the check that follows compares them over the study's own retirements, which both cover, and chapter 12 follows the plain index's two funds day by day from December 1986.

  • 1929 no longer ran out. With withdrawals rising with inflation, the 1929 retirement no longer ran out within twenty years, in any mix or in stocks alone. Prices fell 24% from 1930 to 1932, and the withdrawal fell with them: $30k at the end of 1932, against $44k under the 3% rule. At 70/30 that retirement was left $531k after twenty years; its low point, $419k, came at the end of 1932, 3 yr 11 mo in. Over twenty years 1929 was still the worst start for stocks alone, 70/30 and 60/40; for 50/50 it was already 1965, which left $672k. Over 25 and 30 years stocks alone still ran out for the retirements of 1929 and 1930.
  • Over 25 and 30 years the worst starts were 1965 and 1966, at the start of what the Federal Reserve's history calls the Great Inflation (1965-1982), for 60/40 and 50/50 at both lengths and for 70/30 at thirty years. Inflation averaged 7.0% a year from 1966 to 1981, and the 1966 retiree's withdrawal had reached $114k by the end of 1981, against $62k under the 3% rule. Over thirty years 70/30 was left $101k (the 1966 retirement); 60/40 ran out once (1966) and 50/50 twice (1965 and 1966).
  • Over twenty-five and thirty years more in bonds made the worst start worse, not better. The 10-year Treasury earned 3.6% a year from 1966 to 1981, less than inflation, while the withdrawals kept pace with prices.
  • Over thirty years, bonds alone and cash alone ran out more often than under the 3% rule: in 41 of 69 and 50 of 69 retirements, against 32 of 69 and 35 of 69.

These results read the market once a year, from 1928. Would the same starts be the hardest with the market read month by month, from 1872? Chapter 11 takes the same rule further back, and reads the forty- and fifty-year rows above beside the monthly ones.

Chapter 11. A longer history, and longer retirements

Were chapter 10's hardest starts the hardest of all, or only the hardest the yearly data can reach? Its history begins in 1928 and is read once a year. This chapter follows the same rule and the same plain mixes on a monthly history that begins in 1872, and then over the longest retirements the data allow, of forty and fifty years, whose rows in chapter 10's yearly tables are read here beside the same lengths month by month. Like chapter 10's, its tables carry neither SPY nor the plain index: SPY's prices begin in 1993, and those of Total Bond Market, the plain index's bond fund, in December 1986, long after most of these retirements began.
