Chapter 12 ends with every retirement that ran out in chapters 10 to 12, grouped by the markets they met; appendix G.13 lists each complete one, and the retirements still under way that have already run out.

What the long histories show, and what they do not

They show:

  • The hardest retirements of the century were harder than any of the study's twelve. At 70/30 under the study's rule the plain index's worst twenty-year ending was $835k (chapter 8); over the century one such retirement ran out (the 1929 retirement, in the yearly data; in the monthly data none did).
  • The split mattered most at the worst, and which way depended on what went wrong. In the deflation of the 1930s more in bonds helped: at twenty years under the 3% rule, in the yearly data, 70/30 ran out once and 50/50 never did. In the inflation of 1966-1981 more in bonds hurt: at thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation 70/30 never ran out and 50/50 did twice.
  • Over twenty years, stocks alone was never the better choice at the worst: its worst low point and its worst ending were at or below 70/30's under both withdrawal rules, in both data sets.
  • Over forty and fifty years more in bonds did not protect: as the bond share rose from 30% to 50%, the number of retirements that ran out never fell.

They do not show:

  • Anything about choosing funds. Only the plain mixes can be followed this far back.
  • How Total Bond Market would have behaved. The bond here is a single 10-year Treasury, and over the retirements both cover the long-history 70/30 ended above the plain index every time: in all 12 in the yearly data and in all 9 in the monthly (begun 1995-2003).
  • The future. A century holds only a few retirements that began before a crash or a long inflation, and they are not independent: each twenty-year retirement shares nineteen of its years with the next one.
  • Exact endings or low points for a real portfolio. With no fees the endings read high, and with low points read at year ends or as monthly averages the falls read shallower than daily prices would show.

More in bonds helped at the worst in the 1930s and hurt in the 1970s. A split that moves with the market might keep the first without the second. Chapter 12 tests one such rule, first on the study's own two index funds, day by day, and then on the monthly history from 1872.

Chapter 12. Moving the split: a walk-forward rule

Chapters 10 and 11 held the split fixed for the whole retirement. Their hardest retirements began just before a long fall in stocks or a long inflation, and which split fared better at the worst depended on which of the two came. Can a rule that moves the split as the market moves raise the floor in both? This chapter tests one, and sets it beside the fixed splits on the same monthly history from 1872 and on the study's own two index funds, day by day, from 1987.

Why move the split

A fixed split holds the same share in stocks through every fall. A retiree at 70/30 in 1929 was restored to 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds each January while the S&P 500 lost 81.8% of its value, with withdrawals still due every year. The aim of a moving split is protection: less in stocks while a fall is under way, more while stocks lead.

The rule tested here is walk-forward: every decision is taken only from what had already happened by the day it was taken, and is carried out at the next month's (or the next day's) price, never at a price the rule has already read.

Its settings — the 20% fall, the one- and three-year comparisons, the splits — were declared in advance by the author from a reading of market history, not found by trying many values and keeping the best. Each version was run once, and every version run is reported here: the rule with two defensive splits, and its first version with the same two. Because they were chosen by someone who knows how past falls unfolded, the settings are not free of hindsight; what they are free of is tuning on these results.

The rule

  • 50/50 at first: the rule needs three years of history before it can compare, and compares only at the January check. It held 50/50 through 1989 in the daily data, which begin on 11 December 1986, and through 1874 in the monthly data, which begin in January 1871.
  • Each January, by the S&P 500's lead over bonds: the S&P 500's total return over the past year and over the past three years is compared with that of bonds over the same periods. Ahead on both: 70% stocks, 30% bonds. Ahead on one: 60/40. Ahead on neither: 40/60.
  • A hard stop: the moment the S&P 500 is 20% or more below its highest level so far (since the data begin), the portfolio moves to 20% stocks and 80% bonds, whatever the January comparison says. It stays at 20/80 until a January check finds the S&P 500 less than 20% below its high; from then the January rule applies again. The hard stop applies from the first day, the 50/50 years included.
  • Timing: a decision taken on one month's (or day's) data is traded at the next month's (or day's) price. Between decisions the split drifts with the markets; each January it is restored.

Everything else is chapter 10's retirement: $1M at the start, $40,000 withdrawn at the end of the first year, each later withdrawal 3% larger (or changed by that year's inflation), taken from the whole portfolio at the year end; no fees and no Treasury-bill account.

Three other versions are run beside it:

  • The hard stop to 40/60: the same rule with 40% stocks and 60% bonds as the defensive split.
  • The first version, to 20/80 and to 40/60: it came back from the defensive split as soon as the S&P 500 led bonds over either one or three years, and could switch again only once the S&P 500 was back within 20% of its high.

The exit is what separates them. Day by day the first version switched 18 times, at both defensive splits, and 12 of those switches lasted 10 trading days or less: the S&P 500 was 20% below its high but still ahead of bonds over one year or three (over one year only in 4 of them), so the rule came straight back. On 29 August 2001 it came back with the S&P 500 23.6% below its high, and since it could not switch again until the S&P 500 had recovered to within 20% of that high, it never returned to its defensive split through the fall that followed, to 47.5% below the high on 9 October 2002: the version to 20/80 held 60/40 for the rest of 2001 and, by the January rule, 40/60 through 2002 and 2003. The hard stop held 20/80 from March 2001 until the January check after 2004.

The data, and the checks

  • Monthly, January 1871 to August 2023: the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested and a 10-year Treasury bond — chapter 11's monthly data, built from monthly-average prices. The rule reads them from January 1871; the retirements begin in 1872, as in chapter 11, which uses the complete years 1872-2022. The S&P 500's high and its falls are read from those averages.
  • Daily, 11 December 1986 to 9 October 2026: the study's 500 Index fund and Total Bond Market fund, from their dividend-adjusted closing prices; here the 500 Index fund stands for the S&P 500, and Total Bond Market for bonds.
  • The fixed splits are run the same way as the rule, bought at the January price rather than at the end of the December before, so their monthly figures differ from chapter 11's: a little at the median, a lot at the floor. Over twenty years under the 3% rule their medians are 1.2% to 4.1% lower (70/30: $2.03M against $2.05M), and both name 1929 as the worst start, but that retirement's ending was $45k here against $145k in chapter 11 at 70/30, $191k against $275k at 60/40 and $311k against $380k at 50/50. The month's difference also moves a retirement at the edge from one side to the other, so the counts of retirements that ran out differ too: over thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation the fixed 70/30 ran out in 0 of 122 retirements in chapter 11 and in 1 of 122 here, the retirement of 1966.
  • Neither benchmark reaches back to the monthly data: SPY's prices begin in 1993 and the study's retirements in 1995. Over the retirements both cover, the study's own twelve, the second daily table below sets them beside the rule.
  • Checked against the study's retirements: for every one of the 12 retirements begun 1995-2006, the daily fixed 70/30 ended 0.5% to 2.0% below the study's plain index — the same two funds, without the Treasury-bill account in which the study's retirees hold the coming year's spending, and whose interest they earn.

As in chapter 10, there are no fees, taxes or trading costs. The rule trades more often than a fixed split, at every switch and every January, and in a taxable account each trade could realise a gain.

  • Against the plain index at 50% in stocks and 50% in bonds (chapter 9's table) the hard stop to 20/80 paid no such price: it led on all four measures, with a worst low point of $755k against $662k, a median low point of $905k against $771k, a worst ending of $1.09M against $991k and a median ending of $1.81M against $1.63M. The hard stop to 40/60 led on three: its median low point ($806k), worst ending ($1.01M) and median ending ($1.85M) were above the plain index's, but its worst low point, $645k, was below it.

Twenty retirements that overlap by up to nineteen years are one stretch of market history, not twenty separate ones.

  • Here the order turned over at the floor. The hard stop to 20/80's worst low point was $232k (the 1903 retirement, December 1922, 19 yr 11 mo in), below every fixed mix — $490k for 50/50, $415k for 60/40 and $348k for 70/30, each the 1929 retirement, June 1932, 3 yr 5 mo in — and above only stocks alone's $164k (the 1929 retirement, December 1948, 19 yr 11 mo in). By the measure this book puts first, that is the rule's worst result over twenty years. Its median ending, $1.61M, was the lowest in the table as well.
  • That worst result came from the rule's own timing, not from the market. Begun in 1903, with the same withdrawals, the fixed mixes and stocks alone ended between $813k and $1.01M, against the hard stop's $232k (under the 3% rule, between $903k and $1.10M, against $329k). The rule switched to 20/80 in August 1903 and in August 1907 (each switch traded at the next month's price), and both times the S&P 500 was back at its high by the January check that ended the switch, after December 1904 and December 1908: the retirement held 80% in bonds through both recoveries. It switched again in November 1917 and December 1920, in years 15 and 18 of its twenty, the inflation of 1916-1920 falling in years 14 to 18; the last switch held 20/80 until the check after December 1921, through year 19 (see the retirements begun 1898-1911, below). As over thirty years, in the next section, what mattered was when the rule held stocks, not how much: over its twenty years the split the rule set averaged 53.1% in stocks, more than a fixed 50/50, and was at 20/80 in 57 of 240 months.
  • The hard stop to 40/60 fell to $461k (the 1903 retirement, December 1922, 19 yr 11 mo in): above the fixed 70/30 and 60/40, below the fixed 50/50.
  • The first version held up better here: $382k to 20/80 (the 1966 retirement, December 1985, 19 yr 11 mo in) and $510k to 40/60 (the 1929 retirement, June 1932, 3 yr 5 mo in), the highest worst low point in the table. No retirement ran out over twenty years with withdrawals rising with inflation.

Over thirty years every portfolio ran out at least once, and the hard stop to 20/80 most often: in 7 of 122, against 1 of 122 for a fixed 50/50.
  • Where the hard stop ran out and a fixed 50/50 did not. Over thirty years under the 3% rule it ran out for the retirements of 1881-1883, 1887, 1902, 1903 and 1929, where a fixed 50/50 ran out only for 1929. Yet over the months each of the six begun 1881-1903 lasted, the split the rule set averaged 55%-57% in stocks (and 43%-45% in bonds), more than the 50/50: the difference lay in when the rule held stocks, not in how much.
  • With withdrawals rising with inflation the rule fared worse than every fixed mix. Over twenty-five years the hard stop to 20/80 ran out in 1 of 127 (the 1903 retirement), where no fixed mix ran out, and the hard stop to 40/60's worst low point, $170k (the 1966 retirement, December 1990, 24 yr 11 mo in), was below every fixed mix's (from $348k for 70/30, the 1929 retirement, June 1932, 3 yr 5 mo in, to $469k for 50/50, the 1966 retirement, December 1990, 24 yr 11 mo in). Over thirty years both versions ran out more often than every fixed split: the hard stop to 20/80 in 8 of 122, to 40/60 in 3 of 122, against 1 of 122 for a fixed 70/30, 2 of 122 for 60/40, 2 of 122 for 50/50 and 2 of 122 for stocks alone. The first version ran out in 7 of 122 (to 20/80) and 2 of 122 (to 40/60). Which retirements they were, and what the market did around them, closes this chapter.

  • The longest stay began in March 2001 and lasted 956 trading days, to the January check after 2004.
  • In 2020 the recovery came while the rule held 20/80: by the check that ended that switch, the S&P 500 was back at its high.
  • Over the whole daily history the rule held 20/80 on 23.2% of trading days and 70/30 on 53.8%.

Month by month it switched 15 times, beginning in 1877, 1884, 1893, 1903, 1907, 1917, 1920, 1929, 1937, 1962, 1970, 1974, 1987, 2001 and 2008, and held 20/80 in 19.9% of months. The two longest stays followed 1929 (85 months, to the check after December 1936) and 1937 (79 months, to the check after December 1943). The monthly averages never fell 20% below their high in 2020 or in 2022, so the monthly rule did not switch in either year.

What the rule shows, and what it does not

Is the rule protection, then? It shows:

  • A higher floor where the withdrawals rose 3% a year. Day by day, over the retirements begun 1987-2006, the hard stop to 20/80 had the highest worst low point of every portfolio, with a median between a fixed 70/30's and stocks alone's; over the study's own twelve its worst low point was $755k against the plain index's $492k (both March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), for a lower median ending. Month by month under the 3% rule it had the highest worst low point over twenty and twenty-five years.
  • Day by day, a higher floor with withdrawals rising with inflation too, over twenty and twenty-five years: over twenty its worst low point was $765k, against $666k for a fixed 50/50 (both the 2000 retirement, March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in). Over thirty years, which only 10 daily retirements have run, the fixed 50/50 and 60/40 held more.
  • Month by month, a lower floor where the withdrawals rose with inflation. Over twenty years its worst low point, $232k (the 1903 retirement, December 1922, 19 yr 11 mo in), was below every fixed mix's (from $348k for 70/30 to $490k for 50/50, each the 1929 retirement, June 1932, 3 yr 5 mo in), and over twenty-five years it ran out once where no fixed mix did. Like the fixed splits of chapters 10 and 11, it protected against some histories and not others.
  • Month by month, close to a fixed 50/50 at the median over twenty and twenty-five years, not beyond. At those lengths the 20/80 version's median ending was within a tenth of a fixed 50/50's under both withdrawal rules (over twenty years under the 3% rule, $1.70M against $1.67M); from thirty years on it differed by more, and over forty and fifty years it was 31% and 71% above under the 3% rule and 12% and 25% below with withdrawals rising with inflation. At the floor the withdrawal rule decided: under the 3% rule it was slightly above a fixed 50/50 over twenty years and well above over twenty-five; with withdrawals rising with inflation it was far below over twenty years, and over twenty-five it ran out where the 50/50 did not.
  • It did worse where the retirement was long. Over thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation both versions ran out more often than every fixed split; over forty years under the 3% rule, more often than every fixed mix; over fifty, the 20/80 version still did.

It does not support:

  • That a moving split beats a fixed split in general. On the long history it did not; the daily result covers one stretch of twenty overlapping retirements.
  • That these settings are the best ones. No other values of the fall or the comparison periods were tried, and no defensive splits beyond the two shown; other values would give other results.
  • Anything net of costs. There are no fees, taxes or trading costs, and the rule trades more than a fixed split.
  • The future. The history holds only a few deep falls, and the next need not resemble them.

Every retirement that ran out

Chapters 10 to 12 give, for every portfolio, length and withdrawal rule, how many retirements ran out. Which ones were they, and what did the markets do around them? Appendix G.13 lists every complete one, with the year of the retirement in which it ran out, and beside them the 105 retirements still under way, all cash alone or bonds alone in the yearly data, that have already run out. None ran out in the daily data, under any version of the rule or any fixed split.

Every retirement holding stocks that ran out — stocks alone, a fixed mix or the rule — began in one of four stretches of years. Bonds alone and cash alone ran out far more widely:

A start year counts once for each portfolio, length and data set in which it ran out, so a single hard start can stand behind many of the results counted above. This chapter's fixed splits and stocks alone are counted beside chapter 11's monthly rows: they are the same portfolios on the same monthly data, bought a month later, and 188 of their 227 results repeat a chapter 11 result for the same start year.

Begun 1872-1894: falling prices and withdrawals rising 3% a year

  • Only the monthly data reach these years. All but 2 of the 306 results that ran out were under the 3% rule, over 30 years or more; the exceptions are the hard stop to 20/80's retirement of 1893, over forty and fifty years. They ran out between 1908 and 1942.
  • Prices fell while the withdrawals rose. Consumer prices fell 48.5% from December 1872 to December 1896. The 3% rule raised the withdrawal regardless: by the end of 1896 the 1881 retiree was drawing $62k, where withdrawals rising with inflation would have been $26k. Under withdrawals rising with inflation, no retirement holding stocks that began before 1893 ran out, at any length.
  • Returns were modest. From 1881 to 1920 the S&P 500 earned 5.5% a year and the 10-year Treasury 3.5%; forty years of the 3% rule need 5.4% a year if the return is the same every year.
  • No archived source used in this book names an event for these years, so only the data are described.

Begun 1898-1911: the inflation of 1916-1920, then the crash of 1929

  • Monthly data only: 109 results under the 3% rule and 91 under withdrawals rising with inflation, over 25 to 50 years; they ran out between 1926 and 1960. 125 of the 200 are the rule's own: 75 for the hard stop and 50 for its first version.
  • Consumer prices rose 88.3% from December 1915 to December 1920. From 1903 to 1920 the S&P 500 earned 4.6% a year, about the rate of inflation (4.6%), and the 10-year Treasury 3.3%, less.
  • The fall of 1929-1932 then came late in these retirements, in years 19 to 32 of them, for all but 4 results: the hard stop to 20/80's retirement of 1903, with withdrawals rising with inflation, had already run out, in 1926, year 24, over each length of twenty-five years and more (the section "Twenty years, month by month" shows the rule's timing in it).

Begun 1928-1940: the crash of 1929 and the 1930s

  • Both data sets and both withdrawal rules: 143 results under the 3% rule and 38 under withdrawals rising with inflation, over 20 years and more; they ran out between 1942 and 1985, as early as year 14 of the retirement.
  • The S&P 500, dividends reinvested, fell 81.8% from September 1929 to June 1932 (monthly averages), and did not regain its September 1929 level until January 1945, 15 years later. Consumer prices fell 27.2% from September 1929 to March 1933, and from 1930 to 1940 the S&P 500 returned -0.9% a year and the 10-year Treasury 4.0%. Under the 3% rule the withdrawals kept rising through all of it.
  • The Federal Reserve's history of the crash dates Black Monday to 28 October 1929, and records that the Dow Jones Industrial Average, price only, stood 89% below its peak by July 1932 and did not return to its pre-crash level until November 1954.
  • The retirements begun 1936-1940 ran out only over forty and fifty years, and late. Those begun in 1936 and 1937 met a second fall early — the S&P 500's monthly averages fell 41.6% from March 1937 to April 1938, in the recession the Federal Reserve's history dates from May 1937 to June 1938 and calls the third-worst downturn of the twentieth century — and outlasted it. Those begun in 1939 and 1940 began after that low and met another fall within their first years: from the January they began to April 1942, the monthly averages fell 23.5% to 25.7%. Their 23 results ran out between 1975 and 1985, in years 39 to 49 of the retirement, 20 of them under withdrawals rising with inflation: they ran out during and after the inflation of the late 1960s and 1970s, described for the starts of 1959-1969 below, not in the fall of 1937-38. Across the whole group, 50 of the 181 results ran out in 1965 or later.
  • The hard stop held 20/80 through both: for 85 months after its switch in 1929, to the check after December 1936, and for 79 months after 1937, to the check after December 1943.

Begun 1959-1969: the Great Inflation (1965-1982)

  • Every one under withdrawals rising with inflation: 232 results, over 25 to 50 years, in both data sets; no portfolio holding stocks begun in these years ran out under the 3% rule. They ran out between 1989 and 2012.
  • Inflation outran both stocks and bonds. Consumer prices rose 7.0% a year from 1966 to 1981, while the S&P 500 earned 6.0% a year and the 10-year Treasury 3.6% (yearly data). The withdrawals rose with prices: the 1966 retiree's had reached $114k by the end of 1981 (chapter 10).
  • Within those years the S&P 500's monthly averages fell 39.2% from January 1973 to December 1974, and were back at that level in July 1976.
  • The name is the Federal Reserve's: its history of the period files the years 1965-1982 as the "Great Inflation".

Bonds alone and cash alone

  • Bonds alone ran out in 802 results and cash alone in 335, across the start years in the table above.
  • The 10-year Treasury earned 2.7% a year from 1941 to 1981, less than the 3% yearly rise of the withdrawals and less than inflation (4.7%); from 1982 to 2020 it earned 7.8%. Over forty years under the 3% rule, in the yearly data, which begin in 1928, every bonds-alone retirement begun from 1928 to 1963 ran out, and none begun later; in the monthly data, those begun 1872-1959 and 1961 ran out.
  • The order of the returns mattered as much as their average. Bonds alone begun in 1955 earned 5.7% a year over its forty years, more than the 5.4% a steady return would need, and still ran out, in 1978, year 24 of the retirement: over those 24 years it had earned 3.1% a year.
  • Treasury bills earned 0.3% a year from 1933 to 1945: under the 3% rule cash alone ran out within twenty years for every retirement begun from 1931 to 1938. They earned 0.5% a year from 2009 to 2021, and the forty-year cash retirements begun 1982-1986 ran out late, in years 33 to 40. Those begun 1987-2004, not yet forty years old, have already run out, sooner: in years 22 to 32.

Apart from the bond funds held alone in chapter 8, every portfolio in Part IV holds the market itself, through the indexes or two index funds. Could a retiree have done better by choosing funds, and how can a choice be tested without knowing, as no retiree could, which funds would do well? Part V sets out the method, beginning with the funds that could actually be bought on each date.

Part V: Choosing funds — the method

A rule that picks past winners is easily made to look better than any retiree could have done: rank it on today's list of funds, which holds only the survivors, or let it buy at a price the ranking has already read. How did the study keep out such hindsight, and where could it not? This part sets out how each result is produced, in five steps: the fund universe, the prices, the selection rule, the simulation, and the checks applied to it.

Chapter 13. The fund universe

Which funds could a retiree of 1995 actually have chosen from? Not those on offer today, which are the ones that survived. This chapter defines which funds a retiree may choose from, and limits every choice to the funds that could actually be bought on that date. Without that limit, the results would carry decades of hindsight.

Which funds are eligible

The investable universe is restricted to Vanguard funds:

included excluded
Stock funds broad US stock funds, index or actively managed sector, international, balanced, target-date and tax-managed funds
Bond funds taxable investment-grade bond funds only high-yield and tax-exempt funds

Also excluded:

  • asset-allocation and LifeStrategy funds;
  • funds of funds;
  • ESG-screened and factor funds;
  • Core Bond, which may hold up to 10% in bonds outside US dollars;
  • Core-Plus Bond, by the author's choice (no archived filing of the fund gives a reason);
  • funds offered only to institutions.

Funds are held in their retail share classes:

  • the lower-cost Admiral class where the fund offers one, from the first trading day of 2004, or from the Admiral class's first price if that came later;
  • an older class of the same fund before that, normally the original Investor class;
  • the Investor class throughout for the few funds that never offered Admiral shares, such as Dividend Growth and Selected Value.

Four funds depart from these rules (chapter 14):

  • Morgan Growth offered Admiral shares from 14 May 2001, but the study uses its Investor class's published yearly returns throughout.
  • Long-Term Bond Index is priced on its Admiral class alone, from 7 February 2019, because its Investor class's prices were not available.
  • Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index are priced on their exchange-traded classes until their Admiral classes' first prices, although each also had an Investor class: the price records hold no Investor-class prices for either fund (chapter 16 gives the effect):
    • Dividend Appreciation Index: an Investor class from 2006; priced on the exchange-traded class until December 2013, so the portfolios that held it from 2012 to December 2013 were valued at exchange-traded prices;
    • High Dividend Yield Index: an Investor class from 2006; priced on the exchange-traded class until February 2019, so the portfolios that held it from 2016 to February 2019 were valued at exchange-traded prices.

Funds that later merged or were liquidated are included until the year end before the event (chapter 16).

Only what was available on the day

The governing principle is that a retiree may select only from funds that existed, and were open to new investors, on the date of selection.

A list of today's funds consists of survivors — funds that performed well enough to remain in existence. Applying it to a retiree of 1995 would confer 31 years of hindsight.

The fund menu was therefore reconstructed as it stood at each year end from 1994, fund by fund, from Vanguard's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. For each fund the menu records the date it was:

  • launched;
  • offered to retail investors;
  • closed to and reopened for new investment;
  • merged or liquidated.

Closures and reopenings are those found in the filings that were read. For the 1990s the evidence is thinner. It consists of:

  • the closures of Windsor, PRIMECAP and Trustees' Equity U.S., read in their own filings;
  • Vanguard's family-wide notices of funds not accepting new accounts, which name only Windsor and PRIMECAP — and no such notice was found for October 1996 to April 1998;
  • each other fund's prospectus of late 1998 or early 1999, which shows no closure, though the longer ones were read only in part.

Windsor's reopening on 1 June 1999 is inferred rather than read: its prospectus of February 1999 still shows it closed, and that of June 1999 no longer does. Any date between the two gives the same menus, because the menu changes only in January: Windsor could first be bought in January 2000 either way.

A missed closure of another fund in the 1990s therefore cannot be ruled out (appendix G.2).

Four ways to apply the menu

The menu is applied in four ways, each consistent with the date of selection:

  • the menu each January (chapter 20) — the funds available each January from 1995, ranked afresh every year; this is the principal method;
  • the list frozen at retirement (chapter 19) — the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement (for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994), frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January; a variant reviews the list every 3 or 5 years instead;
  • the 1999 list (chapter 21) — the menu on 31 December 1999, kept throughout; applicable only to retirements beginning in 2000 or later, and presented as a comparison;
  • picked once and kept (chapter 18) — the top funds on the menu on the first day of retirement, held for the whole retirement without re-ranking.

The number of funds that could be picked grew from 17 in January 1995 to 50 in January 2025, as new funds were launched. Closures, mergers and reopenings moved it in both directions along the way.

The full detail is set out in appendix G.2:

  • the complete year-by-year menu;
  • the menus at the 1994-1998 year ends as published by Vanguard;
  • the 1999 list fund by fund;
  • the closures and mergers used, with the sources for them.

When a fund closes or reopens

Three rules govern changes in availability:

  1. Closed at a year end: a fund closed to new investors cannot be purchased in the following January.
  2. Closed while held: a fund already held when it closes is retained until the next January and then sold.
  3. Reopened: a fund that reopens may be purchased again at a January rebalance if it ranks highly enough.

The portfolios picked once and kept (chapter 18) depart from the second rule by design. An existing holder keeps a fund that closes, and adds to it each January only as far as the fund's closure terms allowed. Chapter 18 also applies this keep-a-closed-fund rule, as a variant, to the menu each January and the list frozen at retirement.

The menu settles which funds could be bought. What each of them then returned is a question for the price records.

Chapter 14. Prices and data

Can a database of fund prices be taken on trust? In this study it could not, and every result rests on the price records. This chapter describes where they come from, how they were checked against Vanguard's own published returns, and what that check corrected.

The source

Daily prices are taken from a database of dividend- and distribution-adjusted closing prices. These represent the value of a holding with every distribution reinvested on the date the price records carry it.

The records are used in three forms:

  • as extracted, one series per share class;
  • one continuous series per fund, built from them:
    • the Admiral share class from the first trading day of 2004 (the early Admiral records are unreliable), or from the Admiral class's first price if that came later, as for these funds:
      • June 2005: Inflation-Protected Securities;
      • September 2011: Small-Cap Growth Index, Small-Cap Value Index, Mid-Cap Growth Index and Mid-Cap Value Index;
      • December 2013: Dividend Appreciation Index;
      • February 2019: High Dividend Yield Index;
    • an older class of the same fund before that, normally the Investor class, but the exchange-traded class for Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index (chapter 13);
    • the Investor class throughout for funds that never offered Admiral shares, such as Dividend Growth and Selected Value;
    • the Admiral class alone for Long-Term Bond Index, from 7 February 2019, because its Investor class's prices were not available;
  • the same set extended with the funds added to the menu after 1999.

Daily prices are missing for five funds that later merged into other funds. Each is represented by its published annual returns; two of them, Trustees' Equity U.S. and Morgan Growth, were on the menu in the 1990s.

These are Investor-class returns throughout. For Morgan Growth, the only one of the five any portfolio held (from 2000 to 2018, chapter 16), this is one of the departures from the share-class rule noted in chapter 13. Its Admiral shares date from 14 May 2001, so the share-class rule would have used them from 2004; the study uses its Investor class's published yearly returns instead.

From 2004 it was held by:

  • the top-four portfolios picked once at the 2000 and 2001 starts, from 2004 to 2018, at 17.5% of the funds' value at 70/30 (less at the other splits);
  • the top four of the lists frozen at retirement, at the same share: the list frozen at the 1995 retirement in 2016 and the lists frozen at the 1995 to 1998 retirements in 2018;
  • the top three of the list frozen at the 1995 retirement, at 23.3%, in 2018 alone.

The fund's own prospectuses put the Admiral class's expenses 0.14 to 0.19 percentage points a year below the Investor class's in fiscal years 2004 to 2008 (its 2009 prospectus) and 0.10 to 0.14 in 2014 to 2018 (its 2019 prospectus); the Admiral class's published return was 0.10 points higher in 2008 and 0.10 in 2018. On a 17.5% holding, the understatement is therefore roughly 0.02 to 0.03 points a year of the portfolio's return, and about 0.02 at 23.3% (2018, a gap of 0.10) — an approximation, not a measured figure.

The check against published returns

The prices were verified against Vanguard's published calendar-year returns for every fund from 1985 to 2003.

The verification proved material: the database omitted a substantial number of capital-gain distributions, principally through 1993 (chapter 26). Two corrections followed:

  • Each year that disagreed with the published figure was restated to it.
  • The funds whose earliest years could not be verified begin at the end of 1987 (U.S. Growth) or 1988.

Traceability

The study uses 291 price files across the three forms above:

  • 284 of the funds' mutual-fund share classes (a series can appear in more than one form);
  • two: the exchange-traded classes of Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index (chapter 13);
  • five others: SPY in each form; RSP, an exchange-traded fund extracted as a second benchmark and not used in this book; and the 3-month Treasury-bill rate. Behind the restated series are 31 untouched extracts. Each file is identified by a recorded checksum, so that the inputs to every result can be established exactly.

The share classes used in each period, every data correction and the cross-checks are documented in appendix G.3.

With the menu and the prices in place, one decision remains each January: which of the funds on the menu to hold.

Chapter 15. The selection rule

Does a fund that has led over the past five and ten years go on leading? The selection rule is a wager that it does, and Part VI tests the wager. The rule ranks funds on past return and holds the leaders. This chapter states it exactly.

Each January, separately for stock funds and for bond funds, every fund available that day is ranked using data up to the previous year's final close only:

  • History: a fund requires at least five years of history to be ranked.
  • Ranking: it is ranked on its five-year return and on its ten-year return, and the two ranks are averaged. A fund's rank is one plus the number of funds with a higher return. The ten-year rank is taken only among the funds that have ten years of history; a fund with less than ten years is ranked on its five-year return alone.
  • Example: in January 1998 U.S. Growth was 10th of 13 on five years and 3rd of the 7 funds with ten years: a score of 6.5, the average of the two. The lowest score ranks first.
  • Ties are resolved in favour of the higher five-year return.
  • Holdings: the portfolio holds the top two stock funds and the top two bond funds (the top three or four in alternative versions), in equal amounts within each asset class.
  • Timing: the ranking uses prices up to the last trading day of the old year (31 December, or the last trading day before it). Every purchase — the first one and each later change of holdings, together with the annual rebalance — is made at the close of the first trading day of the new year, so nothing is bought at a price the ranking has read.

The ranking considers return alone; it takes no account of risk, expenses or changes of management.

The table in chapter 13 shows the highest-ranked funds at intervals. Every January's selections at two, three and four funds, with the corresponding holdings of the 1999 list, are set out in appendix G.4.

Old funds ranked as if young

History is counted from the start of a fund's price records, not from its launch. Eight funds ranked in the mid-1990s have price records that begin only at the end of 1987 or 1988, because their earlier years could not be verified (chapter 14).

In the Januaries shown below, each had been running for ten years or more but had no ten-year return in its records, so it was ranked on its five-year return alone. In earlier Januaries a fund launched less than ten years before was genuinely young and is not counted. Did the shortened records reach what was bought? The last column shows when the menu each January picked these funds.

U.S. Growth 1959 1987 1995 to 1997 third or fourth in 1995

Windsor, whose records also start late, was closed to new investors in those years and was not ranked. The lists frozen at retirement and the portfolios picked once used the same scores. How the results would change if these funds had their full ten-year records has not been measured.

Three later funds were also ranked on a record shorter than their lives:

  • Growth Equity joined the menu on 12 June 2000, carrying the record of Turner Growth Equity — but only from 1999, although Turner Growth Equity was launched in 1992. With less than five years of record it could not be ranked in the Januaries of 2001 to 2003. It was then ranked on its five-year return alone in 2004 to 2008: last in 2004 to 2007, and 8th of 22 in 2008.   • Dividend Growth is counted only from 6 December 2002, when it became a diversified stock fund; its earlier record, as Utilities Income, a sector fund, is left out by the rules of chapter 13.   • Long-Term Bond Index, launched in 1994, has usable prices only from 7 February 2019 (chapter 14). It was ranked on its five-year return alone from its first January, 2025: 20th of 22 in 2025 and 2026 among the bond funds, so it was never picked.

The rule decides what is bought each January. How a retirement is then followed for twenty years or more, and by what it is judged, is the subject of chapter 16.

Chapter 16. The simulation and the measures

Twenty years or more of daily values have to be reduced to a few figures before two ways of choosing funds can be compared. Which figures, and in what order should they be read? This chapter describes how the study's own retirements are simulated, and defines every measure reported for them:

  • It covers the retirements begun from 1995 on the daily fund prices: the fund-selection methods of Part VI, and the cash, the single funds, SPY and the plain index of Parts II to IV.
  • Chapters 10 to 12 and 27 state their own data and assumptions, which differ from those below: chapters 10, 12 and 27 each in a section of their own, and chapter 10's section covers chapter 11's monthly data too.

The simulation

The simulation follows one retirement at a time: a start year, a horizon of 20 or 25 years (or "to date", to the last available close), a portfolio, and the withdrawal rule of chapter 1. It walks every trading day and:

  • restores each fund to its target weight at the first close of each January — the only point at which stocks are traded against bonds (the variants of chapter 22 also do so every six or three months);
  • takes the withdrawal at the last close of each year, from every fund in proportion to its value, so the withdrawal leaves the weights unchanged;
  • pays the T-bill account out monthly and accrues its interest.

It is run for every start year from 1995 to 2025 and for every portfolio; Part VI reports the results.

A complete retirement is one whose whole horizon lies inside the price records. Only complete retirements enter the median and the worst. With a 20-year horizon there are twelve of them, starting from 1995 to 2006 (seven for the 1999 list, which starts in 2000).

All figures for the simulated retirements are in nominal dollars, before taxes and before trading costs. The after-inflation figures of chapters 5 and 6 come from yearly index returns, not from this simulation.

The measures

Every measure reported for these retirements is defined once, here:

measure meaning
ending balance the money left in the funds at the end of the retirement, after that year's withdrawal
lowest value at any point the lowest value the portfolio reached on any day: funds + T-bill account - spending still owed this year. Beside a worst low point, "N yr M mo in" is how far into that retirement it fell: the calendar months from January of the start year to the month of the lowest value, in whole years and months ("0 yr 11 mo in" is the December of the first year)
biggest fall the largest fall from a high to a later low of that value — withdrawals included, so in every complete retirement larger than the fall of the holdings themselves, the same portfolio with nothing withdrawn
time to recover months from the high before the biggest fall back to the same value, withdrawals included; a median time to recover is taken over the retirements that got back only. Those that never did are counted under "never back", and where their months are shown they are a lower bound, the months to the end of the retirement, written "n+"
never back the portfolio had not regained that high when the retirement ended; tables give the number of start years for which this was so
longest underwater the longest stretch, in months, below any earlier high
ran out a year-end withdrawal larger than what was left
ahead of the plain index the retirement ended with more money than the plain index with the same stock/bond proportions and start year
share of what was left (taken out ÷ assets) everything withdrawn so far divided by what is left in the funds
median / worst the middle and the lowest outcome over the complete retirements; with twelve retirements the median is the average of the 6th and 7th, so no single retiree had it. Where methods are compared, the worst low point is read first and the median ending last (below)

Withdrawals are included in every measure. A portfolio that declines 40% while paying out $40,000 a year or more takes longer to recover than an index chart suggests. The time to recover reported here reflects that.

The median ending and the lowest point answer different questions. The median ending is what a typical retirement left behind. The lowest point is what the retiree had to live through, and the moment at which a retiree is most likely to abandon the plan or return to work. Wherever methods are compared, the book therefore reads the table above in this order:

  1. the worst lowest value at any point, with when it came;
  2. the median lowest value;
  3. the worst ending;
  4. the median ending, given as the cost of a higher floor, never as the verdict on its own.

Where the floor and the median point opposite ways, both are stated; "The ranking and the comparison" below gives a case.

What the simulation assumes

Every retirement this chapter covers rests on the assumptions below. Each is a choice, and a different choice could change the figures.

The retiree

  • Follows the rule mechanically for twenty years or more: never sells in a fall, never changes the spending, and has no other assets or income in the model.
  • Holds the funds directly with Vanguard, one account per fund, with no transaction fees.
  • Pays no tax. Distributions are reinvested in full; switching gains, rebalancing gains and Treasury-bill interest are untaxed; withdrawals are gross.

The figures therefore describe a tax-deferred account such as an IRA, before tax on withdrawals and without required minimum distributions. In a taxable account the realised gains would be taxed. That cost falls mostly on the selection methods: a switch sells a whole holding, while the plain index's January rebalance sells only the excess. Tax on distributions falls on both.

The money

  • All simulated figures are in nominal dollars. The withdrawal rises a fixed 3% a year, not with measured inflation. A balance that grows from $1M to $2M has not doubled in purchasing power.
  • The first year's spending is set aside on top of the $1M. The retiree effectively starts with about $1.04M, and the first sale from the funds comes after a year of growth — gentler than the common 4% rule, which withdraws at the start.
  • The ending balance excludes the next year's spending, already moved to the Treasury-bill account.
  • Withdrawals come from every fund in proportion, not from bonds first or from a separate reserve. Only the January reset (and the in-year resets of chapter 22) trades stocks against bonds.
  • The Treasury-bill account earns the previous trading day's 3-month Treasury rate, without fees or tax.
  • Only two of these retirements have run thirty years inside the price records: those begun in 1995 and 1996. Later starts are followed to the last close and projected beyond it (chapter 24), so what the fund-selection results say about money running out rests mainly on the twenty- and twenty-five-year retirements. The long histories of chapters 10 to 12 follow far longer retirements; chapter 12 says which of them ran out, and appendix G.13 lists every one.

Trading and timing

  • Every purchase is made one trading day after the ranking. The ranking reads the last close of the old year; the funds are bought at the close of the first trading day of the new year. An earlier version bought the first holdings at the ranking's own close, a trade no retiree could have made; chapter 26 describes the correction.
  • The picks depend on the exact date of the ranking. Ranking one trading day earlier changes the top two in 7 of the 32 Januaries and the top four in 12. (Six of the seven top-two changes come from returns; in the other, January 2003, Mid-Cap Growth falls one trading day short of five years of history and drops out of the ranking.)
  • Fees on purchases, redemptions and short-term trading, and Vanguard's limits on frequent trading, are not modelled.
  • Admiral share prices are used wherever a fund's series has switched to them (chapter 14), although smaller holdings may at times have been below the Admiral minimum. Those holdings are overstated: in the price records the Admiral classes' returns led the older classes' by 0.07 to 0.16 percentage points a year, measured from each fund's switch to the last close. Morgan Growth, kept on its Investor class's published returns, is understated instead: its prospectuses put the Admiral class's expenses 0.10 to 0.19 points a year lower (chapter 14).
  • Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index are priced on their exchange-traded classes before their switch (chapter 13), because the price records hold no Investor-class prices for them. Those years are overstated against the Investor class the rule would have used: after the switch the exchange-traded classes' returns led their own Admiral classes' by 0.02 and 0.05 points a year respectively, and in every other fund the Admiral class led the older class. By how much these years are overstated has not been measured.
  • With rebalancing every six or three months (chapter 22), a fund that closed during the year is topped up at the in-year resets without the $25,000 limit of chapter 18.

Prices

  • Prices are total returns: distributions are reinvested on the date the price records carry them, and fund expenses are already deducted.
  • The five funds without daily prices are built from their published calendar-year returns, at a constant rate inside each year, so a fall within a year is not seen. Only Morgan Growth was ever held (see "The fund list" below); the case where this matters most is set out next.
  • Old funds ranked as if young: eleven funds were ranked on their five-year return alone in Januaries when they were older than their records (chapter 15).
  • A fund's record includes its predecessor's where it took one over: Mid-Cap Growth carries the record of PIC Mid Cap (a load fund), and Growth Equity that of Turner Growth Equity, but only from 1999 (chapter 15). Dividend Growth counts only from 6 December 2002, when it became a diversified stock fund.

Morgan Growth's smoothed prices

The top four picked once at the 2000 start held Morgan Growth from 2000 to 2018, at 17.5% of the funds' value at 70/30 (its share at each January reset). Its biggest fall, 58.0%, runs from a high on 1 September 2000 to its lowest value, $443k on 9 March 2009. Both days fall inside a calendar year, where Morgan Growth's price is smoothed. Does the smoothing make the fall look smaller or larger than it was? The first two rows set the smoothed price beside what two daily-priced funds did on the same days:

U.S. Growth / the 500 Index over the same days rose 14.1% / rose 5.4% fell 19.1% / fell 26.9%
Morgan Growth's share of the funds that day 15.2% 20.9%

Giving Morgan Growth U.S. Growth's or the 500 Index's move over those days, all else unchanged, puts the biggest fall at an estimated 61.0% to 62.1% (the range over either fund at either end). This is an estimate, not a simulation. It would make this retirement's fall the worst of the top four picked once, above the 58.4% of the 1999 start.

The 2001 start and the 60/40 and 50/50 versions of both starts held it too, and share the low of 9 March 2009, where they are affected in the same direction. Only the two days of this retirement's fall — the high of 1 September 2000 and the low of 9 March 2009 — are re-estimated. The smoothing on other days, such as inside 2001 and 2002 and at the 2001 start's highs of 2007, has not been examined; nor has the effect on the portfolios that held Morgan Growth for only a year or two.

The fund list

  • US funds only, and Vanguard only. No international funds, in a period when US stocks did exceptionally well. The absolute figures do not carry over to a globally diversified retiree; the comparison with the plain index is less affected.
  • Long-Term Bond Index was on the menu from 1994, but its usable prices begin only on 7 February 2019, so it is first ranked in January 2025, on five years alone (chapter 15) — although a long-term bond fund ranked first on the bond side in 26 of the 32 Januaries from 1995 to 2026.
  • The three Admiral-only Treasury funds ($50,000 minimum) are left out by the author's choice, not by a rule of chapter 13. Launched in 1992, they had five years of history only from January 1998, and were exchanged into the Admiral shares of the ordinary Treasury funds on 1 June 2001, so they would have left the menu at the year end before. They could have been ranked only in the Januaries of 1998 to 2000, and the choice affects only those three menus.
  • A fund that merged away or was liquidated leaves the menu at the year end before the event. It applied to five stock funds, all of which merged into other Vanguard funds:

U.S. Value 29 July 2020 into Value Index, 5 February 2021 2020 -- (already closed)
  • For Morgan Growth, the one such fund ever held, this used no hidden knowledge. A prospectus supplement dated 17 December 2018, two weeks before the 31 December 2018 ranking, announced its merger into U.S. Growth and closed it to new accounts with immediate effect, so it could not have been bought by a new account in January 2019 in any case; existing accounts could keep buying until shortly before the merger. Had it stayed open, it would have ranked 3rd of 28 that January.
  • Trustees' Equity U.S. and Capital Value left the menu a January before they closed and merged. Had they stayed, they would have ranked 11th of 14 in January 1998 and 28th of 28 in January 2020; Capital Value had the lowest five- and ten-year returns on the menu.     • in 2016 and 2018, under a few lists frozen at the 1995 to 1998 retirements;
    • by the top-four portfolios picked once at the 2000 and 2001 starts, from their start to 2018 (chapter 18).
  • Closures in the 1990s rest on thinner evidence than later ones (chapter 13).

The ranking and the comparison

  • The ranking rule was chosen after earlier versions had been seen. Of the scores tried on the lists then in use, it did best (appendix E), which biases the results in favour of the selection methods.
  • A five-year return alone — the score of any fund with less than ten years of history — favours new funds with one strong stretch, the kind of fund that weighed on the menu each January (chapter 20).
  • The plain index holds the S&P 500 as its stock share, while the selection methods can hold small-company, mid-cap and value funds. The comparison therefore mixes fund selection with company size and style.
  • The ranking favoured long-term bond funds, a bet on falling interest rates. Measured by calendar year, the two bond funds held by the menu each January's top two grew to 5.14 times their starting value from 1995 to 2020, against 4.05 times for Total Bond Market, although they trailed it in 10 of those 26 years, by as much as 12.8 percentage points in 2009. They were level with it in 2021 (0.1 points behind) and trailed it by 12.5 points in 2022 (chapter 20). The same shares in stocks and bonds do not mean the same risk.
  • The order of the measures is a choice, and it can decide a comparison. At 70/30 over twenty years the menu each January's top two had a higher worst low point than the plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January): $515k (the 2000 retirement; March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in) against $492k (the 2000 retirement; March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in). Its median low point was higher too, $755k against $674k. Its worst ending was lower, $692k against $835k, and so was its median ending, $1.78M against $2.10M; it ended ahead in 2 of the 12 retirements. Read with the floor first, the menu leads; read by the endings, the plain index does. Chapter 25 sets out the comparison for every method.
  • Only twelve overlapping twenty-year retirements are complete; together they amount to only one or two independent observations of the market.
  • The five retirees of chapter 23 were chosen to show the best start of the study (1995) and the starts around the 2000 and 2008 falls.

Each of these assumptions is a choice, stated so that it can be weighed. An undetected error would be stated nowhere; chapter 17 sets out how the study looks for one.

Chapter 17. Checks and reproducibility

How would anyone know if a figure in this book were wrong? A backtest can be wrong in ways that produce entirely plausible figures: a fund bought while it was closed, a purchase at a price the ranking had already read, a table left over from an earlier version of the method. This chapter lists the controls that guard against that.

The following controls are applied to every result of the fund-selection tests (appendix B):

  • Independent rebuilds. For a few retirements per test, the portfolio's growth is recomputed from the raw prices by a separate, independent calculation. It must agree with the simulation to six digits.

  • Availability compliance. Every holding in every year is checked against its closure periods, menu dates and merger or liquidation dates. A fund bought while it could not have been bought is an error. A fund is held while closed in two cases only:

    • it closed during a year in which it was held, and is kept until the next January (rule 2 of chapter 13) — under the menu each January, for example, PRIMECAP in 1998;
    • an existing holder keeps it on purpose (chapter 18); the January additions to it stay within its closure terms, but the in-year resets of chapter 22 top it up without that limit (chapter 16).

    Across the tests, tens of thousands of yearly holdings were checked; none failed.

  • Unchanged means identical. When the method changes, every result it should not affect is rerun and must come out exactly the same as before. For example, when new measures were added, every existing measure in every set of results had to come out unchanged.

  • Full reproduction. Every test and every table was once regenerated from scratch and compared with the recorded results: nothing differed. After each correction described in chapter 26 every test still in use was rerun, and each later test was checked against an independent rebuild.

  • The ends of every derived series. The first and last values of any curve built for a chart or a table are printed and checked before anything is quoted from it.

  • Benchmarks in every comparison of the fund methods. SPY and the plain index sit beside every table that compares the fund-selection methods. The long histories of chapters 10 to 12 and 27 reach back before either benchmark existed; each of those four chapters says how it handles that.

The long histories were checked against the study's own retirements over the years both cover: chapter 10 sets its mixes beside SPY and the plain index, and chapter 12 compares its daily fixed 70/30 with the plain index.

Every figure taken from the results, the price records or the archived filings is computed when the book is assembled, and assembly stops if a sentence no longer matches the data. The other figures are the study's own settings (chapter 1) or dates and terms typed from the filings and research notes listed in appendix C, each with its source recorded. Independent reviews have recomputed the book's figures (chapter 26).

Not every test was declared in full before it was run. A group of earlier tests changed the holding method without declaring it; they were repeated with re-ranking every January, and every test from that repeat onwards was declared in full before it was launched. The earliest of the group were not repeated on their own: they differ from a repeated test only by its closure rule, and once funds are re-ranked every January that rule changes no holding, because a closed fund cannot rank among the open ones. Each test's method and results are recorded, so the exact method behind every result can be recovered; appendix B lists every test.

With the menu, the prices, the rule, the measures and the checks set out, the results can be read. The floor and the median ending can point opposite ways, and not the same way for every method. At 70/30 over twenty years, against the plain index, the menu each January's top two has a higher worst low point and a lower median ending (chapter 16); the top two picked once and kept (chapter 18) has a lower worst low point and a lower worst ending, but a higher median ending. Part VI therefore gives both for every method, beside SPY and the plain index, beginning with the simplest way to choose: the top funds of the first day of retirement, kept.

Part VI: Choosing funds — the results

Does choosing funds by their records do better than simply holding the plain index — at the worst moment on the way, at the end, or both?

Every retirement in this part follows the same rules:

  • Starting capital: $1,000,000, invested at the close of the first trading day of its first year.
  • Withdrawals: $40,000 at the end of that year, rising 3% a year thereafter — $1.07M over twenty years.
  • Measure of outcome: the capital remaining.
  • Amounts: nominal dollars, before taxes and trading costs.

The chapters move from the simplest way of choosing funds to the most active:

  • Picked once and kept (chapter 18) — the top funds chosen on the first day and kept, a fund being replaced only if it merges away.
  • The list frozen at retirement (chapter 19) — the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement (for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994), frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January; also the list reviewed every 3 or 5 years.
  • The menu each January (chapter 20) — everything Vanguard offers, re-ranked each January; the principal method.
  • The 1999 list (chapter 21), which serves only as a comparison.

Chapters 22 to 24 then test rebalancing more often than once a year, follow five individual retirees, and ask how long the money lasts.

Chapters 18 and 19 also ask the question of chapter 9 for the chosen funds: should the mix be restored every year?

Each chapter presents the principal result and its charts. The detailed tables are in appendix G.

Counts of retirements "ahead of the plain index" turn, in a few cases, on margins under 1% of the plain index's ending balance. With 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, 2003 is such a near-tie for 15 of the 45 methods reported in this part and appendix G (each number of funds, each way of restoring the mix and each closure rule counted separately), and 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998 or 1999 for a few others. At the other splits the near-ties fall mostly in other years: with 60% in stock funds and 40% in bond funds, 1997 for eight of the 33 methods reported; with 50% in each, only 1996 and 1998.

A count alone is therefore not a meaningful difference when it moves by one or two between methods. What matters is the margin behind each retirement that changes sides.

Chapter 18. Picked once and kept

The simplest approach of all is to choose once and keep the choice. Can the funds picked on the first day of retirement simply be held for twenty years?

A result that depends heavily on luck. The method in this chapter produced the deepest worst low point and the lowest worst ending among the 70/30 portfolios, and also the highest median of any method in the study apart from two variants of itself (only the stock / bond split restored, $2.87M; a closed fund topped up without limit, $2.84M). All three come from a handful of decisions made once, on the first day of retirement. Whether those first picks happened to include a fund that would outperform for the next twenty years was not knowable from the ranking; the same rule, applied at the start of 2000, chose the two that fared worst over the twenty years that followed, of the 13 stock funds that could be picked that January (with nothing withdrawn: U.S. Growth 1.94 times its starting value, Growth Index 2.97 times; the other 11 between 3.15 and 5.26 times). The retiree of 1999 had chosen the same two, again the worst two of the 12 that could be picked that January. The figures below describe what happened to twelve retirements, not what the method can be expected to deliver.

The rule

On the first day of retirement the retiree buys the two (in a second version, four) highest-ranked stock funds and bond funds on that January's ranking. The retiree keeps them for the whole retirement, restoring the 70/30 allocation each January.

Two events can change a holding:

  • A fund closes to new investors: it is kept, since a closure stops new accounts and an existing shareholder is never required to sell.
  • A fund merges away: it is replaced by the fund it merged into, or, if that fund is already held, by the highest-ranked fund of the same type on that January's menu.

In practice only one merger touched a holding: Morgan Growth, merged into U.S. Growth on 5 April 2019, in the 2000 and 2001 retirements holding the top four. The merger was announced on 17 December 2018, so the replacement at the January 2019 ranking used only what a retiree could have known. No fund picked was liquidated.

Morgan Growth's prices are known only as calendar-year returns, so its moves inside a year are smoothed. For the top-four retirement that began in 2000 (70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds), this hides part of the fall from its high in September 2000 to the 2009 low: chapter 16 estimates its lowest value at $414k to $421k rather than $443k, and its biggest fall at 61.0% to 62.1% rather than 58.0%, which would make it the worst fall of the top four (estimates, not simulated results). The 2001 top-four retirement's low on 9 March 2009 is affected in the same direction (its 2007 high has not been examined); that effect has not been measured.

Buying more of a closed fund

Keeping a closed fund raises a second question. Restoring the allocation each January means buying more of any fund that lagged the rest of the portfolio in the year just ended. Whether an existing shareholder could still buy depended on the terms of each closure.

Vanguard's closure notices, filed with the SEC, set those terms out. The closures that affect these retirements:

  • PRIMECAP: 1995-1996, 1998-2001 and 2004-2024.
  • Capital Opportunity: March 2004 to April 2013, and again from December 2013 (still closed).
  • Explorer: 2006-2008.

For these closures an existing shareholder could add up to $25,000 a year. Reinvested dividends were exempt from the limit wherever a notice addresses them.

Dividend Growth (2016-2019), which some of the re-ranking retirements below keep, stayed open to existing shareholders without limit. Selling was never restricted.

The method is therefore measured three ways:

  • Limited: the January purchase of a closed fund limited to $25,000 a year, as the notices provided. This is the version shown first.
  • Unlimited: without any limit.
  • None: with no purchase at all.

Whatever a closed fund cannot take goes to the open funds of the same kind — stock or bond — in proportion to their targets. When every stock fund held is closed, there is no open stock fund to take it: what cannot be bought stays in the bond funds, and the split is not fully restored that January. That needs both conditions at once — every stock fund closed, and one of them below its target by more than the $25,000 it may still take:

  • The 2002 retiree, holding PRIMECAP and Capital Opportunity: both were closed in every January from 2005, 17 in all, but money stayed in the bond funds only in January 2009 and 2012. With no purchases at all it would have stayed there in eight Januaries.
  • The 1995 retiree, holding PRIMECAP and Explorer: both were closed in January 2007 and 2008, and money stayed in the bond funds only in January 2008.

Twelve retirements

Nearly the highest median of any method (only two variants of itself end higher) — but how low did it go on the way? Over the twelve completed retirements, against the plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January), the top two picked once had:

  • Worst low point: $352k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $492k (9 yr 2 mo in) for the plain index — lower.
  • Median low point: $753k, against $674k — higher.
  • Worst ending: $408k, against $835k.
  • Median ending: $2.83M, against $2.10M.

The high median came with the deepest floor. Holding two stock funds for twenty years is a concentrated position, and its outcomes are correspondingly wide.

What the closure terms change

The closure terms make little difference, and none at the floor:

  • Worst low point: $352k (9 yr 2 mo in) under all three — the $25,000 limit, no limit, and no purchases at all.
  • Median low point: between $752k and $753k.
  • Worst ending: $408k under all three.
  • Median ending: $2.83M under the limit; without any limit on buying a closed fund it would have been $2.84M, and with no purchases at all $2.82M.
  • In 7 of 12 retirements the three versions end within $10,000 of one another.

The largest effect is on the 2002 retirement, which bought Capital Opportunity and PRIMECAP two years before both closed:

The six retirements that began with PRIMECAP or Capital Opportunity — two funds managed by the same firm and closed to new investors for most of 2004-2024:

  • all ended with $2.78M or more (the column for the top two picked once, a closed fund topped up by at most $25,000 a year; the lowest is the 1998 retirement's $2,786,850, printed there as $2.79M);
  • five of them are among the six largest outcomes. The sixth is the 1996 retirement, which began with Explorer and Small-Cap Index.

A retiree who already held PRIMECAP or Capital Opportunity kept them through those closures and through two decades of strong performance.

In the other six retirements:

  • Median: $1.83M for the method, against $1.78M for the plain index over the same start years.
  • Ahead of the plain index: in only two of the six.
  • SPY: a median over the same six of $1.84M, about the same as the method's.

The bond funds picked on the first day also contributed. In 11 of the 12 retirements at least one of the two was Long-Term Treasury or Long-Term Investment-Grade (both, in 7), held for twenty years, most of them years of falling interest rates. With nothing withdrawn and the two restored to equal shares each January, the bond part grew more than Total Bond Market in all 12 retirements: for the 1995 retiree 5.03 times its starting value against 3.25, for the 2000 retiree 4.31 against 2.61. In the 11 retirements holding a long-term fund, that was a bet on long-duration bonds while rates fell; chapter 20 shows how it reversed in 2022.

The 2000 retirement began with Growth Index and U.S. Growth, the leaders of the late-1990s advance, bought at the top of the technology market. It ended with $408k.

Two further qualifications

First, this comparison changes two things at once. The re-ranking methods of chapters 19 to 21 sell a fund the January after it closes. This method keeps it and never re-ranks.

The two can be separated. Allowed to keep a closed fund for as long as it still ranks among the top two (with the same $25,000 limit on buying it), the results become:

With the top four of each type, keeping closed funds matters more, though not at the floor. At every split it leaves the worst low point and the worst ending unchanged, and it never lowers the median low point. With 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds it raises the median low point — from $718k to $724k on the menu each January, from $704k to $713k on the list frozen at retirement — and leaves the median ending unchanged; at 60/40 it raises the median ending by up to $20k, and at 50/50 by up to $68k (appendix G.11).   • On the list frozen at retirement: from 8 of 12 to 9 of 12.

  • Top four, list frozen at retirement, closed funds sold: 1996 ($13,590 ahead).
  • Top four, list frozen at retirement, closed funds kept: none.

Second, the selection rule itself — five- and ten-year records, the number of funds — was settled after earlier versions of the study had been examined. The twelve retirements also overlap heavily in time.

Picking once had the deepest worst low point and, apart from two variants of itself, the highest median of any method. Chapter 19 repeats the same ranking each January, within a list fixed on the first day of retirement, and follows what that does to the floor and to the median.

Chapter 19. The list frozen at retirement

The method of chapter 18 tied each retirement to its first choices. A middle course fixes the list of funds on the first day of retirement but re-ranks within it each January, so a fund that falls behind is replaced. Does freezing the list, instead of rebuilding it from the whole menu each January, change the outcome?

The principal method of the study, set out in full in chapter 20, is the menu each January: every January the retiree re-ranks all the funds Vanguard offers that day and holds the top two stock funds and the top two bond funds.

Against it, reviewing the list at intervals changes little, and where it moves the floor it lowers it. Retaining the list without review held less at its worst moment — less even than the plain index — but ended higher than the menu each January, at the median and in the worst ending. Is that a better result? The answer depends on which measure comes first.

How the list is compiled

An alternative to the menu each January is to compile the list once, at retirement, from the menu of that day — for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994. The list is then either retained or reviewed at intervals.

Within the list the funds are still re-ranked each January and the top two of each type held.

The list frozen at retirement is the list retained: the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement, frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January.

Reviewing every three or five years

Reviewing the list every three or five years held up no better than the menu each January at the worst moment, and in places worse:

  • Worst low point: every three years $515k, the same as the menu's; every five years $506k, against $515k (each 9 yr 2 mo in).
  • Median low point: every three years $748k, against the menu's $755k; every five years $755k, the same.
  • Worst ending: every three years $692k, the same as the menu's; every five years $660k, against $692k.
  • Median ending: $1.78M for all three.

Retirement by retirement, in every complete retirement but one, both reviews end the same as the menu each January or slightly lower:

  • Every three years: six of the 12 retirements end lower, by up to $67k; six end the same; none ends higher.
  • Every five years: eight end lower, by up to $58k; three end the same; one ends higher (2003, by $1,530).
  • Ahead of the plain index: the list reviewed every 5 years in 3 of 12, against 2 of 12 for the menu each January and for the list reviewed every 3 years.

The whole difference in that count is the 2003 retirement, which is a near-tie: all three end within about $2,000 of the plain index's $2.32M (every 5 years $1,170 ahead of it, the other two $360 behind it).

With a review every three years the whole difference comes from one fund. A new fund normally cannot be picked until it has five years of history. By then, a list reviewed at least every five years already contains it.

Mid-Cap Growth broke that pattern. It joined the menu in mid-2002 carrying the five-year record of its predecessor, and was among the top two in January 2003:

  • The 2003-2006 retirees compiled their lists after it joined, so it was on them from the start.
  • The 1997 and 2000 retirees had a three-yearly review that January and picked it up.
  • The 1995, 1996, 1998, 1999, 2001 and 2002 retirees picked it up only at a later review. These are the six that end lower with a review every three years.

With a review every five years, two further funds contribute besides Mid-Cap Growth: the Long-Term Treasury Index and Long-Term Corporate Bond Index funds, which the menu each January held in 2016 and 2017 and which some five-yearly lists did not yet contain. They account for the one retirement that ends higher, and for the 1998 retirement ending $400 lower.

Keeping the original list

Retaining the original list without review gives a different result: lower on the way, higher at the end. In March 2009 it fell further than the menu each January:

  • Worst low point: $476k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $515k (9 yr 2 mo in) for the menu each January and $492k (9 yr 2 mo in) for the plain index — below both.
  • Median low point: $721k, against $755k for the menu each January (the plain index's: $674k).
  • Worst ending: $943k, against $692k. With everything restored once a year, each January, no top-two method available to a 1995 retiree has a higher worst ending.
  • Median ending: $2.07M, against $1.78M.
  • Ahead of the plain index: in 7 of 12, one of them by under 1%: 1998 ($13,750 ahead).

It leaves out every fund added to the menu after the retirement began:

  • Some weighed on the menu each January, Dividend Growth above all (chapter 20).
  • Some helped, such as Mid-Cap Growth: the lists reviewed every 3 years that picked it up late ended up to $67k lower than the menu (above).

On balance the exclusions helped the endings and cost the floor.

Against the plain index, in each split's own proportions, the comparison depends on the split (appendix G.6):

  • With 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds: worst low point $476k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $492k (9 yr 2 mo in); median low point $721k, against $674k; median ending $2.07M, against $2.10M (1.1% below).
  • With 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds: worst low point $578k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $573k (9 yr 2 mo in); median low point $791k, against $721k; median ending $1.96M, against $1.91M (2.4% above).
  • With 50% in each: worst low point $691k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $662k (9 yr 2 mo in); median low point $847k, against $771k; median ending $1.71M, against $1.63M (4.8% above).

Only at 70/30 does the list fall below the plain index at its worst moment, and only there does it end lower at the median.
