Against the menu each January, then, the frozen list gave up some of the floor for a higher ending. Chapter 20 turns to the menu itself, the study's principal method, and sets it beside the plain index at its worst moment as well as at the end.

Chapter 20. The menu each January

Does re-picking the best-ranked Vanguard funds every January do better than simply holding the plain index? The method has been available to any retiree since 1995, and it is the principal result of the study. Which held up better in March 2009, the menu or the plain index — and which ended with more? The lowest-value and ending columns of the table below answer both, and they point in opposite directions.

How the menu is built

Each January the retiree:

  • reviews the funds Vanguard offers that day;
  • retains those with at least five years of history;
  • ranks them on their five- and ten-year records;
  • holds the two highest-ranked stock funds and the two highest-ranked bond funds.

The process is repeated every year. No information unavailable at the time is used, as far as the filings allow, with one exception: a fund that later merged or was liquidated leaves the menu at the year end before the event (chapter 16). Apart from that, every fund selected was open to investors on the date of selection. For the 1990s the closures come from the filings read for three funds (Windsor, PRIMECAP and Trustees' Equity), from Vanguard's family-wide notices — with none found for October 1996 to April 1998 — and from each other fund's late-1998 or early-1999 prospectus, the longer ones read only in part; a missed closure of another fund cannot be ruled out (chapter 13, appendix G.2).

The method needs no list fixed at any date. It applies identically to every start year from 1995.

The result

Across the 12 retirements that have completed twenty years (1995 to 2006), with 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, against the plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January):

  • Worst low point: $515k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $492k (9 yr 2 mo in) for the plain index — higher.
  • Median low point: $755k, against $674k — higher.
  • Worst ending: $692k, against $835k — lower.
  • Median ending: $1.78M, against $2.10M — lower: the cost.
  • Ahead of the plain index at the end: in only 2 of 12. The 2003 retirement is a near-tie: $360 behind the plain index's $2.32M.

With 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, holding the top three or top four of each type instead of the top two moves the worst low point little, and in both directions — down to $503k with the top three, up to $528k with the top four, against $515k (all three 9 yr 2 mo in) — and lowers the median low point, to $709k and $718k against $755k. What it improves is the worst ending: $789k and $931k, against $692k. The median ending barely moves ($1.77M and $1.80M, against $1.78M). The top four also finish ahead of the plain index more often: in 7 of 12, against 2 of 12 with the top three and 2 of 12 with the top two. Some of the top four's retirements end within 1% of the plain index's ending (Part VI's opening): 1995 ($17,590 ahead), 1996 ($16,400 behind) and 2003 ($1,310 ahead). With 50% in stocks and 50% in bonds the worst low point does not move both ways: the top three and the top four both lower it, to $699k (3 yr 2 mo in), against $725k (9 yr 2 mo in) with the top two (the low-point table below).

The top four's worst low point, at every split, is the 2000 retirement's, which held Morgan Growth; its smoothed prices make that low look higher than it was (chapter 16), so the true figures are lower still and the verdicts are unchanged.

This is the low point along the way, not the balance at the end. The low point is what a retiree has to sit through without selling. The ending is a separate measure: the top two's worst ending, $692k, is below the plain index's $835k.

The edge came from the bond funds, not the stock funds. Taking the 2000 retiree's top two apart, without withdrawals, from the start to 9 March 2009:

  • Stock funds selected: each dollar was worth 53.6 cents, against 54.5 cents in the 500 Index fund.
  • Bond funds selected: each dollar was worth 184.1 cents, against 169.7 cents in Total Bond Market.

The ranking mostly favoured long-term Treasury and corporate bond funds, which gained as interest rates fell. At least one of the two bond funds held was long-term in nine of the ten Januaries from 2000 to 2009; the rest of the bond picks were GNMA, intermediate-term and inflation-protected funds. That is a bet on long-duration bonds, and it cuts both ways: in 2022 the menu's two bond funds, Long-Term Corporate Bond Index and Long-Term Investment-Grade, lost 25.8% and 25.5%, against 13.2% for Total Bond Market. The same allocation is not the same risk.

Over those same seven the plain index's median low point was $645k, $700k and $755k at 70/30, 60/40 and 50/50 (SPY's $500k): both 1999-list rows are below it at 70/30 and above it at the other two splits. The worst low points compare like with like as they stand: the plain index's is a 2000-2006 retirement's at every split.

Where the shortfall comes from

If the menu held up better at the worst moment, why did it end lower? Part of the shortfall comes from the funds the menu each January admits after 1999. The 1999 list never admits them. Set against it, the menu's top two with 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds trail by:

  • 27.7 percentage points of return in total from 2000, year by year from each January's purchase (first close to first close).
  • 22.2 of those points from the five years in which Dividend Growth, in scope only from the end of 2002, was among the top two (appendix G.5).

The ranking rewards a strong five-year record. A fund can reach the top on such a record close to its peak relative performance.

The funds the menu added after 1999, every January's holdings, the results at every stock / bond split and over 25 years, and the retirement-by-retirement table are in appendix G.5.

The menu each January admitted every fund Vanguard added; a list fixed at the end of 1999 admitted none of them. Chapter 21 applies that list to the retirees of 2000-2006, and explains why no one could have chosen it in advance.

Chapter 21. The 1999 list, from 2000

What if every retiree from 2000 onwards had used one list, Vanguard's menu at the end of 1999? Applied from 2000, the 1999 list ended ahead of the plain index in every one of its seven retirements. Was it the safer choice as well? At its worst moment it held less. This chapter sets out both, and explains why the list is presented only as a comparison.

The list

The 1999 list is a single list: Vanguard's menu at 31 December 1999, retained throughout and re-ranked within itself each January.

Only retirements beginning in 2000 or later could have used it. For earlier retirements it contains funds added to the menu after the retirement began. It therefore covers only 7 complete retirements, 2000 to 2006.

For the 2000 retiree it is identical to the list frozen at retirement, and produces exactly the same result.

The record

Over those seven retirements, with 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, against the plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January) over the same seven:

  • Worst low point: $476k (9 yr 2 mo in), against $492k (9 yr 2 mo in) — lower.
  • Median low point: $634k, against $645k — lower.
  • Worst ending: $943k, against $835k — higher.
  • Median ending: $2.54M, against $2.13M — higher.
  • Ahead of the plain index at the end: in 7 of 7.

The endings favour the list; the floor favours the plain index.

Against SPY the order reverses. The floor is far higher — a worst low point of $476k (9 yr 2 mo in) against SPY's $290k (9 yr 2 mo in), a median low point of $634k against $500k — and so is the worst ending, $943k against $385k. But the median ending, $2.54M, is below SPY's $2.96M, and the list ended ahead of SPY in only 3 of the seven retirements.

The table below also gives the list frozen at each retirement and the menu each January over the same seven retirements. Which of its columns favours the 1999 list over those two, and which favours them over it?

Column by column, the floor — the worst and median low points and the biggest fall — favours the menu each January on all three, and the frozen list on the median low point only. Both lead the 1999 list on the median low point. The menu each January also leads it on the worst low point ($515k, against the 1999 list's $476k) and on the biggest fall (53%, against 57%); the frozen list ties it on both, the two figures being the 2000 retiree's, who holds the same list under either name. The endings favour the 1999 list: its worst ending, $943k, is the frozen list's too and above the menu's $692k, and it leads both on the median ending and on the count ahead of the plain index — 7 of 7, against 4 of 7 for the frozen list and 2 of 7 for the menu.

Why it is only a comparison

The endings, however, reflect a single and favourable date. The menu at the end of 1999 contained:

  • the funds added to the menu in 1995-98 that subsequently performed well;
  • none of the later additions, such as Dividend Growth, that weighed on the menu each January.

Over the same seven retirements, the same rule applied to the list frozen at each retirement (chapter 19) and to the menu each January ended lower at the median than the 1999 list's $2.54M, despite their higher median low points: the frozen list $1.94M, the menu lower still, $1.76M.

The 1999 list is therefore presented as a comparison, not as a choice a retiree could have made in advance.

The 1999 list's funds, its holdings year by year and all its tables are in appendix G.7.

Every method so far restores its weights once a year, each January. Is once a year often enough? Chapter 22 tries every 6 and every 3 months.

Chapter 22. Rebalancing every 6 or every 3 months

Would resetting the weights more often than once a year cushion the worst moment? In the table below it did the opposite: for all four methods (the 1999 list over 2000-2006), every 6 and every 3 months lowered both the worst and the median low point — the plain index's worst low point from $492k to $482k and $485k (each 9 yr 2 mo in), its median low point from $674k to $668k and $664k. The worst ending fell every 6 months for all four and moved by under 1% every 3 months.

The median ending moves little, but in a consistent direction. With the top two and 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, against once a year, every 3 months ended higher in most complete retirements — 8 of 12 for the plain index, 10 of 12 for the top two from the menu each January, 11 of 12 for the list frozen at retirement and 7 of 7 for the 1999 list — and every 6 months ended lower in 12 of 12, 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 6 of 7.

With three or four funds of each type, and at 60/40 and 50/50, every 3 months still ended higher in most complete retirements (in at least 9 of 12). Every 6 months did not always end lower: with the top four, in as few as 8 of 12, and on the 1999 list with the top three or four in only 3 to 4 of 7 (appendix G.8).

Elsewhere the portfolio is restored to its target weights once a year, in January. Rebalancing every 6 or every 3 months keeps the weights closer to target but sells more of whatever has been rising. A fund that closes during a year is kept until the next January, and the resets every 6 or 3 months top it up in full, without the purchase limit that the closure notices set (chapter 18).

With the same funds held, the largest move of a median ending in the table below from once a year is 2.84%: the 1999 list's median every 3 months, $2,616,110 against $2,543,830 once a year ($2.62M and $2.54M in the table). The next largest is 2.77%: the list frozen at retirement's median every 3 months, $2,130,960 against $2,073,610 ($2.13M and $2.07M in the table). Every other median ending moves less. The 1999 list covers only the retirements of 2000-2006, so SPY and the plain index are shown over those seven as well, directly above it:

Year by year

Because these medians share the same calendar years, the appropriate comparison is year by year. Is the difference a steady one, or the work of a few years?

Each year's figure is the calendar-year return of that year's holdings, without withdrawals: from the last close of the previous year to the last close of the year, one trading day before the simulations buy at the first close of January. Both sides are measured the same way; only the rebalancing dates differ.

For the plain index:

  • Every 6 months: outperformed annual rebalancing in only 9 of 31 calendar years (-3.19 points in total) — a small, consistent cost.
  • Every 3 months: outperformed in 14 years and was approximately neutral in total (+0.17 points). Three V-shaped years, 2020, 1998, 2011, gained 3.52 points, more than the whole net; the other 28 years together lost 3.35. Its worst year was 2008 (-1.39).

The pattern is the same for the top two from the menu each January:

  • Every 6 months: outperformed in 12 of 31 years (-4.24 points).
  • Every 3 months: outperformed in 18 years (+0.26 points).

Retirement by retirement (twenty years, or to date for the later ones), the picture is less even than the yearly sums suggest:

  • Every 3 months ended higher than once a year in 8 of 12 complete retirements for the plain index, and in 10 of 12 for the top two from the menu each January. Counting every start to date: 23 of 31 and 22 of 31.
  • Every 6 months ended lower in 12 of 12 complete retirements for the plain index, and in 12 of 12 for the top two. Counting every start to date: 31 of 31 and 30 of 31.

The yearly sums weight every calendar year equally; each retirement covers only its own twenty years and pays its withdrawals along the way, so the two measures can disagree.

Transaction costs and taxes, which would rise with each additional rebalance, are not included.

Every split, both horizons and the year-by-year tables are in appendix G.8.

Medians and floors summarise many retirements at once. What did the same methods look like to one retiree, year by year — above all to the one who retired in January 2000, at the top of the technology market? Chapter 23 follows five retirees.

Chapter 23. Five retirees

How did the methods compare for one retiree at a time, through the declines of 2000-02 and 2008? Summary statistics conceal the experience of individual retirements. This chapter follows five of them, from the first day to 9 October 2026:

  • Start: $1M, invested at the close of the first trading day of 1995, 2000, 2006, 2007 or 2008.
  • Allocation: 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds.

The 1995 portfolios never fell below the $1M they started with: their lowest value is the first day's. For the retirees of 2006, 2007 and 2008 the answer is yes: SPY, all stocks, ended with the most and fell the lowest. For the retiree of 2000 the answer is no: SPY fell the lowest and ended with the least, and its low, $191k, came not in 2009 but on 30 March 2026, 26 yr 2 mo in. Among this retiree's portfolios holding bonds, though, the answer is yes again: the list frozen at retirement (for this retiree the same list as the 1999 list) ended with the most, $1.29M, and fell the lowest, to $476k, against $492k for the plain index and $515k for the menu each January. That does not hold for every retiree: among the 2007 retiree's portfolios holding bonds, the plain index ended with the most, $2.48M, and fell the least, to $600k (2 yr 2 mo in).

Retiring in 1995

The most favourable start in the study. Every portfolio benefited from the late-1990s advance before meeting the 2000-02 decline with a substantial margin.

The 2008 crash still cut the top two from the menu each January by 45% from its peak in June 2007. The gains of the 1990s absorbed it: after twenty years of withdrawals that portfolio held more than three times its initial value.

Retiring in 2000

The most difficult start for every portfolio:

  • Timing of the ranking: the ranking at the end of 1999 placed the growth funds that had led the advance at the top immediately before the 2000-02 decline.
  • A second decline: the 2008 decline arrived before the portfolio had recovered.

For this retiree, the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list are the same list, so their lines coincide in figure 23.2.

Neither the menu each January nor SPY had regained its 2000 peak by 9 October 2026. The plain index regained it about 21 years after that peak (256 months), and the list frozen at retirement about 20 years after it (238 months).

Retiring in 2006, 2007 and 2008

Three retirements that met the 2008 decline early.

The 2008 retirement holding the top two from the menu fell to $596k by March 2009, 41% below the peak. Yet, like the other 2006-2008 portfolios holding bonds, it recovered and continued to meet its withdrawals.

What each of them held every year, what was left at each year end, and the 2000 retiree's ranking in detail are in appendix G.9.

The retiree of 2000 has by now withdrawn more than the $1M with which the retirement began. How long can that continue, and from which portfolio? Chapter 24 follows that retiree.

Chapter 24. Money taken out, and how long it lasts

How long does the money last once the withdrawals have exceeded the starting capital? This chapter follows the retiree of 2000 to find out. Every portfolio in it holds 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds — the menu each January and the list frozen at retirement with the top two funds of each type, the plain index as 70% in the 500 Index and 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January — except SPY, which is all stocks.

What has been taken, and what is left

A retiree following this rule withdraws $1.07M over twenty years — more than the initial capital. By the end of 2025 the retiree of 2000 had withdrawn $1.54M.

Whether that can continue depends on the capital remaining. On 9 October 2026 the 2000 retiree had:

  • Menu each January: $719k.
  • List frozen at retirement (for a 2000 retiree, the same as the 1999 list): $1.29M.
  • Plain index: $1.03M.
  • SPY alone: $236k.

A simple measure is cumulative withdrawals divided by the capital remaining, shown here for 2000, every fifth year from 2004, and 2025. Which column passes 100% first, and which stands lowest in 2025?

A ratio above 100% means the portfolio has paid out more than its current value. SPY's passed 100% first, at the end of 2008; the other portfolios' ratios not until 2015 or 2016. The ratio of the list frozen at retirement then dipped back below 100% at the end of 2020 and 2021, and passed it again at the end of 2022 (Figure 24.1 shows every year). In 2025 the list frozen at retirement — for this retiree, the 1999 list — stands lowest.

How long it lasts

Because the withdrawal rises by 3% a year, a portfolio lasts indefinitely only if what is left after the 2026 withdrawal, earning a constant return, can pay every later withdrawal, each 3% larger than the one before, for ever. From the balances of 9 October 2026 (no growth in the rest of 2026, as in Figure 24.2), the lowest constant return that does so is about (70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, top two; SPY all stocks):

  • List frozen at retirement: 10% a year.
  • Plain index: 12%.
  • Menu each January: 17%.
  • SPY alone: 62%.

At any lower constant return each of the four runs out eventually. The question is when.

The next figure projects the 2000 retiree's portfolios forward from 9 October 2026 at a constant return. It is a projection, not an observation.

Every way of choosing funds in this part has led on one measure and trailed on another. Taken together, what do the results support, and what do they not? Part VII weighs them, the low point first.

Part VII: Assessment

Twenty-four chapters of figures leave two questions: what do they show when taken together, and how far can they be trusted? Part VII steps back from the individual methods: what the study's twelve retirements and the long histories of chapters 10 to 12 support, what they do not, the errors found and corrected along the way, and the seven known limitations not yet corrected.

Chapter 25. What the results show, and what they do not

The book set out to answer one question: does a retiree who holds whichever Vanguard funds have done best recently, re-selected each January, fare better than one who holds the plain index of chapter 8? The answer depends on what "better" means — the lowest point the money reached on the way, or what was left at the end — and this chapter gives the low point first, because it is the one a retiree lives through, and the median ending as its price.

Over twenty years at 70/30 with annual rebalancing, the methods that re-rank the funds and were available to a retiree from 1995 mostly held a higher worst low point than the plain index — the menu each January's top two fell to $515k at its worst, the plain index to $492k — but none of them ended above the plain index at the median. SPY fell lowest of all, to $290k, and had a higher median than any of them. Picking once and keeping fell below the plain index at its worst, to $352k, and had the highest median of all but two variants of itself; that median rests on a few early choices, not on a repeatable method. Each of those worst low points is the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in.

Over twenty-five years the medians rank differently, but only seven retirements are complete at that length, too few to settle anything (below).

Before any fund is chosen: Parts II-IV

The same $1M and the same rising withdrawal, before any fund is selected: the study's retirements begun 1995-2006 in chapters 2-9, and the long index histories, from 1872 month by month and from 1928 year by year, in chapters 10 to 12. For comparison, over the study's retirements SPY's worst low point was $290k (9 yr 2 mo in), its median low point $515k, its worst ending $385k and its median ending $2.42M; the plain index's at 70/30 (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January), in the same order, $492k (also 9 yr 2 mo in), $674k, $835k and $2.10M. The long histories begin before either benchmark existed and carry neither.

  • Cash alone ran out (chapter 2). Its median after twenty years was $189k. The ten retirements begun 1995 to 2004 and held in cash all lasted twenty years and then ran out, between year 22 and year 27.
  • Bond funds alone had not run out by 9 October 2026, though four Short-Term Treasury retirements held less than the withdrawal due at the end of 2026 (chapter 3). All but the three short-term funds held a higher floor than the plain index, and every one left less at the median (chapters 3 and 8). Total Bond Market, Long-Term Treasury and Long-Term Investment-Grade fell at worst to $545k (19 yr 11 mo in), $743k (19 yr 11 mo in) and $830k (2 yr 9 mo in), against $492k (9 yr 2 mo in). The first two of those lows are not a crash but the end of the retirement: they are the twenty-year endings of the retirements begun in 2005 and 2006, still falling under the withdrawals, while the plain index's came in March 2009. Their median low points were $899k, $947k and $925k, against $674k; their worst endings $545k, $743k and $1.03M, against $835k. The price was the median ending: $906k, $1.77M and $1.78M, against $2.10M. In the plain index's worst start years the long-term funds also ended higher: Long-Term Treasury ended above it for the retirements of 1998-2001, Long-Term Investment-Grade for 1998-2002. For the 2000 retiree 6 of the 9 bond funds did, every one except the three short-term funds, Total Bond Market among them ($1.08M against $835k; chapter 8). That was a period of falling interest rates.
  • The S&P 500 over 1928-2025 (chapters 5 and 6), dividends reinvested, nothing withdrawn, before inflation, lost money over 5 of 89 ten-year periods, in two episodes (periods starting 1928-1930 and 1999-2000), and over none of its 79 twenty-year periods.
  • A 70/30 mix gave up the best outcomes to avoid the worst (chapter 7). Its worst ten-year period earned +1.1% a year, against -1.7% for the S&P 500 alone; over thirty years its worst (+7.0%) trailed the S&P 500's worst (+8.0%). In the retirements (chapter 8) the plain index held a higher floor than SPY at both the worst and the median low point, and a higher worst ending (the figures above); its price was a lower median ending.
  • Letting the split drift (chapter 9) raised the plain index's worst low point at 70/30 ($544k against $492k, both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), while its median low point barely moved ($681k against $674k); its worst ending fell ($762k against $835k), and so did its median ($2.05M against $2.10M). At 50/50 the drifting mix also held the higher worst low point ($727k against $662k, again both 9 yr 2 mo in) and median low point ($778k against $771k), with a lower worst ending ($866k against $991k), but it ended higher at the median ($1.73M against $1.63M).
  • A century of retirements (chapters 10 and 11): the same rule on the long index histories, with no fund selection — 79 twenty-year retirements begun 1928-2006 in the yearly data, with no fees and a 10-year Treasury as the bond. At 70/30 the 1929 retirement ran out in its last year in the yearly data; month by month it ended with $145k. Bonds alone and cash alone ran out in long retirements: under the 3% rule the 10-year Treasury held alone ran out in 21 of 74 twenty-five-year retirements and 32 of 69 thirty-year ones, and cash alone in 8 of 79 twenty-year ones. With withdrawals rising with inflation, the hardest thirty-year retirements began in 1965 and 1966, and there more in bonds made the worst outcome worse; over forty and fifty years, from 70/30 to 60/40 to 50/50, more in bonds never meant fewer retirements running out. Over the study's 12 retirements the long-history 70/30 ended 2.3% to 16.1% above the plain index, in every one, so these mixes flatter.
  • A moving split (chapter 12): a walk-forward rule that moves to 20/80 when the S&P 500 falls 20% or more below its high, and holds it until a January check finds the index less than 20% below. With withdrawals rising 3% a year, over the study's 12 retirements the rule's worst low point was $755k, against the plain index's $492k (both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in); its median low point $905k against $674k; its worst ending $1.09M against $835k. The price was a lower median ending, $1.81M against $2.10M. On the two index funds over the retirements begun 1987-2006, its worst low point, $755k (the 2000 retirement, March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), was the highest of every portfolio, with a median of $2.50M (fixed 70/30: $2.42M). Over the retirements begun from 1872 month by month, its median ending was close to a fixed 50/50's over twenty and twenty-five years, but with withdrawals rising with inflation its worst twenty-year low point, $232k (the retirement of 1903, 19 yr 11 mo in), was below every fixed mix's. Over long retirements it ran out more often than the fixed splits: over thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation in 8 of 122, more than every fixed split, and over forty years under the 3% rule in 24 of 112, against 7 to 16 for the fixed mixes.

The medians are below the plain index in 8 of the nine cells; where they are not, the menu is at most $3k above.

Where the count is high, the wins and the losses are each concentrated in a few start years. With the top four at 70/30, against the plain index:

  • the two largest wins: +$525k (2001) and +$543k (2002);
  • the three losses that matter: -$313k (2004), -$576k (2005) and -$772k (2006);
  • the other seven start years: between -$33k and +$95k.

Twelve overlapping retirements cannot settle which measure a retiree should prefer.

Over twenty years the methods that re-rank the funds, among those available to a retiree from 1995, mostly held a higher floor than the plain index, but none outperformed it at the median at 70/30 (70% in stocks, 30% in bonds) with annual rebalancing; the floor is taken up below, under "At the worst moment". At the median the list frozen at retirement edges ahead only with more bonds or with rebalancing every 3 months:

  • At 60/40 with the top two ($1.96M against $1.91M), but not with the top three ($1.84M) or four ($1.82M).
  • At 50/50 with all three: $1.71M, $1.74M and $1.72M, against $1.63M (appendix G.6).
  • At 70/30 rebalanced every 3 months (chapter 22), with the top two: $2.13M against the plain index's $2.11M on the same schedule, though on that schedule its worst low point, $465k, stayed below the plain index's $485k (both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in). The menu each January stays below, at $1.79M. Rebalanced every 6 months, the list frozen at retirement stays below too: $2.04M against $2.06M.

At 70/30 with annual rebalancing, over twenty years, by method:

  • The highest-ranked funds from the menu each January held a higher worst low point than the plain index ($515k against $492k, both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in) and a higher median low point ($755k against $674k), but a lower worst ending ($692k against $835k) and a lower median ($1.78M against $2.10M). They finished ahead of it in only 2 of 12 retirements.
  • A list reviewed every three or five years reached the same worst low point as the menu each January when reviewed every three years, and a slightly lower one, $506k (also March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), every five. It gave the same median (chapter 19) and ended the same or slightly lower in every complete retirement but one:
    • every three years: lower in 6, the same in 6, higher in none;
    • every five years: lower in 8, the same in 3, higher in 1 — the 2003 retiree, by $1,530. That is enough to put it ahead of the plain index in 3 of 12 retirements, against 2 of 12 for the yearly review.

Of the re-ranking methods available to a retiree from 1995, the list frozen at retirement with the top two fell lowest at its worst, and came closest to the plain index at the median, over twenty years.

  • Its worst low point, $476k, was below the plain index's $492k (both the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in) and below the other top-two methods'.
  • With everything restored once a year, each January, it had the highest worst ending of the top-two methods available to a 1995 retiree, $943k (tied with the 1999 list, whose worst retirement, 2000, is the same).
  • It finished ahead of the plain index in 7 of 12 retirements, but its median remains below the plain index's.

Its edge at the median lies in what it excludes: funds added to the menu after the retirement began. Several of those reached the top of the ranking shortly before a period of underperformance.

Over the same twenty-year retirements SPY fell lowest and ended lowest — the lowest worst low point ($290k, 9 yr 2 mo in) and the lowest worst ending of every portfolio holding stocks compared — the price of a higher median than any re-ranking method. Only portfolios without stocks did worse on both counts: cash and Short-Term Treasury held alone fell lower and ended lower at their worst (chapters 2 and 3).

  • The 2000 retirement ended with $385k. Its balance fell 72.6%, withdrawals included, from 24 March 2000 to 9 March 2009; over the same dates the fund itself, with nothing withdrawn, fell 48.5%.
  • The market's own deepest fall within these retirements was 55.2%, over a shorter interval: from 9 October 2007 to 9 March 2009.
  • None of the 70/30 portfolios declined as far, and none exhausted its capital.

The 1999 list fell lower than the plain index at its worst, yet ended ahead of it in 7 of 7 retirements, and its record reflects a single date. Over the same seven retirements its worst low point was $476k, against the plain index's $492k (both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), and its median low point $634k against $645k; its worst ending was higher, $943k against $835k, and so was its median, $2.54M against $2.13M: here the floor and the endings point opposite ways. It ended ahead of SPY in only 3 of 7. It is one list, compiled at an unusually favourable moment, and it was not available to any retirement that began before 2000.

With the top two at 70/30, rebalancing every 6 or every 3 months lowered both the worst and the median low point of every method. Every 6 months also ended lower than once a year in almost every retirement; every 3 months ended slightly higher in most, the exceptions falling mainly in the weakest start years (chapter 22). Over the complete twenty-year retirements, top two at 70/30, once a year, every 6 months and every 3 months:

  • the worst low point (each the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in): the plain index $492k, $482k and $485k, the menu each January $515k, $502k and $503k, the list frozen at retirement $476k, $465k and $465k and the 1999 list $476k, $465k and $465k;
  • the median low point, in the same order: $674k, $668k and $664k; $755k, $742k and $746k; $721k, $705k and $712k; and $634k, $629k and $627k (over the 1999 list's seven retirements);
  • every 6 months ended lower in 12 of 12 for the plain index, 12 of 12 for the menu each January, 12 of 12 for the list frozen at retirement and 6 of 7 for the 1999 list;
  • every 3 months ended higher in 8 of 12, 10 of 12, 11 of 12 and 7 of 7 respectively, by up to 4.5%;
  • where every 3 months ended lower, by up to 1.8%, five of the seven cases are the retirements of 1999 and 2000, the two weakest start years.

With the top two, every 6 months also ended lower in almost every retirement at 60/40 and 50/50. With more funds it is less consistent. At 70/30 with the top three, every method but the 1999 list still ended lower in every retirement, the 1999 list in only 3 of 7 (4 of 7 with the top four); with the top four, the menu each January and the lists reviewed every three or five years ended lower in only 8 or 9 of 12. Every 3 months ended higher in most retirements at every split and number of funds.

At the worst moment the re-selected funds mostly held up better than the plain index.

  • Re-ranked from the menu each January, the top two, three or four reached a lowest value of $515k, $503k and $528k (the 2000 retirement, 9 March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in).
  • The plain index reached $492k, on the same day.
  • The same is true at 60/40 and 50/50, and for lists reviewed every three or five years (chapter 20).
  • The exceptions:
    • at 70/30 with the top two, the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list each reached $476k, below the plain index's $492k; both lows are the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in, a retirement for which the two lists are the same;
    • picking once and keeping fell below the plain index at every split (at 70/30: $352k with the top two, $443k with the top four, both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in).

The weaker endings come after that low point, not at it. Which part of the portfolio held the low point up: the stock funds or the bond funds? Each dollar the menu's top two invested at the first close of 2000 was worth, at the low of 9 March 2009:

  • in its stock funds, 53.6 cents, against 54.5 cents in the 500 Index fund — they had fallen at least as far;
  • in its bond funds, mostly long-term, 184.1 cents, against 169.7 cents in Total Bond Market.

The edge at the low came from the bond funds, and that bet on long-duration bonds reversed in 2022 (chapters 16 and 20).

Over twenty years, picking once and keeping (chapter 18) fell below the plain index at its worst moment and had the lowest worst ending of the 70/30 portfolios, against the highest median of any method, SPY included, apart from two variants of itself: only the stock / bond split restored each January ($2.87M) and a closed fund topped up without limit ($2.84M). The top two picked on the first day of retirement and held thereafter had:

  • a worst low point of $352k (9 March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), the lowest of the fund-selection methods at 70/30, against the plain index's $492k;
  • a worst ending of $408k, against $835k;
  • a median of $2.83M, against $2.10M.

The median rests on the retirements whose first picks happened to include PRIMECAP or Capital Opportunity. Those funds went on to outperform for two decades while closed to new investors. The result is evidence of how much a single early choice can matter, not of a repeatable advantage.

It does not depend on how a closed fund is treated. Under each rule for further purchases of a closed fund the worst low point and the worst ending are the same, and the medians differ by at most $16k:

picked once and kept, top two (closure terms) $3.33M / $232k; low $963k / $232k (24 yr 11 mo in); ahead in 5 of 7 $3.09M / $735k; low $965k / $457k (9 yr 2 mo in); ahead in 5 of 7 $2.82M / $1.11M; low $965k / $578k (9 yr 2 mo in); ahead in 7 of 7
  • The menu each January is above the plain index at the worst low point and at the median in all nine cells, against one of nine at the median over twenty years. Yet with the top two at 70/30 it ended ahead in only 2 of 7 retirements.
  • The list frozen at retirement, top two at 70/30, fell lower at its worst than the plain index, $476k against $492k (both in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), yet has a median of $2.54M, above both the plain index ($1.70M) and SPY ($1.80M), and a worst ending of $1.11M, against the plain index's $892k: here the floor and the median point opposite ways.
  • Picking once and keeping, top two at 70/30, now has the lowest worst low point of the portfolios holding stocks, $232k against SPY's $244k (both 24 yr 11 mo in), and the lowest worst ending, $232k against SPY's $244k — and still the highest median but for the same two variants of itself ($3.43M and $3.34M). Both low points are the 2000 retirement's twenty-five-year endings: neither balance had stopped falling, so for these two the worst low point and the worst ending are one and the same figure.

The seven retirements overlap by up to twenty-four years. This comparison cannot tell which method is better over twenty-five years; it shows only that the twenty-year ranking is not stable.

What the results do not support

  • That any method will beat, or trail, the plain index in future. Twelve overlapping twenty-year retirements amount to only one or two independent observations of the market (chapter 16).
  • A ranking that holds at every length of retirement. Over twenty-five years the medians rank differently: the menu each January is above the plain index in all nine cells and the list frozen at retirement above SPY. But only seven retirements are complete at that length, and the menu's top two at 70/30 ended ahead of the plain index in only 2 of 7; that experiment cannot tell.
  • That the ranking reliably finds the same funds. Moving the ranking back by one trading day changes the top two in 7 of the 32 Januaries and the top four in 12 (chapter 16).
  • A verdict beyond one fund family and one market. Every fund on the menus is a Vanguard US fund, and SPY tracks the same US market, in a period when US stocks did exceptionally well.
  • That the edge at the low point will recur. It came mostly from long-term bond funds during a long fall in interest rates, and it reversed in 2022 (chapter 16).
  • Anything about real or after-tax wealth. All dollar figures are nominal and pre-tax, as in a tax-deferred account, where switching funds triggers no tax. In a taxable account the tax on gains realised by switching would fall mostly on the selection methods; tax on distributions falls on every portfolio, the plain index included (chapter 16).
  • A rule free of hindsight. The ranking rule, the number of funds and the annual re-selection were settled after earlier versions had been examined (appendix E), which favours the selection methods.
  • Picking once and keeping as a method. Its median rests on a few early choices of two funds run by the same firm.
  • That the long histories show what the study's funds would have done (chapter 10). Over the retirements both cover, the long-history 70/30 ended 2.3% to 16.1% above the plain index, for reasons not measured. It has no fees and no Treasury-bill account, and its low points are read at year ends or from monthly-average prices, which miss the bottoms of falls. It is one country's market, and its benchmarks cannot reach back that far.
  • That a moving split protects in general (chapter 12). Its strong daily result covers one stretch of twenty overlapping retirements, 1987-2006, in years when the 10-year Treasury's yield fell from 7.08% (January 1987) to 0.62% (July 2020), before rising again from 2022, to 4.17% in August 2023, the last full month of the archived series. Over the long history its median was close to a fixed 50/50's over twenty and twenty-five years, its floor was below every fixed mix's when withdrawals rose with inflation, and it ran out more often over long retirements. There are no fees, taxes or trading costs, and the rule trades more than a fixed split. Its settings were declared before it was run, but by an author who knew how past falls unfolded, so they are not free of hindsight.

All fund figures use the restated prices of chapter 26, verified against Vanguard's published returns. The study's detailed findings, at every allocation and horizon, and its full list of caveats are in appendix G.12.

The restated prices were one correction among many. Chapter 26 sets out each error found, what it changed, and what is still known to be wrong.

Chapter 26. Errors and known limitations

Why should any figure in this book be trusted? Not because none was ever wrong: a backtest that has never been found in error has usually not been examined closely. This one was in error several times, and in almost every case the error produced plausible figures.

What can be offered instead is the record. The errors are listed below by subject, with the date each was identified and its effect where it was measured, because the corrections form part of the result. Seven known limitations, not yet corrected, follow them, and the chapter ends with how the errors were found.

Errors of method

An undeclared change of holding method (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The method specified by the author re-ranks the funds every January. After one comparison favoured selecting the funds once and holding them throughout retirement, a series of tests used that alternative without declaring it.
  • Correction. Every one of them still in use was repeated with annual re-ranking. The others had already been superseded for a different reason (appendix E).
  • Since then. No method is adopted because it scored better, and every test declares its holding method. Picking once and keeping (chapter 18) is now studied as a declared method of its own.

Closed funds topped up without limit (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Picking once and keeping restores each fund to its target every January, which can mean buying more of a fund closed to new investors. The first version allowed unlimited purchases. The closure notices allow an existing shareholder $25,000 a year, and unlimited purchases only for Dividend Growth (2016-2019).
  • How it was found. A question from the author: whether a closed fund allowed money in at all. Every closure notice the tests depend on was then read.
  • Correction. The closure terms are now the headline rule; the unlimited and no-purchase versions are shown beside it (chapter 18, appendix G.11).
  • Effect. The top two at 70/30: median from $2.85M to $2.84M (before the purchase-timing correction below; currently $2.84M without a limit and $2.83M under the terms). No conclusion changed.

The first purchase made at the ranking's own close (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The ranking reads prices up to the last close of the old year, and every later change of holdings was made a trading day later, at the first close of the new year. The first purchase of each retirement, however, was made at the ranking's own close — a trade no retiree could have made.
  • How it was found. An audit of the assumptions, comparing what the simulation does with what the book says.
  • Correction. The first purchase is now made at the close of the first trading day of the year, like every other purchase; SPY and the plain index are bought on the same day. Every test was rerun. Which funds are held each year did not change.
  • Effect. Every retirement starts one trading day later. Over twenty years SPY's median moved by 2.3%; the medians of the plain index and of every selection method moved by up to 1.8% at 70/30, 2.6% at 60/40 and 2.1% at 50/50. The worst endings in the table below moved by up to 9% (SPY's). No conclusion changed.

Among the figures in this book, the largest change in relative terms is SPY's 2000 retirement measured to 9 October 2026: $152k before the correction, $236k after. SPY fell 0.98% on the first trading day of 2000, so the later purchase bought more of it, and on a balance that small a one-day difference is magnified.

Errors in the data

Incomplete closure records (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Closures to new investors were missing:
    • PRIMECAP was closed not only from 2004 but also in 1995-96 and 1998-2001;
    • Capital Opportunity in 2000-01;
    • Explorer in 2006-08.
  • Correction. Each date was established from the SEC filings.
  • Effect. In test 14 (the 30-fund list compiled in 2026, the top two at 70/30, picked once with a closed fund replaced; appendix B), the worst 20-year ending fell from $1.25M to $672k. That test was later superseded (appendix E).

An erroneous daily price (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The database recorded a gain of 9.76% for U.S. Growth on 3 April 2019, against 0.71% for its own Admiral class on the same day.
  • Correction. With the author's approval, that day's return was replaced by the Admiral class's return.
  • Effect. The tests run on the faulty series overstated their results by up to about 9%. Every result in this book uses the corrected series.

Unreliable early Admiral prices (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The stock Admiral classes trail their own Investor classes by up to 14% a year in 2000-01. The bond Admiral classes omit dividends in 2001-03.
  • Correction. Every series therefore uses the older class before 2004 and the Admiral class thereafter, or from the Admiral class's first price where that came later (June 2005 for Inflation-Protected Securities; September 2011 for Small-Cap Value Index, Small-Cap Growth Index, Mid-Cap Growth Index and Mid-Cap Value Index; December 2013 for Dividend Appreciation and February 2019 for High Dividend Yield, which use their exchange-traded class before). Long-Term Bond Index has Admiral prices only, from February 2019, and no usable older class. Appendix F gives each fund's date.

Distributions missing from Mid-Cap Index prices (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The prices gave the fund -3.28% for 2001 and -15.18% for 2002. Vanguard's annual reports give -0.50% and -14.61%.
  • Diagnosis. The ratio of price to published NAV was constant at every report date from the end of 2000 to mid-2002. The prices were therefore unadjusted NAVs. Three distributions had not been reinvested:
    • $0.21 a share in March 2001;
    • $0.105 in December 2001;
    • $0.082 in March 2002.
  • Correction. The distributions were restored: the first on its date, 23 March 2001, which the day's price move identifies; the other two on the days that best fit the published returns, 24 December 2001 and 15 March 2002 (another day in early 2002 fits almost as well). The exact day of those two changes no result, because the ranking reads only year-end prices. With them restored, the prices reproduce every published half-year and full-year return to within 0.03 percentage points.
  • Effect. On the corrected prices, Mid-Cap Index entered the top four in January 2006, and Extended Market replaced Small-Cap Index in the 1999 list's top two in January 2012. No 20-year result changed by more than about 1%, and no conclusion changed.

The same omission in 31 funds (identified 12 October 2026)

  • How it was found. A comparison of every fund's calendar-year returns from 1985 to 2003 with Vanguard's published figures found 91 fund-years differing by more than 0.10 percentage points.
  • What was wrong.
    • chiefly, capital-gain distributions omitted through 1993: PRIMECAP in every year 1986-93; Small-Cap Index 1985-87 and 1989-90, by up to 17 points a year; 500 Index 1985-86; Extended Market 1988-90;
    • some later omissions: Intermediate-Term Treasury 1993, Inflation-Protected 2001-02, Strategic Equity 2000;
    • distributions recorded on the wrong side of a year end;
    • a few years slightly overstated.
  • Correction.
    • Each was restated to Vanguard's figure.
    • Eight funds whose 1985-88 returns could not be verified now begin at the end of 1988: Windsor, Windsor II, Explorer, GNMA, Long-Term Investment-Grade, Long-Term Treasury, Short-Term Federal and Short-Term Investment-Grade.
    • Three funds whose early prices had been excluded (Mid-Cap Index, Strategic Equity, U.S. Growth) had their history restored, U.S. Growth's to the end of 1987. Chapter 15's eight funds ranked as if young in the mid-1990s are therefore a different set: U.S. Growth is among them, and Windsor, closed to new investors in those years, is not.
  • Effect on the rankings. The menu's January rankings changed in 1995-1999, 2002-2007 and 2010-2011:
    • the top two stock funds in 1996-1999, 2003 and 2004;
    • the top two bond funds in 2006, 2007 and 2011;
    • only the third or fourth place in the other years.
  • Effect on the results, with 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, before the purchase-timing correction above:
    • the top two from the menu each January: median from $1.76M to $1.79M, still ahead of the plain index in only 2 of 12 retirements;
    • the list frozen at retirement: from $1.95M to $2.05M, ahead in 7 of 12 (previously 5);
    • the 1999 list: from $2.64M to $2.53M;
    • the benchmarks' medians: unchanged to the nearest $10k (the plain index's worst ending moved from $811k to $810k).
  • The current figures, after both corrections: $1.78M, $2.07M and $2.54M; the plain index's worst ending $835k.
  • Conclusions. They stand.

Errors in the fund lists

Survivorship in lists compiled in 2026 (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. A list of today's funds contains only survivors.
  • Correction. The study accordingly moved to lists as they existed at the time: first the 1999 list, then the menu at every year end.
  • Effect. The results on lists of survivors are not used anywhere in this book (appendix E).

An incorrect menu date in the list frozen at retirement (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The first version took each fund's menu date from the start of its price series. For three funds whose reliable price history begins after they were first offered, the list compiled at a 1996-2000 retirement was therefore incomplete.
  • How it was found. That list should equal the 1999 list for a 2000 retiree, and did not.
  • Correction. After correction it reproduces the 1999-list results exactly. The list frozen at retirement is the corrected version throughout this book.

The 1999 list applied to retirements beginning 1995-1999 (identified by the author, 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. A list compiled at the end of 1999 did not exist when a 1995-1999 retirement began, and it contains six funds launched in 1995-98, after some of those retirements had begun.
  • Effect.
    • The headline had reported 12 of 12 complete retirements ahead of the plain index (1995-2006). The valid figure is 7 of 7 (2000-2006).
    • For the four start years 1995-1998, with the top two at 70/30, the 1999 list ends $0.05M to $0.52M above the list those retirees could actually have compiled (current figures; $0.15M to $0.62M when the error was found).
    • With the top three it ends between $117k below and $395k above it.
  • Correction. The 1999 list is now shown only for retirements from 2000.

The 1999 list's rebalancing comparison begun in 1995 (identified 11 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The first year-by-year comparison of rebalancing for the 1999 list began in 1995, within the affected years.
  • Correction. It was recomputed from 2000 (chapter 22).

Errors in reporting

A published table that showed retirements running out (identified 14 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. A change made on 14 October to the program that writes appendix G's tables left it reading the single-start results from a place where they no longer were, and it printed a missing value as "ran out". In appendix G.6's table of single start years run to today, fifteen rows — SPY, the plain index and the 1999 list's top two, three and four, at each of the three splits — read "ran out" in every column, though none of those retirements ran out. The three editions of the book published on 14 October before the eleventh review carried it; no other table was affected.
  • How it was found. The eleventh review of the book: the table contradicted appendix G.12, which says that nothing on the 1999 list ran out.
  • Correction. The program reads the results by name again, and the rows came back identical to those printed before the change; the corrected book was published the same day. A missing value now stops the book being built instead of printing, and appendix G's tables may say "ran out" only where a retirement's own results record a run-out, which the program that writes them checks.
  • Effect. None outside that table.

Stored results from the old prices (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. To save time, the study kept a copy of each simulation it had run, identified by the funds held but not by the prices. After the price restatement a stored copy could therefore return figures from the old prices.
  • How it was found. A self-check that recomputes the benchmarks: the plain index differed by $3,460.
  • Correction. The stored copies were discarded, and each is now identified by the prices and the Treasury-bill rates as well. Every table in the book, recomputed afterwards, came out identical.

Statements broader than the data (identified 12 and 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Earlier versions said:
    • in Part II, that even the best bond fund held alone left less than the plain index, and that the longer the bonds, the more was left. Both hold only at the median: in the plain index's worst start years Long-Term Investment-Grade ended above it (the retirements of 1998-2002), and for the 2000 retiree 6 of the 9 bond funds did, Total Bond Market among them. Corrected 12 October;
    • in chapter 6, that SPY fell slightly less than the index because the fund holds dividends as cash until it pays them out. Nothing in the data separates that from its fee or from small differences in the price data; since 13 October chapter 6 names all three as possible causes;
    • in chapter 25, that where the menu each January often ended ahead of the plain index, its wins were small and its losses large. With the top four at 70/30 the two largest wins were +$525k (2001) and +$543k (2002), of the same order as the losses;
    • in chapter 25, that at the low point the re-selected funds held up better than the plain index. There were exceptions: the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list each reached $476k in the 2000 retirement, and picking once and keeping $352k, against the plain index's $492k (each in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in);
    • in chapter 25, that lists reviewed every three or five years gave slightly lower individual results. The list reviewed every five years ended higher in one retirement (2003, by $1,530);
    • in chapter 25, that no re-ranking method beat the plain index at the median, without saying that this holds over twenty years (over twenty-five years the medians rank differently), or that it excludes the 1999 list, which re-ranks too and ended ahead of the plain index in 7 of 7 retirements, 2000-2006. Since 13 October the verdicts cover the methods "available to a retiree from 1995";
    • in chapter 7, that with withdrawals the worst retirements fared far better with the 70/30 mix "at every length this book can test". Over forty and fifty years stocks alone ran out no more often than the mix in 7 of the 8 comparisons (chapter 11);
    • in chapters 16 and 17, that every simulated retirement in the book rests on the assumptions chapter 16 lists, and that SPY and the plain index sit beside every table that compares methods. The long histories of chapters 10 to 12 and 27 hold no Treasury-bill account and carry neither benchmark, and their yearly and monthly data charge no fees; both statements now cover the fund methods only;
    • in this chapter, that two limitations were known; the count is now taken from the list itself.
  • How it was found. Reviews of the text against the results; the last three, the tenth review of the book.
  • Correction. Each chapter now states the exceptions, and chapter 25 the length of retirement and the methods each verdict covers.
  • Effect. None on any figure.

Verdicts read from the endings first (identified 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Earlier versions compared the methods by their median endings and gave the low points after them, although a retiree lives through the low point first. Read in the order chapter 16 now sets — the worst low point, the median low point, the worst ending, then the median ending as the cost — several verdicts change:
    • the menu each January holds a higher floor than the plain index (a worst low point of $515k against $492k, a median low point of $755k against $674k), though it ends lower;
    • with the top two at 70/30, rebalancing every 6 or every 3 months lowered both low points of every method (chapter 22);
    • leaving the split to drift held a higher worst low point than restoring it each January at every split (chapter 9), at the cost of a lower worst ending.
  • How it was found. The author's ruling that the lowest point matters more to a retiree than a lower median ending, and the tenth review of the book, which found comparisons still led by the endings.
  • Correction. The comparisons from "The answer in brief" to this chapter were rewritten to give the floor first.
  • Effect. None on any figure; the verdicts above.

Answers corrected (identified 14 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Earlier versions said, or left out:
    • in chapter 15, that a long-term bond fund held one of the top two bond places in every January up to 2020. It held one in every January 1995-2022 except 2004;
    • in chapter 16, after the eleventh review, that the bet on long-term bonds hurt in 2021 as well as 2022. The long-term funds did lose money in 2021 (Long-Term Treasury -4.6%, Long-Term Investment-Grade -2.3%), but so did Total Bond Market, and the two bond funds the menu each January held ended 2021 level with it (0.1 points behind); the bet reversed in 2022, by 12.5 points;
    • in "The answer in brief", that the list frozen at retirement fell deeper at its worst than the plain index and the menu at 70/30 only. It fell deeper than the menu each January at every split, and deeper than the plain index at 70/30 only;
    • in chapter 23, when the 2000 retiree's SPY balance reached its low, among lows that all came in March 2009. It came on 30 March 2026, 26 yr 2 mo in;
    • in Part II's closing summary, that cash "lasted twenty years, then ran out", beside a figure in which $1M in cash grew. Both were true of different things — the figure withdrew nothing; the summary followed the retiree of chapter 1 — and neither said so. The summary now gives both, Figure 3.2 now follows the retiree of 1995 with the withdrawals taken out, and the chart with nothing withdrawn is Figure 27.1.
  • How it was found. The eleventh review of the book, which recomputed each answer from the results; the last, the author's own reading of the page.
  • Correction. Each sentence now gives the answer the results support, with a check that stops the book being built when they no longer do.
  • Effect. None on any figure.

Estimates and counts corrected (identified 12 and 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong.
    • Morgan Growth's estimated fall (chapter 16) re-estimated the 2009 low but not the September 2000 high, although Morgan Growth's price is smoothed at both. With both re-estimated (12 October), the biggest fall of the top four picked once at the 2000 start is an estimated 61.0% to 62.1%, not 60.1% to 60.7%.
    • The funds ranked as if young (chapter 15) were counted as eight. Growth Equity and Dividend Growth were added on 12 October and Long-Term Bond Index on 13 October: eleven in all.
    • The tables of picking once and keeping (chapter 18, appendix G.11) read the lowest value and the biggest fall of the funds alone, leaving out the Treasury-bill account. Since 13 October they read the whole portfolio's, as every other table does; the two differ by at most $79 in any retirement's lowest value and 0.07 percentage points in its fall.
    • The retirements on the 1999 list were counted in appendix G as 297: the start years 2000-2006, followed both for twenty years and for twenty-five or to date, were counted twice. They are 234 retirements, 26 start years at nine settings (13 October).
  • How it was found. Reviews of the text against the results; the last, the tenth review of the book.
  • Effect. No conclusion changed. What the first two mean for the results has not been simulated (below).

A time to recover that mixed two measures (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Chapter 25's median time to recover counted every retirement, including the months of those that never got back as though they had: SPY 161 months.
  • Correction. The median now counts only the retirements that got back; the others are counted separately, their months marked "+" as a lower bound. SPY: 85 months, the longest 237+. The same rule is used throughout the book.
  • Effect. The menu each January from 82 to 78 months, the list frozen at retirement from 81 to 78 (top two at 70/30). No conclusion changed.

A rebalancing summary corrected (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. An earlier summary said that more frequent rebalancing did not improve results reliably. That held for rebalancing every 6 months with the top two, which ended lower than once a year in almost every complete retirement for every method (less consistently with more funds), but not for every 3 months, which ended higher in most of them for every method and number of funds (chapters 22 and 25).
  • Correction. Chapter 25 now reports the two schedules separately.
  • Effect. None on any figure.

Two descriptions corrected (identified 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Earlier versions said:
    • that the 2002 retiree picked once and kept had the split left unrestored in every January from 2005. Money stayed in the bond funds only in January 2009 and 2012 (chapter 18);
    • that cash and bonds held alone had no crash to live through. That was wrong only for bonds: Total Bond Market fell 13.2% in 2022.
  • How it was found. A review of the text against the results. For the first, a replay of the simulation's January rebalancing, which reproduces the simulation's endings, showed which Januaries left money in the bond funds.
  • Correction. Chapter 18 now gives those Januaries, and "The answer in brief" describes cash and bonds separately.
  • Effect. None on any figure.

The first records of the long-history runs (identified 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. The study's first records of the runs behind chapters 10 to 12 said:
    • that stocks alone on the long history matched SPY to within about 3% over the study's retirements. In 10 of the 12 it ended between 1.8% below and 5.8% above SPY, and for those begun in 2000 and 2001 9.1% and 10.1% lower;
    • that the long-history 70/30 ended above the plain index because the 10-year Treasury did better than Total Bond Market. Over 1995-2025 the 10-year Treasury earned 4.44% a year and Total Bond Market 4.55%; the cause of the gap has not been measured (below);
    • that the hard stop's thirty-year run-outs came from too little in stocks. The six retirements begun 1881-1903 that ran out over thirty years under the 3% rule held on average 55%-57% in stocks (and 43%-45% in bonds), more than a fixed 50/50 (chapter 12);
    • in the walk-forward rule's list of its switches, that the S&P 500 was 26.0% below its high when the rule moved to its defensive split in May 1970; the rule's own month-by-month record gives 25.1%;
    • in the descriptions of the study's tools, that the yearly inflation series is the change in the year's average prices. It is the change from December to December (2008: 0.09%, where the change in the average was 3.8%), the same convention as the monthly data.
  • How it was found. Writing chapters 10 to 12 against the results; a comparison of the list of switches with the rule's own record; and the tenth review of the book, which compared the inflation series with the monthly data's.
  • Correction. Each record was corrected, and the book states the corrected versions, each computed and checked at every build.
  • Effect. None on any figure: the results were right, the descriptions of them were not.

The run-outs of 1936-1940, and two measures of saving (identified 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong.
    • The chapter on the walk-forward rule (now chapter 12) said that the retirements begun in 1936-1940 that ran out had begun just before a second fall, the recession of 1937-38. They ran out between 1975 and 1985, during and after the inflation of the late 1960s and 1970s.
    • In chapter 27, the median lowest value of $1M left alone was the starting $1M in every row of the yearly table, because most accounts never ended a year below it, so the column said nothing.
    • In chapter 27, a saver's largest fall from a high counted each new deposit as recovery: over ten years the median fall was 0.0% for every portfolio, stocks alone included.
  • How it was found. The tenth review of the book.
  • Correction. Chapter 12 now dates those run-outs and groups every run-out by the markets it met. Chapter 27 now counts the accounts that went below the starting $1M and shows how low those went, and gives the saver's floor, the lowest value as a share of the money deposited so far, from a replay of every account that must reproduce the results each time the book is built.
  • Effect. None on any ending or return; two columns of chapter 27 were replaced.

Checks that could not fail, and a note printed on the page (identified 13 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. Two of the checks behind chapter 10's comparison with the study's retirements could never stop the book being built: a failure inside them was discarded. The checks behind appendix G's tables ran only when those tables were written, not when the book was built, and a failure inside some of them went unnoticed. And a note left for the author in the source of chapter 13 was printed on the page, because two dashes inside it ended it early; it named records of the study.
  • How it was found. A review of the checks themselves, and the tenth review of the book.
  • Correction. Each of those checks now stops the build when it fails, each proved by a deliberately broken input, and building the book now rewrites appendix G and runs its checks. The note was removed, and the build now refuses any note that reaches the page.
  • Effect. None on any figure; every check passes.

An overstated claim about picking once (identified 12 October 2026)

  • What was wrong. An earlier version said that the six largest endings of picking once and keeping were exactly the six retirements that began with PRIMECAP or Capital Opportunity.
  • Correction. Of the six, five began with one of those funds; the other is the 1996 retirement, which began with Explorer and Small-Cap Index. The 1998 retirement, which began with PRIMECAP, ranks seventh.
  • Effect. None on any figure; the conclusion that the median rests on those two funds stands.

Identified, not corrected

Seven limitations are known but have not been corrected (as of 14 October 2026, the date to which the list of errors above also runs). The effect of the first two on the results has not been simulated; for the others, each entry gives what has been measured.

  • Old funds ranked as if young (chapter 15). In some Januaries, eleven funds that had existed for more than ten years were ranked on their five-year return alone. For ten of them the cause is a price record that begins later than the fund did, and a rerun that extends those records with their published yearly returns, as is done for Morgan Growth, is possible. The other, Dividend Growth, is short by rule: it is counted only from 6 December 2002, when it became a diversified stock fund, because its earlier record, as Utilities Income, is that of a sector fund, which chapter 13 leaves out. Extending its record would break that rule, so the rerun would cover only the other ten.
  • Morgan Growth's smoothed in-year prices (chapter 16). Built from its published calendar-year returns, its price moves at a constant rate within each year, so a fall inside a year is not seen. For the top four picked once at the 2000 start, chapter 16 estimates the lowest value at $414k to $421k rather than the simulated $443k, and the biggest fall at 61.0% to 62.1% rather than 58.0%. These are estimates, not simulations.
  • The long-history mixes end higher than the plain index, for reasons not measured (chapter 10). Over the study's 12 retirements the long-history 70/30 ended 2.3% to 16.1% above the plain index. The two differ in the bond held, in fees, in the Treasury-bill account and in when each year is measured; how much each explains has not been measured, and the 10-year Treasury did not earn more than Total Bond Market over 1995-2025 (above).
  • No Treasury-bill account and, on the index histories, no fees (chapters 10-12 and 27). The long histories take each withdrawal from the portfolio at the year end, without the Treasury-bill account in which the study's retirees hold the coming year's spending, and the yearly and monthly index data charge no fees. Over the study's twelve complete twenty-year retirements the daily fixed 70/30 of chapter 12 — the plain index's two funds without that account — ended 0.5% to 2.0% below the plain index, and over its seven twenty-five-year ones 0.8% to 3.5% below.
  • Low points read at year ends or from monthly averages (chapters 10-12 and 27). The yearly data see only year ends and the monthly data average each month's prices, so their lowest values read higher, and their falls shallower, than they were: with withdrawals rising with inflation, the 1929 retirement at 70/30 fell to $368k month by month (3 yr 5 mo in) but only to $419k at year ends (3 yr 11 mo in; chapters 10 and 11), and monthly averages themselves smooth the bottoms of falls.
  • Two timings in chapter 27's monthly comparison. The rule's savings accounts are timed as in chapter 12, a month later than the fixed mixes'. In chapter 12's retirements that difference alone left the fixed splits' twenty-year medians 1.2% to 4.1% lower; the savings accounts were not run on both timings.
  • An undocumented early price index (chapters 10 and 11, appendix C). Month by month, the withdrawals rising with inflation and chapter 27's deposits follow the series Shiller's archived file heads "Consumer Price Index", and the file does not say how its early years were compiled. Its December-to-December changes equal the yearly data's inflation in every year 1914-2022 (above); for the years before 1914, which only the monthly data reach, nothing checks them.

How the errors were found

How many of these errors showed themselves as a figure that looked implausible? Only two:

  • a one-day gain of 9.76% in a diversified fund;
  • a Mid-Cap Index return for 2001 that looked low for the market it tracks.

The others were found by a control:

  • an independent recalculation that disagreed;
  • a list that should have matched another and did not;
  • a date that had to be confirmed in the original filing;
  • a comparison with published returns;
  • an audit comparing what the simulation does with what the book says;
  • a self-check that recomputes the benchmarks;
  • a review of the text against the results, or of the checks themselves;
  • or a question from the author.

Every retirement in this book has had money taken out. One question remains before the book closes: what did the same markets do for money left to grow, or still being put in?

Part VIII: Before retirement

This last part turns the book's question round, as a short preview of possible further work: the same markets and the same portfolios, in the years before retirement, with money being saved instead of withdrawn.

Chapter 27. Saving instead of spending

A retiree fears running out. A saver's fear is different: putting money in for years and finding the account worth less than what went into it. How often did that happen, how far did the accounts fall, and what did saving earn in the end? Two savers are followed, over 10, 20, 30 and 40 years, from every start year the data allow:

  • Savings 1.0: $1M invested once, with nothing added and nothing withdrawn.
  • Savings 2.0: an account that starts empty; $10,000 is deposited at the end of the first year, and each later deposit is the one before it changed by that year's inflation (the change in consumer prices from December to December), so that every deposit buys about the same; nothing is withdrawn.

The portfolios are those of chapters 10 to 12: stocks alone, 70/30, 60/40 and 50/50 restored each January, bonds alone and cash alone, and the rule of chapter 12 with its hard stop to 20/80 or to 40/60. Figure 27.1 adds the four safe holdings of chapters 2 and 3, left alone.

The data, and what they are not

  • Yearly, 1928-2025: the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested, a 10-year Treasury bond and 3-month Treasury bills, as in chapter 10; values are seen only at year ends, so a fall within a year is not seen.
  • Monthly, from 1872: the S&P 500 and the 10-year Treasury from monthly-average prices, with no cash series. The fixed mixes are timed as in chapter 11 and the rule as in chapter 12, which buys at the January price rather than at the end of the December before. In chapter 12's retirements that difference alone left the fixed splits' twenty-year medians 1.2% to 4.1% lower; the savings accounts were run on one timing each, so month by month the rule and the fixed mixes differ in their timing as well as in their rule.
  • Daily, from 1987: the study's 500 Index fund and Total Bond Market fund, bought on the first trading day of the start year and restored each January. The fixed rows are therefore the plain index of chapter 8, in each row's proportions; with nothing withdrawn, its Treasury-bill account holds nothing.
  • Daily, from 3 January 1995, for Figure 27.1 only: the safe holdings of chapters 2 and 3 — the study's cash series, which earns the 3-month Treasury-bill rate, and its Short-Term Treasury, Total Bond Market and Long-Term Treasury funds — each bought once and left alone, priced at every close to 9 October 2026 (the figure plots the month ends).
  • No SPY row: the yearly and monthly data begin decades before SPY; in the daily data the 500 Index fund alone, which follows the same index, stands in its place.
  • What they are not: there are no taxes or trading costs, and the yearly and monthly index data carry no fees (the daily fund prices are net of the funds' own costs); every figure is in nominal dollars; the bonds are a single 10-year Treasury in the yearly and monthly data; and the history is that of one country's market.

It dipped below the $1M more often (100 of 132 against 91 of 132), but never as far: the median low point of the accounts that fell below it was $970k against $937k. Its worst ending was lower, $1.77M against $2.19M, and so was its median, $3.94M against $4.36M: month by month the higher floor came with a lower ending at both the worst and the median. Day by day, from 1987, against the plain index at 70/30: a worst low point of $899k (the account begun in 1990, October 1990, 0 yr 9 mo in) against $731k (the account begun in 2006, March 2009, 3 yr 2 mo in), a median low point (of the accounts that fell below the $1M) of $972k against $926k, and a higher worst ending, $3.18M against $2.97M; the cost was a lower median, $4.59M against $4.68M.

Does money left alone in the safe holdings of chapters 2 and 3 ever stand below what was put in? Figure 27.1 places $1M in each of the four, priced daily, at the start of 1995. Long-Term Treasury fell 46.0% from its peak, more than twice the 10-year Treasury's largest year-end fall in the table above (21.5%), yet after its first month it never stood below the $1M: its lowest value, $999,951, came on 24 January 1995, before its rise had begun. After January 1995 none of the four closed below the $1M on any day.

Savings 2.0: $10,000 a year, changed by inflation

For a saver the account starts empty, so its own lowest value is the empty account and says nothing about a loss. What does is whether the account was ever worth less than the money put into it so far, and by how much: the last column, the lowest value as a share of the deposits made up to that point. Did a saver ever hold less than had been put in? That column answers before the returns do.

The measure of the outcome is the annual return on the deposits: the single yearly rate at which the deposits, each compounded from the year it was made, would have grown to the ending.
