  • Savers, too, stood below what they had put in. At year ends, 44 of 79 twenty-year stocks-alone savers were at some point worth less than their deposits so far. The deepest, begun 1928, held 45.4% of its deposits in December 1931 (3 yr 11 mo in); the worst at 70/30 held 60.1%, at 50/50 70.9%, in bonds alone 91.7%, and cash alone never fell below its deposits. Month by month the stocks-alone floor was lower still: 35.5%, for the saver begun 1927, in June 1932 (5 yr 5 mo in).
  • The more in stocks, the higher the median return, at every length: over twenty years 11.4% a year for stocks alone, 9.7% at 70/30, 8.0% at 50/50, 4.1% for bonds alone and 3.6% for cash alone. Figure 27.2 follows that return start by start: stocks alone earned more than cash alone for 76 of 79 start years.
  • Over ten years the worst stocks-alone saver lost money: begun 1999, it earned -4.3% a year on its deposits. Over twenty years the worst stocks-alone saver earned 3.3% a year, less than the worst at 70/30 (3.6%) or 50/50 (3.7%), but more than the worst for bonds alone (0.9%) or cash alone (0.4%).
  • Over forty years the worst stocks-alone saver (begun 1935) earned 9.3% a year, more than the median saver in bonds alone (6.4%) or in cash alone (4.8%). The lowest forty-year stocks-alone ending, as a multiple of the deposits, was 5.9 times (begun 1969). The multiple counts every dollar deposited alike, whenever it went in, while the annual return allows for how long each deposit was invested, so the lowest multiple and the lowest return belong to different savers.
  • The rule of chapter 12 against a fixed 70/30 (appendix G.14). Over twenty years month by month, the hard stop to 20/80 kept its savers at no less than 82.8% of their deposits, against 51.9% at 70/30. Yet its worst return on the deposits, 2.0% a year, was the lowest of every portfolio holding stocks (70/30: 3.6%; stocks alone: 3.0%), and its median, 6.6%, was below the 70/30's 7.7%: month by month the floor and the returns point opposite ways. Day by day, against the plain index at 70/30, the rule's floor was 85.5% against 68.6%, and its worst return 6.3% against 5.3%; the cost was a lower median return, 7.3% against 7.6%.

What the preview shows, and what it does not

It shows, the floor first:

  • The road was not smooth. Over twenty years 36 of 79 accounts of $1M left alone in stocks stood below the $1M at some year end, the lowest at $352k (December 1932, 3 yr 11 mo in). A stocks-alone saver could hold less than half of what had been put in (45.4% at the worst year end, 35.5% month by month), and the rule of chapter 12, which kept the saver's floor far higher, earned less at the median.
  • Time changed the ending for stocks. Left alone for ten years, $1M in stocks sometimes ended below where it started; left for twenty years or more, in this history, it never did, however far it had fallen on the way.
  • Regular saving into stocks earned more than saving into bonds or cash at the median at every length, and over forty years even the worst stocks-alone saver earned more than the median one in bonds or cash.

It does not show:

  • What a saver should do. How much to save, for how long, in what mix, and when to move from saving to spending are left for further work — the point at which this preview hands over to the retiree of chapter 1.
  • Anything net of costs, taxes or inflation. Every dollar figure is nominal and before taxes; the yearly and monthly data carry no fees.
  • The future. One country's market over one century and a half holds only a few long savings periods that do not overlap.

That further work would start from three questions, with the same data and the same checks to put them to: how much a saver must put in, and for how long, to arrive at the $1M with which every retirement in this book began; what a fall like 1929's or 2008's does in the last years before the first withdrawal; and whether choosing funds, tested here only on money being taken out, fares any better on money being put in. The saver's side is the part of the story this preview has only begun to tell.

Appendices

The appendices hold the reference material: a glossary, every test, the sources, how to reproduce the results, the earlier analyses that were superseded, every fund's returns, and the detailed tables behind each chapter.

biggest fall (worst fall) the largest fall from a high to a later low of the portfolio's value, withdrawals included; "worst" is the largest over the retirements compared chapter 16
bond term (short, intermediate, long) how long a bond runs before it is repaid; the longer, the more its price moves when interest rates change chapter 3
closure a fund closed to new investors: it cannot be bought; a holder who already owns it may keep it, and may add to it only as far as the closure terms allow chapter 13, chapter 18
closure terms what an existing shareholder could still buy while a fund was closed, from the closure notices: up to $25,000 a year in the closures that matter here, without limit for Dividend Growth chapter 18
company size and style (small-cap, mid-cap; value, growth) the size of the companies a stock fund holds, and whether it favours cheaply priced (value) or fast-growing (growth) companies; the plain index's stock half is large companies only chapter 16
complete retirement a retirement whose whole length ends inside the data. In the study's own retirements, twelve of 20 years starting 1995-2006 (seven for the 1999 list, 2000-2006) and seven of 25 years starting 1995-2001; in the long histories of chapters 10 to 12, retirements of 20 to 50 years from every start year the data allow (for example 79 of 20 years in the yearly data, 132 in the monthly), and in chapter 27 savings periods of 10 to 40 years counted the same way chapter 16, chapter 10, chapter 11
defensive split the split the walk-forward rule moves to when the S&P 500 falls 20% or more below its high: 20/80 in the book's headline version, 40/60 in the other; the headline version (the hard stop) holds it until a January check finds the index less than 20% below, the first version only until the S&P 500 leads bonds again chapter 12
distribution (capital-gain distribution) a fund's payout to its shareholders of the income (dividends, interest) or the capital gains it has realised; the price falls by the amount paid, so a price series that leaves a payout out understates the return chapter 14, chapter 26
duration (long duration) how strongly a bond's price reacts to a change in interest rates; long-term bonds have long duration and move most chapter 18, chapter 20, chapter 25
ending balance (remaining) the money left in the funds at the end of the retirement, after that year's withdrawal chapter 16
ETF (exchange-traded fund) a fund whose shares trade on a stock exchange throughout the day, like a company's shares chapter 6
first version (of the walk-forward rule) the rule as first run: back from the defensive split as soon as the S&P 500 led bonds over one or three years, rather than at a January check; run with both defensive splits chapter 12
five-year minimum a fund needs five years of history before it can be ranked chapter 15
float-adjusted market value share price times the shares available to the public (chapter 4's words for it); what the S&P 500 weights by chapter 4, appendix C
floor the worst low point: the lowest value at any point, the lowest over the retirements compared; the first of the four measures the book reads, before the median low point, the worst ending and the median ending chapter 16, chapter 25
Great Inflation the years 1965-1982, as the Federal Reserve's history names them chapter 10, chapter 12
hard stop in the walk-forward rule, the move to 20/80 (or 40/60) whenever the S&P 500 is 20% or more below its highest level so far, held until a January check finds it less than 20% below chapter 12
hindsight (survivorship) using knowledge not available at the time, such as a list of the funds that still exist today — the survivors chapter 13, chapter 26
Index Committee the S&P Dow Jones Indices staff committee that decides which eligible companies are in the S&P 500 chapter 4
index fund a fund that holds the securities of an index in the index's proportions, rather than choosing among them chapter 8
investment-grade bonds of borrowers judged likely to repay; companies with good credit, paying a little more than the government chapter 3
Investor shares Vanguard's original retail share class; used before the Admiral class, and for funds without Admiral shares; Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index use their ETF share class instead chapter 14
largest fall from a high (saving) for $1M left alone, the largest fall of the account from an earlier high to a later low; nothing is withdrawn, unlike the biggest fall of a retirement; named by the years it fell chapter 27
left to drift a mix bought once and never restored to its split; withdrawals taken from every fund in proportion chapter 9
list frozen at retirement the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement (for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994), frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January chapter 19
list reviewed every three or five years the list frozen at retirement, extended every three or five years with the funds added to the menu since chapter 19
load fund a fund that charges a sales commission when it is bought or sold chapter 16
longest underwater the longest stretch below an earlier high chapter 16
lowest value as a share of the deposits for a saver who adds money every year, the account's lowest value divided by the money deposited up to that point; below 100%, the account was worth less than had been put in chapter 27
lowest value at any point (low point) in the study's retirements, the lowest value on any trading day of the funds plus the Treasury-bill account, less the spending still owed that year; in the long histories of chapters 10-12 and 27, the lowest value at a year end (yearly data), at a month end of monthly-average prices (monthly data) or on any trading day (daily data), with no Treasury-bill account. "Worst" is the lowest over the retirements compared, and "N yr M mo in" beside it is how far into that retirement it fell: the calendar months from January of the start year to the month of the lowest value chapter 16, chapter 10
median / worst (worst ending) the middle and the lowest ending over the complete retirements compared; "worst" alone is the worst ending, and the worst low point is the lowest of their low points How to read, chapter 16
menu the funds a retail investor could buy from Vanguard at a year end, within the universe of chapter 13 chapter 13
menu each January (menu rebuilt every year) each January, the top funds from that day's menu; the principal method chapter 20
merger replacement a fund that merges away is replaced by the fund it merged into, or by the next-ranked fund of its kind chapter 18
monthly-average prices Shiller's monthly S&P 500 is the average of the month's daily closes, so a fall, and the bottom of a fall, read shallower than they were chapter 10, chapter 11
multiple of the deposits a saver's ending divided by the total deposited chapter 27
N yr M mo in beside a worst low point, how far into that retirement it fell: the calendar months from January of the start year to the month of the lowest value, written in full ("9 yr 2 mo in", "0 yr 11 mo in") How to read, chapter 16
NAV (net asset value) a fund's value per share, struck once a day at the close; the price at which it is bought and sold chapter 26
never back had not regained the high before its biggest fall by the end of the retirement chapter 16
nominal dollars dollars as paid, not adjusted for inflation; every dollar figure in this book is nominal; chapters 5 and 6 also give the S&P 500's returns after inflation chapter 16, chapter 5, chapter 6
percentage point the difference between two percentages: from 5% to 7% is 2 percentage points chapter 14
picked once and kept the top funds on the first day of retirement, held for the whole retirement without re-ranking chapter 18
plain index 500 Index (VFIAX) + Total Bond Market Index (VBTLX), in the same stock/bond proportions as the portfolio it is compared with (70/30, 60/40 or 50/50), restored each January chapter 8
ran out a year-end withdrawal larger than what was left chapter 16, chapter 12, appendix G.13
rebalancing restoring each fund to its target weight: once a year (the book's rule), every 6 or every 3 months chapter 1, chapter 9, chapter 22
re-ranked every January each January the funds are ranked again and the portfolio holds that year's top two, three or four chapter 15
rolling periods (holding periods) every stretch of a given length, one for each possible start year chapter 6
S&P 500 the index of 500 large U.S. companies chosen by the Index Committee and weighted by float-adjusted market value; in the yearly and monthly long histories (chapters 5-7, 10-12 and 27) its total return, dividends reinvested (the daily data of chapters 12 and 27 hold the 500 Index fund instead) chapter 4, chapter 5
Savings 1.0, Savings 2.0 $1M invested once and left alone; $10,000 a year from an empty account, each deposit the one before it changed by that year's inflation; nothing withdrawn in either chapter 27
score the average rank on trailing 5- and 10-year return; ties go to the better 5-year return chapter 15
share class one of several versions of the same fund, differing only in costs and minimum investment chapter 14
share of what was left (taken out ÷ assets) everything withdrawn so far divided by what is left in the funds chapter 16, chapter 24, appendix G.10
SPY the SPDR S&P 500 ETF, an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 (not a Vanguard fund); 100% stocks, dividends reinvested; the all-stock benchmark The answer in brief, chapter 6
tax-deferred account an account, such as an IRA, in which gains are not taxed until money is withdrawn; the setting the figures describe chapter 16
T-bill account where each year's withdrawal waits, paid out monthly and earning the 3-month Treasury-bill rate chapter 1
time to recover months from the high before the biggest fall back to that high, withdrawals included; a median of these counts only the retirements that got back, and a retirement that never got back is counted under "never back", its months shown with "+" as a lower bound chapter 16
top two / three / four the two, three or four best-ranked stock funds plus as many best-ranked bond funds How to read
total return price change plus every distribution, reinvested chapter 5, chapter 16
V-shaped year a year with a sharp fall and a recovery within the same year, such as 2020; in such years rebalancing every three months bought low and sold high chapter 22
walk-forward rule a rule whose every decision uses only what had already happened, carried out at the next month's or day's price; here, the split moved each January by the S&P 500's lead over bonds, with a hard stop chapter 12
withdrawal $40,000 at the end of year 1, then 3% more each year; chapters 10 to 12 also run a withdrawal rising with inflation chapter 1
withdrawal rising with inflation $40,000 at the end of year 1, each later withdrawal the one before it changed by that year's inflation (consumer prices, December to December) chapter 10, chapter 12
yield the interest a bill or bond pays, as a percentage a year of its price chapter 1, chapter 3

Appendix B. Every test

Every test from the repeat of tests 14-19 onwards was declared with all its settings and approved by the author before it was run, and its settings and results were recorded. Tests 12-19 changed the holding method without declaring it; repeating tests 14-19 with re-ranking every January corrected that (chapter 26).

The tests of fund selection

27 the menu each January and the list frozen at retirement, keeping a held closed fund while it still ranks: the ranking recomputed, with that fund's closure lifted, only in Januaries when a held fund is closed; the same three purchase rules current (chapter 18, appendix G.11)

Test 26 in brief. With the top two at 70/30, the worst low point was $352k under each rule for further purchases of a closed fund, below the plain index's $492k and above SPY's $290k (each the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in); the median low point under the closure terms was $753k, against $674k and $515k. The worst ending was $408k under each rule, against $835k and $385k. The median was $2.83M under the closure terms, $2.84M without a limit and $2.82M with no further purchases, against $2.10M for the plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January) and $2.42M for SPY: the floor below the plain index's, the median above it. The result is driven by PRIMECAP and Capital Opportunity, kept through their closures. The purchase rule moves the 2002 retirement most: $3.75M under the terms, $3.88M without a limit, $3.57M with none.

Test 27 in brief. Keeping a closed fund leaves every worst low point where it was, at 70/30: with the top two $515k for the menu each January and $476k for the list frozen at retirement, with the top four $528k and $509k (each the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in, against the plain index's $492k and SPY's $290k). It leaves every worst ending where it was too: with the top two $692k and $943k, with the top four $931k and $1.02M (the plain index $835k, SPY $385k). For the top two the medians barely move: the menu each January $1.78M selling it and $1.78M keeping it; the list frozen at retirement $2.07M and $2.08M (the plain index $2.10M, SPY $2.42M). For the top four at 70/30, keeping closed funds raises the number of retirements ahead of the plain index:

  • the menu each January: from 7 of 12 to 9 of 12; the retirements that change sides are 1996 (0.7% behind the plain index with closed funds sold, 8.3% ahead with them kept) and 1998 (2.1% behind, 9.9% ahead);
  • the list frozen at retirement: from 8 of 12 to 9 of 12; the retirement that changes sides is 1995 (4.7% behind the plain index with closed funds sold, 2.5% ahead with them kept).

The medians do not move at 70/30, but rise by up to $20k at 60/40 and $68k at 50/50.

Appendix C. Sources

The fund lists, inception dates, closures, mergers and the yearly returns of the five funds that later merged away come from Vanguard's filings with the SEC, read in its public filing database (EDGAR):

  • annual and semiannual reports;
  • prospectuses, and the prospectus supplements that amend them between editions (a closure, for example, is announced in one).

The study's research notes cite each fact's filing line by line, in five parts:

  • the menu on 31 December 1999 (appendix G.2);
  • the menus at the 1994-1998 year ends (appendix G.2);
  • the funds added and removed 1995-2026, their closures, and the yearly returns of the five funds that later merged away;
  • the closure periods and their filings (appendix G.2, "Closures and mergers");
  • what an existing shareholder could still buy during each closure: the closure notices and prospectus supplements for Windsor, PRIMECAP, Capital Opportunity, Explorer and Dividend Growth (chapter 18, appendix G.11).

The prices were checked against, and where necessary restated to, Vanguard's published calendar-year returns (chapters 14 and 26):

  • the annual total returns in the funds' prospectuses;
  • the financial highlights in their annual reports;
  • the return tables in those reports.

A copy of every filing cited is kept with the study's records.

The prices and rates behind every retirement:

  • Prices are dividend- and distribution-adjusted daily closes from the author's end-of-day price database, checked as above. The database itself is not distributed.
  • The 3-month Treasury-bill yield is the 3-month rate in the daily Treasury yield-curve series published by the U.S. Treasury (treasury.gov).

Chapter 1's inflation figure, the chapters on safe money, the S&P 500, mixing and the long histories (Parts II-IV), chapters 25 and 26, and the preview of Part VIII also draw on:

  • Long-run annual returns, 1928-2025: Aswath Damodaran's "Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills" (New York University), for the S&P 500 with dividends, 3-month Treasury bills, 10-year Treasury bonds and inflation (the change in consumer prices from December to December, from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), and for the 10-year Treasury's yield at each year end in chapter 3, which the same workbook takes from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
  • Monthly U.S. market data since 1871: Robert Shiller (Yale University) — the S&P 500's monthly prices and dividends, the 10-year Treasury's yield and the monthly total return of a 10-year Treasury bond built from it, and the series the file heads "Consumer Price Index" (its December-to-December change is the monthly data's inflation). The archived file does not document how that index was compiled for its early years; it names no source for any of its series beyond "various public sources". Used to check the long-run series, to follow the retirements of chapters 11 and 12 and the savings of chapter 27 month by month, and for the 10-year Treasury's yield in chapter 25.
  • The S&P 500 itself: S&P Dow Jones Indices and S&P Global — the index methodology, factsheets from 2012 to 2026, and their published histories of the index and research on its concentration, sectors and dividends; the SEC's notices in the Federal Register on the move to float-adjusted weighting (2004-05); the Global Industry Classification Standard documents of MSCI and S&P; Yardeni Research for some price-only falls (named where used); Morningstar for one sector weight (named where used).
  • Recessions and market events: the National Bureau of Economic Research's business-cycle dates, and the Federal Reserve's histories of the 1929 crash, the 1937-38 recession, the 1987 crash and the 2007-09 recession, with a Federal Reserve Board working paper on the 1987 crash. The name "Great Inflation (1965-1982)" is the Federal Reserve History site's own, from its list of time periods (chapters 10 and 12).

Appendix D. How the results can be reproduced

Every result in this book can be rebuilt from four things: the prices, the long-run market histories, the fund lists with their dates, and the rules. Of these, only the prices are not public:

  • The prices come from the author's end-of-day price database, adjusted for dividends and distributions and verified against Vanguard's published returns (chapter 14). The database itself is not distributed. They are identified by a checksum of every one of the 291 price files and of the 31 untouched extracts behind the restated ones (chapter 14), so a rebuild can prove it starts from exactly the same inputs.
  • The long-run market histories are Damodaran's annual returns and Shiller's monthly data, each kept as downloaded with its checksum, and the Treasury's daily yield files, kept as downloaded (appendix C).
  • The fund lists are fixed by the menu dates, closure periods, mergers and liquidations of chapter 13, each tied to an SEC filing (appendix C).
  • The rules are the withdrawal rule, the Treasury-bill account and the January rebalancing of chapter 1; the ranking of chapter 15; the alternatives of chapter 9 (left to drift) and chapter 22 (every six or three months); the closed-fund and merger rules of chapter 18; the simulation and measures of chapter 16; the withdrawals rising with inflation of chapter 10; the walk-forward rule of chapter 12; and the deposits of chapter 27. Appendix B describes each test.

The order of a full rebuild is the order of the tests:

  1. the 3-month Treasury-bill series, from the Treasury's daily yields;
  2. the raw prices and their repairs (chapter 14);
  3. the price series that join each fund's older share class to its Admiral class (chapter 14);
  4. the 1999 list and its tests;
  5. the plain index;
  6. the menu each January (rebuilt at every year end);
  7. the list reviewed every three or five years, or never;
  8. the rebalancing schedules;
  9. picking once and keeping, with the re-ranking methods keeping closed funds, under each of the three purchase rules for a closed fund;
  10. safe money held alone: a cash series built from the Treasury-bill rate, and each bond fund (Part II);
  11. the S&P 500, Treasury bonds and bills since 1928, over every holding period and in mixes (Part III);
  12. the rebalancing choices: the plain index left to drift, and the selection methods with only the split, only the funds within each part, or nothing restored (chapters 9, 18 and 19);
  13. the retirement rule on the long index histories (chapters 10 and 11), the walk-forward split (chapter 12) and the savings accounts (chapter 27).

After each of steps 4-9 and 12, the tests of fund selection and of the rebalancing choices, the checks of chapter 17 must pass:

  • independent rebuilds to six digits;
  • availability compliance;
  • identical results wherever nothing was meant to change.

The other steps have narrower checks. The prices of steps 2 and 3 are compared with Vanguard's published returns (chapter 14). Step 10 runs the same simulation as the tests of fund selection, on a cash series and on each bond fund; no independent rebuild of it was recorded. The 1995 retirement behind Figure 3.2 was traced again day by day in each of the four holdings, and each time the book is built every trace must reproduce the test's own result: the ending, the lowest value and its date, the biggest fall, and the date the money ran out where it did. Step 11's holding-period returns are reproduced by the first check of step 13 below.

Step 13 has checks of its own:

  • the yearly long-history calculation, with nothing withdrawn, reproduces the holding-period returns of step 11 in all 1,776 periods compared, to the six decimals those returns are recorded to;
  • adding the forty- and fifty-year retirements left every earlier result unchanged, line for line, and the walk-forward calculation, changed to add the hard stop, still reproduces its first version's results exactly when it is run again with the first version's rule, each time the book is assembled;
  • the daily fixed 70/30 ends 0.5% to 2.0% below the plain index in every one of the study's twelve complete twenty-year retirements, and 0.8% to 3.5% below in each of its seven twenty-five-year ones, the difference being the Treasury-bill account (chapter 12);
  • every savings account of chapter 27 is replayed independently each time the book is assembled, and the replay must reproduce each account's ending, lowest value and largest fall.

Appendix E. Earlier analyses, superseded

None of these analyses is used anywhere else in this book; their tables are kept in the study's records.

  • Lists compiled in 2026 (tests 12-20): the 30-fund list and the growing list of today's open funds contain only funds that survived to 2026 — hindsight (chapter 26).
  • Picked once without saying so (tests 12-19): the first picks held for the whole retirement, although the author's method re-ranks every January. Picking once and keeping, declared and on each retiree's own menu, is chapter 18.
  • Other scores (tests 15-18): averages of the 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-year ranks, or of the 3-, 5- and 10-year ranks, tried on the 2026 list only. Re-ranked every January with the top two at 70/30, every one ended lower at the median than the 5- and 10-year score ($1.93M to $2.03M against $2.34M), yet two of the four held a higher worst low point; with the top three or four, four of the eight comparisons ended higher at the median. On a list of survivors, none of these readings is free of hindsight.
  • Older share-class prices (test 7): the first plain index used the Investor share classes throughout; over 2004-2025 their prices returned 0.11 percentage points a year less than the Admiral classes', for the 500 Index and for Total Bond Market alike. The plain index of test 22 and every portfolio here use the same prices, each fund's older class joined to its Admiral class (chapter 14), except Morgan Growth, for which the study uses its Investor class's published yearly returns.
  • Results computed before the corrections of chapter 26, including the 1999 list applied to retirements before 2000: every test still in use was rerun after each correction.

Appendix G. The detailed tables, chapter by chapter

The chapters give the short answer; this appendix keeps every long table behind them, grouped by the chapters they support.

G.1. A worked example

One retirement followed year by year: a retiree who started in January 2000 with the two best-ranked stock and bond funds on the list of that day — the 1999 list, which for a 2000 retiree is also the list frozen at retirement — re-ranked within it every January (chapter 19). It is not the menu each January (chapter 20), which chapter 23 follows beside the other methods.

  • Day 0: the ranking uses prices up to the last close of the old year; the whole $1,000,000 is invested at the close of the first trading day of the start year; year 1's spending is assumed already set aside.
  • End of year 1 (last close of the year): sell 4% of the initial $1M = $40,000 from the funds, from each fund in proportion to its value.
  • Every later year end: the previous year's amount +3%, regardless of the market ($53.8k in year 11, $72.2k in year 21, $81.3k in year 25), sold at that day's close.
  • The money goes into a T-bill account, paid out 1/12 at the start of each month; the balance earns the previous day's 3-month Treasury yield (treasury.gov, 1990-2026); any interest left at the next year end reduces that year's sale.
  • Ending balance = the funds only; ran out = a sale larger than what is left.

Example — top two at 70/30 on the 1999 list, retiring in January 2000 (first holdings, stocks / bonds: Growth Index, U.S. Growth / Long-Term Treasury, Long-Term Investment-Grade), re-ranked within the list every January:

The PRIMECAP 1995 and 1998 closures and its 1996, 2001 and 2024 reopenings, the Capital Opportunity 2000 closure, the Explorer 2006 closure and 2008 reopening, the Strategic Equity 2006 closure and reopening and the Morgan Growth 2018 closure were checked by reading the filings. PRIMECAP's 1998 notice is dated and filed 22 April 1998 and takes effect immediately (purchases made before that day do not count towards its limit); the fund's semiannual report filed 14 August 1998 says the fund closed "as of April 21, 1998". The table gives the notice's date; the simulations close the fund from 21 April 1998, one day earlier, which changes no January's ranking. Not modelled: the $25,000 minimum first purchase when PRIMECAP and Capital Opportunity reopened in 2001 and Selected Value's from 2001 (every purchase here is larger), exceptions for advisory clients, and purchase / redemption fees: Small-Cap Growth and Value Index 0.5% purchase fee and Extended Market / Small-Cap Index fees around 1999-2000; Aggressive Growth 1% redemption fee under 5 years until 2001; PRIMECAP's 1% fee on shares bought from 23 April 2001 and redeemed within five years of purchase, cut to one year from 23 March 2005; Capital Opportunity's 1% fee on shares redeemed within five years of purchase, in its prospectuses of February 2002 and February 2004. The re-ranking methods sell at a January switch, and every method sells part of each fund for the withdrawals and the yearly rebalancing, so some of these fees would have been paid. For the 1990s the closures rest on the filings read by hand: the closures of Windsor, PRIMECAP and Trustees' Equity U.S.; Vanguard's family-wide "new accounts are not currently accepted" notices, none of which covers October 1996 to April 1998; and each fund's late-1998 or early-1999 prospectus, long ones read only in part. A missed closure of another fund cannot be ruled out.

G.3. The prices, in detail

  • Prices: the author's price database (dividend- and distribution-adjusted daily closes). One series per fund: the Admiral class from its first close in 2004 or later, the older class of the same fund before that, scaled to meet it. Early Admiral data is broken (the Admiral classes trail their own Investor classes by up to 14% a year in 2000-2001 for stocks and 2.4-4.7% a year in 2001-2003 for bonds, missing dividends); from 2004 they lead by 0.07-0.16% a year, the fee difference. Every daily return of a joined series equals that of the share class it was taken from.
  • Morgan Growth (no daily prices available): built from its 34 published calendar-year returns — exact at every year end, constant growth inside each year, so its within-year drawdowns are not measured; after 2018 it follows U.S. Growth, the fund it merged into.
  • Data fixes: U.S. Growth's Investor class (VWUSX) had a false +9.76% on 3 April 2019 in the database (its Admiral class: +0.71% that day), replaced by the Admiral class's return.
  • Payouts restored: every fund's calendar-year return 1985-2003 was set against the figure Vanguard published, and the 91 periods in 31 funds that differed by more than 0.10 points — payouts the database had missed or put in the wrong year — were set to the published return. Mid-Cap Index (VIMSX) keeps its record from its launch on 21 May 1998: its 1998-2000 payouts were restored that way, and three distributions of 2001-02 that the database also lacked ($0.21 on 23 March 2001, $0.105 on 24 December 2001, $0.082 on 15 March 2002, from Vanguard's reports) were added back: 2001 -0.49% and 2002 -14.63% against the published -0.50% and -14.61%.
  • Series starts: U.S. Growth from 31 December 1987; Explorer, Windsor, Windsor II, GNMA, Long-Term Investment-Grade, Long-Term Treasury, Short-Term Federal and Short-Term Investment-Grade from 30 December 1988 (the years before could not be verified against published returns); Long-Term Bond Index from 7 February 2019, its Admiral class's first close (the older class's prices are not available); of the funds the menu each January adds (chapter 20), Dividend Growth from 6 December 2002 (a sector fund, out of scope, before that) and Growth Equity from 31 December 1998 (its published yearly returns; the fund dates from 1992); every other fund from its first close. For six funds — Growth Index, Value Index, PRIMECAP, Intermediate-Term Investment-Grade, Short-Term Bond Index and Intermediate-Term Bond Index — the price record begins one trading day before the launch date in appendix G.2, at the launch day's own price, so that first day adds no return.
  • Cross-checks: a sample of these retirements was recomputed independently from the daily prices and agreed to six digits, and every fund held in every year was checked against its launch, closure and merger dates; none was held when it could not have been bought.

G.4. The ranking, every January

Every January, separately for stocks and bonds, using only data up to the last close of the year before:

  1. Who can be picked: a fund on the 1999 list with at least 5 years of history at that year end, that still exists, and that is open to new investors then.
  2. Two rankings: trailing 5-year and trailing 10-year annualised total return; 1 = best. A fund with less than 10 years of price record has only its 5-year rank (for some older funds that is not their age; see below).
  3. Score = the average of its ranks; lower is better. Ties go to the higher 5-year return.
  4. Hold the N best (N = 2, 3, 4), equal weights within the part, filled at the close of the next trading day (the first trading day of the year) together with the yearly rebalance.

Return is the only criterion — drawdown, volatility, fees and manager changes are not considered.

The rule is written for the 1999 list. For the menu each January (chapter 20), read "a fund on that January's menu" in place of "a fund on the 1999 list"; everything else is the same.

Where a price record is shorter than the fund. Step 2 follows the price record, not the fund's age. A fund launched more than ten years before a ranking date whose price record here starts later (chapter 14) has no 10-year return that January and is ranked on its 5-year return alone, as a young fund is. Scoring that one rank alone, it can place above a fund with the better 5-year return whose 10-year rank is weaker. Every such fund and January on the menu each January (chapter 20), with the Januaries it was among the top two picks there — and, from 2000, on the 1999 list for a fund on it:

G.5. The menu each January, in full

The 1999 list (chapter 21) is one list, kept unchanged from 31 December 1999. Here the menu is instead rebuilt at every year end from 1994 to 2025: a fund can be picked in year Y only if, at the last close of Y-1, it was on Vanguard's retail menu, open to new investors, not yet merged away and had 5 years of history. Funds launched after 1999 enter once they have 5 years; funds that merged away leave at the last year end before the merger. That uses one piece of later knowledge for two funds, which left the ranking a January before they closed: Trustees' Equity U.S. Portfolio (from January 1998; closed 21 May 1998) and Capital Value (from January 2020; closed 23 March 2020). Neither would have ranked among the top four in those Januaries, and no holding changed. Everything else is as for the 1999 list: score = mean of the 5-year and 10-year ranks, ties on the 5-year return, re-ranked every January, the same closure periods, the same price series (one per fund, the older share class joined to the Admiral class; the 1999-list series plus the series below). Sources: Vanguard's SEC filings.

At top two at 70/30 one fund carries most of it: Dividend Growth (VDIGX) was in top two on the menu each January in 2009, 2010, 2012, 2016, 2023; the yearly gaps in those years (stock and bond parts together) sum to -22.2 points of the -27.7 total. The 1999-list fund it took the place of, by year: 2009 Small-Cap Value Index, 2010 Mid-Cap Index, 2012 Extended Market Index, 2016 Equity Income, 2023 500 Index.

The ranking also moves when a fund is merely added, because the score is a mean of ranks: in 1996 Trustees' Equity (never held) had a better 10-year return than Small-Cap Index and pushed its 10-year rank down a place. Small-Cap Index stayed in the top two (score 2.5, behind Explorer); without Trustees' Equity the two would tie at 2.0, so only the order changes.

What the menu each January shows:

  • A wider menu lowered the endings, not the floor. On the complete 20-year starts both lists have (2000-2006), top two at 70/30 on the menu each January against the 1999 list: worst low point $515k against $476k (both 9 yr 2 mo in), median low point $686k against $634k; worst ending $692k against $943k, median ending $1.76M against $2.54M. The holdings differ from the 1999 list in 19 of the 26 years 2000-2025; the portfolio on the menu did better in 6 of them and worse in 13, almost all of it on the stock side (summed over the years: stock part -26.6 points, bond part -1.1). Top two at 70/30 on the menu each January ends below the plain index in 10 of 12 complete 20-year starts (1995-2006); the 1999 list, on the 7 starts it is valid for (2000-2006), ends above it in all 7 (chapter 21).
  • The 1999 list's lead over the plain index depended on its list. Every fund on it was genuinely available on 31 December 1999, so for a retiree starting in 2000 the list was a real choice; but the date itself carries hindsight — it was picked in 2026, and a list fixed then kept the later-launched funds out, several of which reached the top of the ranking and then lagged. Neither list is "right": the 1999 list is what a retiree who fixed the list in 1999 would have had; the menu each January is what one who took the whole menu every year would have had.
  • Not shown: that a rebuilt menu is always worse — this is one fund family, one score and 7-12 complete start years, and most of the top two gap is one fund in five years. The menu each January is also only as complete as the filings searched for it (of the added funds' closures before 2001 only Trustees' Equity U.S.'s, in 1998, was read in its filing; the others were not searched).

G.6. The list frozen at retirement, in full

Between the two extremes — one list for ever (chapter 21) and the menu each January (chapter 20) — here each retiree builds the list from the retail menu at the last close before their start and reviews it every 3 or 5 years of their own retirement, or never. A retiree starting in 1995 builds the list at the end of 1994; reviewed every 3 years, the new list first applies in 1998, then 2001, 2004, ...; every 5 years, in 2000, 2005, 2010, ...; for a 1996 retiree, the first new list applies in 1999 (every 3 years) or 2001 (every 5 years), and so on. A review only adds the funds that joined the menu since; between reviews everything is as on the menu each January — re-ranked every January within the current list, closures at every year end, funds that merged away leave at the last year end before the merger, a fund on the list but younger than 5 years enters when it has 5 years. Versions: every year (the same as the menu each January; checked to be identical), every 3 years, every 5 years, and never — the list frozen at retirement: the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement (for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994), frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January.

Complete retirements (20 years: starts 1995-2006; 25 years: 1995-2001; the 1999 list only from 2000: 2000-2006 and 2000-2001), with withdrawals. Each cell: the median over the start years / the worst one.

How to read the tables:

  • Ending: the funds at the end of the retirement.
  • Lowest: the lowest value the portfolio reached on any day during the retirement (funds + T-bill account - payments still owed), with the start year and the date of the worst one, and how far into that retirement it fell ("N yr M mo in": the calendar months from January of the start year to the month of the lowest value).
  • Biggest fall: the largest fall from a high to a later low during the retirement.
  • Time to recover: months from the high before that fall back to the same value (withdrawals included). The median counts only the retirements that got back; "k of N never back" says how many did not.
  • Worst time to recover: the longest of all, its start year in brackets. When any retirement never got back, its time is not known, and the worst is shown as a lower bound, "n+ mo": the longer of the longest recovery and the months from the high to the end of the retirement of those never back; the start years in brackets are then those of the retirements never back. "--" = none got back.
  • Longest underwater: the longest stretch below any earlier high.
  • Above plain: the complete starts that ended above the plain index in the same start year — 500 Index (VFIAX) and Total Bond Market Index (VBTLX) in the portfolio's own stock/bond proportions (70/30, 60/40 or 50/50), restored each January.

What reviewing the list shows:

  • For top two at 70/30 over 20 years, the review interval leaves the median ending unchanged and moves the worst low point by at most 1.8%. Reviewed every year, every 3 years and every 5 years: worst low point $515k, $515k and $506k (each 9 yr 2 mo in); median low point $755k, $748k and $755k; worst ending $692k, $692k and $660k; median ending $1.78M at all three. Start by start the 3- and 5-year reviews end the same or lower in every complete retirement but one (the 5-year review ends $1,530 higher for the 2003 retiree): every 3 years by up to $67,370 (the 2002 retiree; 2.8%) or 3.5% (the 1999 retiree; $27,633), and every 5 years by up to $57,980 (the 1995 retiree; 1.7%) or 4.6% (the 2000 retiree; $31,659). At the other splits and numbers of funds the intervals differ more (the tables above). A new fund normally needs 5 years of history before it can be picked, so a list reviewed at least every 5 years already holds it by then. The exceptions are funds offered to retail investors with years of history already behind them: Mid-Cap Growth, which joined the menu on 29 June 2002 with its predecessor's record and was among the top two stock funds on the menu of January 2003, and three of the seven index bond funds launched in 2009 and offered to retail investors from 16 October 2013 (Intermediate-Term Corporate Bond Index, Long-Term Treasury Index and Long-Term Corporate Bond Index). Complete 20-year starts, top two at 70/30: every 3 years ends lower than every year in 6 of 12 and higher in 0; every 5 years lower in 8 and higher in 1.
  • Never reviewing it (the list frozen at retirement) has the lower floor but the higher endings (top two at 70/30, complete 20-year starts): worst low point $476k against $515k reviewed every year (both 9 yr 2 mo in), median low point $721k against $755k; worst ending $943k against $692k, median ending $2.07M against $1.78M. It ends above reviewing it every year in 11 of 12 complete 20-year starts, because it keeps out the funds launched after the start — the ones that reached the top of the ranking and then lagged (chapter 20). It is above the plain index in 7 of 12 at 70/30.
  • The 1999 list is a favourable list date. Only the lists built at the 1998 and 1999 year ends contain all the funds launched in 1995-1998 — Capital Opportunity, Strategic Equity, Selected Value, Mid-Cap, Small-Cap Growth and Small-Cap Value Index, which the 1999 list held in top two in 2002-2017 — and none of those launched from 2000 on. A retiree whose list dates from 1994-1997 lacks some of the first group, and one whose list dates from 2000 or later has the second (below the 1999 list in all 25 starts 2001-2025 for top two at 70/30 and top two at 60/40, and in 21-24 of the 25 at the other settings). The 1999 list is therefore shown only for starts from 2000: for a 1995-1998 retiree it holds funds launched after they retired.
  • Not shown: that the list frozen at retirement is a good rule in general — it helped here because this fund family's later launches happened to disappoint; the review interval itself mattered little for top two at 70/30.

G.7. The 1999 list, in full

Complete retirements only, and only the start years this list exists for: 20 years for the 7 start years 2000-2006, 25 years for the 2 start years 2000-2001. Retirements starting 1995-1999 are not shown: those retirees could not have had this list — it did not exist until the end of 1999, and it holds six funds launched 1995-1998 (chapter 19 has a list every start year could build).

How to read the tables:

  • Ahead: the complete start years in which the portfolio ended above the plain index with the same stock/bond proportions and start year.
  • Portfolio value: funds + T-bill account - payments still owed; the lowest value, biggest fall and both times use it.
  • Lowest value, worst: in brackets, how far into that retirement it fell: "N yr M mo in" = the calendar months from January of the start year to the month of its lowest value.
  • Time to recover: months from the high before the largest fall back to that value, withdrawals included. The median counts only the retirements that got back; "never back" says how many did not.
  • Worst time to recover: the longest of all. When any retirement never got back, its time is not known, and the worst is shown as a lower bound, "n+ mo": the longer of the longest recovery and the months from the high to the end of the window of those never back. "--" = none got back.
  • Longest underwater: the longest stretch below any earlier high.

Plain index = two Vanguard index funds, 500 Index (VFIAX) for the stock part and Total Bond Market Index (VBTLX) for the bond part, in the same stock/bond proportions as the portfolio it is compared with (70/30, 60/40 or 50/50), restored each January — e.g. 70/30 = 70% in 500 Index + 30% in Total Bond Market Index (their older share classes, VFINX and VBMFX, before 2004). Same withdrawals and the same spliced prices as the portfolios.

"k of N never back" = in k of the N start years the portfolio never got back to the high it had before its largest fall by the end of the retirement (e.g. "1 of 7" at 70/30 = the 2000 start: high 1 September 2000, low 9 March 2009, still below that high when its 20 years ended).

G.8. Rebalancing, in full

Everywhere else the portfolio is reset to its targets once a year, at the first close of January. Here the portfolio keeps exactly the same holdings (the same January picks; funds still switch only in January) but resets every 6 months (first close of January and July) or every 3 months (January, April, July, October): each stock fund back to its equal share of the stock part, each bond fund likewise, and stocks / bonds back to the split. The plain index (500 Index and Total Bond Market Index in the portfolio's stock/bond proportions) is rebalanced on the same schedule; SPY has nothing to rebalance. Trading costs and taxes of the extra rebalancing are not modelled — the 3-month schedule trades four times as often.

What the rebalancing schedules show:

  • Rebalancing more often lowered the floor: the worst lowest value at any point is lower with either schedule, and the worst biggest fall mostly larger. Over every method, number of funds and split and the plain index (102 comparisons with once a year), the worst lowest value is lower in every one, by up to 2.8%, and the worst biggest fall is larger in 101 of them, by up to 1.6 points. The median lowest value is lower in every one as well, the worst ending in 73.
  • Against that lower floor, every 3 months ended higher than once a year in most complete retirements, with the top two, three and four alike. Of the complete 20-year retirements at 70/30 it ended higher in 8 of 12 for the plain index; for the menu each January, the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list, in 10 of 12, 11 of 12 and 7 of 7 with the top two, 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 7 of 7 with the top three and 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 7 of 7 with the top four. With the top two and the plain index it ended higher by up to 4.5%, and where it ended lower, by up to 1.8%. In the calendar years the gain comes mostly from a few years with a sharp fall and rebound inside the year (the best years in the table above: 2020, 1998 and 2011 for the plain index; the two top-two portfolios also have 2010 and 2001 among theirs), where buying stocks after the quarter-end drop paid; without them it is behind. Its largest shortfall is in 2008, rebalancing into a falling market.
  • Every 6 months lowered the floor without that gain: with the top two it also ended lower than once a year in almost every complete retirement, in 12 of 12, 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 6 of 7 of them, in the same order; in most calendar years it does a little worse. With more funds it is not as uniform: lower in 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 3 of 7 with the top three, and in 8 of 12, 12 of 12 and 4 of 7 with the top four (menu, list frozen at retirement and 1999 list).
  • Not shown: that every 3 months will come out ahead in another period — its edge rests on a handful of V-shaped years, and trading costs and taxes (not modelled) would cut it.

G.11. Picked once and kept, under each closure rule

Chapter 18 keeps a fund after it closes to new investors. Each January the allocation is restored, which can mean buying more of a closed fund.

The closure notices allowed an existing shareholder to add up to $25,000 a year (Dividend Growth, 2016-2019: without limit). The rows below show every method that can hold a closed fund under three rules:

  • under that limit;
  • without any limit;
  • with no purchases at all.

Whatever a closed fund cannot take goes to the open funds of the same kind. The re-ranking methods here keep a closed fund only for as long as it still ranks among the top two or four.

G.12. The study's own findings and caveats

  • The 1999 list matters (chapter 20), and its floor and its endings point opposite ways. On the complete 20-year starts both have (2000-2006), top two at 70/30 with the menu each January has the higher floor — worst low point $515k against $476k on the 1999 list (both 9 yr 2 mo in), median low point $686k against $634k — and the lower endings: worst $692k against $943k, median $1.76M against $2.54M. At 70/30 the menu's top two, top three and top four end below their 1999-list counterparts in 26, 24 and 25 of the 26 start years 2000-2025 (20 years, or to date), and top two at 70/30 on the menu is above the plain index in only 2 of 12 complete 20-year starts.
  • For top two at 70/30 over 20 years, reviewing the list every 3 or 5 years instead of every year (chapter 19) leaves the median ending unchanged and moves the worst low point by at most 1.8%. Reviewed every year, every 3 years and every 5 years: worst low point $515k, $515k and $506k (each 9 yr 2 mo in); median low point $755k, $748k and $755k; worst ending $692k, $692k and $660k. Start by start the 3- and 5-year reviews end the same or lower in every complete retirement but one (the 5-year review ends $1,530 higher for the 2003 retiree): every 3 years by up to $67,370 (the 2002 retiree; 2.8%) or 3.5% (the 1999 retiree; $27,633), and every 5 years by up to $57,980 (the 1995 retiree; 1.7%) or 4.6% (the 2000 retiree; $31,659). At the other splits and numbers of funds the intervals differ more. For top two at 70/30, the 12 complete 20-year retirements (1995-2006): median $1.78M reviewed every year, $1.78M every 3 years, $1.78M every 5 years. Every 3 years ends lower than every year in 6, the same in 6 and higher in 0; every 5 years lower in 8, the same in 3 and higher in 1. Above the plain index: 2 of 12 reviewed every year, 2 every 3 years, 3 every 5 years. On the starts all three share (the complete 20-year retirements 2000-2006), the list frozen at retirement has a lower floor than the menu each January and a median ending between the menu's and the 1999 list's (top two at 70/30: worst low point $476k against $515k for the menu and $476k for the 1999 list (each 9 yr 2 mo in); median ending $1.94M against $1.76M and $2.54M) — the 1999 list date is a favourable one.
  • At the worst moment most of the re-selected portfolios held up better than the plain index. The lowest value a complete 20-year retirement reached at any point (fund + T-bill account - spending still owed this year; for the plain index the 2000 start, on 9 March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), 70/30: menu each January top two / top three / top four $515k / $503k / $528k (each 9 yr 2 mo in), against $492k for the plain index (SPY $290k, 9 yr 2 mo in). Of the 51 method and split combinations (the menu each January, the list reviewed every 3 or 5 years, the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list, each with top two, top three and top four; picked once and kept, top two and top four; each at 70/30, 60/40 and 50/50), 8 fell lower than the plain index in the same stock/bond proportions (the table after this list). The low point is what a retiree has to sit through; the weaker endings come after it. The edge came from the bond side: for the 2000 start on the menu each January, from the first purchase to 9 March 2009 with no withdrawals, the top two stock funds were worth 53.6 cents per dollar against 54.5 for the 500 Index fund, the top two bond funds 184.1 against 169.7 for Total Bond Market Index — mostly long-term Treasury and corporate bond funds (11 of the 20 yearly bond holdings 2000-2009), gaining as rates fell; in 2022 Long-Term Treasury lost 29.5% and Long-Term Investment-Grade 25.5%, against 13.2% for Total Bond Market Index.
  • Rebalancing more often lowered the floor; with the top two, every 6 months also ended lower than once a year in almost every complete retirement, while every 3 months ended higher in most (chapter 22). At 70/30 the worst low point of the complete 20-year retirements was lower under both schedules, by up to 2.6%, for the plain index and for the top two from the menu each January, the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list. Every 6 months ended lower in 12 of 12, 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 6 of 7 and every 3 months higher in 8 of 12, 10 of 12, 11 of 12 and 7 of 7 of the complete 20-year retirements of the plain index and of the top two from the menu each January, the list frozen at retirement and the 1999 list, respectively — by up to 4.5%, and where every 3 months ended lower, by up to 1.8%. With more funds the 6-month result is not as uniform: every 6 months ended lower in 12 of 12, 12 of 12 and 3 of 7 with the top three and in 8 of 12, 12 of 12 and 4 of 7 with the top four (the same three methods), while every 3 months ended higher in most of them at every number of funds. In the calendar years most of the 3-month gain comes from a few years with a sharp fall and rebound inside the year. Trading costs and taxes are not modelled.
  • Picking the top two funds once at retirement and keeping them (chapter 18) had the lowest floor of the fund-selection methods and, apart from two variants of itself, the highest 70/30 median ending of any method, over the twelve complete 20-year starts. Worst low point $352k (the 2000 start, 9 March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), against $492k for the plain index; median low point $753k against $674k; worst ending $408k against $835k — the worst low point and the worst ending both the lowest of the fund-selection methods; median ending $2.83M against $2.10M, the highest of any method, SPY included, except picking once with only the stock / bond split restored ($2.87M, the next bullet) or with a closed fund topped up without limit ($2.84M). The result rests on the starts that began with PRIMECAP or Capital Opportunity, kept through their closures. How a closed fund is topped up each January (the closure notices' $25,000 a year, unlimited, or not at all) barely matters, and keeping closed funds inside the re-ranking methods changes their 70/30 medians by at most $9.3k (at 60/40 and 50/50 by up to $67.9k; single 70/30 retirements by more: the top-four 1995-1998 starts change by +$183k to +$320k).
  • Letting the stock / bond split drift raised the floor and lowered the median; restoring the funds inside each part as well as the split changed little. Picked once, top two at 70/30, worst low point / median low point / worst ending / median ending: everything restored $352k (9 yr 2 mo in) / $753k / $408k / $2.83M; only the split restored $356k (9 yr 2 mo in) / $754k / $424k / $2.87M; only the funds inside each part restored, the split left to drift $449k (19 yr 0 mo in) / $749k / $501k / $2.62M; nothing restored $450k (19 yr 0 mo in) / $752k / $510k / $2.66M. Drifting gave the higher worst low point and the higher worst ending, at the cost of a lower median ending. For the list frozen at retirement (everything restored $476k (9 yr 2 mo in) / $721k / $943k / $2.07M; only the funds inside each part restored, the split left to drift $539k (9 yr 2 mo in) / $700k / $749k / $1.89M) and for the plain index, one fund in each part ($492k (9 yr 2 mo in) / $674k / $835k / $2.10M restored, $544k (9 yr 2 mo in) / $681k / $762k / $2.05M left to drift), drifting also raised the worst low point and lowered the median ending, but lowered the worst ending as well.
  • The 1999 list is used only for retirements starting 2000 or later: a 1995-1999 retiree could not have had it — it did not exist until the end of 1999, and it holds six funds launched 1995-1998. That leaves 7 complete 20-year retirements (2000-2006) and 2 complete 25-year retirements (2000-2001).
  • On those, top two on the 1999 list ended above the plain index every time, from a lower floor. 20 years at 70/30, worst low point: top two $476k, plain index (70% in the 500 Index, 30% in Total Bond Market, restored each January, on the same Admiral prices) $492k, SPY $290k (each 9 yr 2 mo in); median low point $634k, $645k and $500k. Ending, median / worst: top two $2.54M / $943k; plain index $2.13M / $835k; SPY $2.96M / $385k. Top two ended above the plain index in 7 of 7 complete 20-year starts and 2 of 2 complete 25-year starts at 70/30; 7 of 7 and 2 of 2 at 60/40; 7 of 7 and 2 of 2 at 50/50.
  • Top three and top four on the 1999 list do not, reliably. 70/30, worst low point: top three $494k, top four $509k and plain index $492k (each 9 yr 2 mo in); ending, median / worst: top three $2.16M / $918k (above the plain index in 5 of 7), top four $2.17M / $1.02M (5 of 7): adding the 3rd and 4th-ranked funds dilutes the leaders.
  • The worst start is 2000: the lowest ending at every split and number of funds, over 20 and 25 years, and the lowest low point too, except for top three and top four at 50/50 over 20 years, whose lowest low point comes in the 2006 start — the year-end-1999 ranking put Growth Index and U.S. Growth on top just before the 2000-02 crash, and PRIMECAP was closed to new investors until April 2001.
  • Later starts (2007-2025, to date): top two at 70/30 on the 1999 list is above the plain index in 10 of 19; it trails for the 2007, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2021, 2022, 2025 starts.
  • Nothing ran out in any of the 234 simulated retirements on the 1999 list (26 start years, 2000-2025, at nine settings: three splits, top two to top four), each followed for 20 and 25 years or, while still running, to date. More bonds raises the floor and lowers the typical outcome.
  • The bond side is a long-duration bet. Long-Term Treasury was among the bond funds held by top two on the 1999 list in 19 of the 27 years 2000-2026 and Long-Term Investment-Grade in 17 (chapter 20): the 5- and 10-year record favoured long bonds through falling rates. That helped from 2000 to 2020 and hurt in 2022.
  • Not shown: that this will hold. It rests on 7 complete start years; the score (5- and 10-year records), the number of funds and the yearly re-ranking were settled after earlier tests were seen; fees and taxes on the yearly switches are not modelled; and the 1999 list is a single, favourable point in time (chapter 21) — with the menu each January instead it does much worse (chapter 20).

Caveats that apply to every number:

  • The 1999 list is one list: the funds a retail investor could choose from on 31 December 1999, used only for retirements starting 2000 or later. The menu each January (chapter 20) is the principal result and is much weaker; the date carries hindsight — 31 December 1999 was picked in 2026, with what followed it known, and it turned out to be a favourable list date (chapter 21). For a retiree starting in 2000 the list itself was a real choice: it is that day's menu, the list frozen at retirement.
  • Funds without daily prices — Morgan Growth on the 1999 list, and four more that the menu each January adds (Trustees' Equity U.S., Growth Equity, Capital Value, U.S. Value) — are modelled from their published yearly returns (exact at year ends, smooth inside the year), so their within-year falls are not measured.
  • Closures: sourced from Vanguard's SEC filings — for the 1999 list's funds 2000-2026 (PRIMECAP's 2024 reopening from a prospectus supplement filed on 18 June 2024), for the funds the menu each January adds 2001-2026 (of their closures before 2001 only Trustees' Equity U.S.'s, in 1998, was read in its filing; the others were not searched; chapter 20). For the 1990s: the closures of Windsor, PRIMECAP and Trustees' Equity U.S., the family-wide "new accounts" notices (none covering October 1996 to April 1998) and each fund's late-1998 or early-1999 prospectus, read in part — a missed closure cannot be ruled out.
  • Fees and taxes: purchase and redemption fees — among them PRIMECAP's and Capital Opportunity's 1% on shares redeemed within five years of purchase, which their archived filings show in force in 2001-2005 and 2002-2004 — and taxes on the yearly switches are not modelled; fund expenses are inside the prices. Everything is pre-tax and in nominal dollars — a tax-deferred account (an IRA), no required minimum distributions.
  • Every purchase is made the trading day after the ranking (the close of the first trading day of the year). The picks themselves are sensitive to the date: ranking one trading day earlier changes the top two in 7 of 32 Januaries and the top four in 12. In one of the seven, 2003, the change comes from the five-year history rule, not from returns: Mid-Cap Growth's price record starts on the last close of a year, so a ranking one trading day earlier finds it a day short of five years (the same holds for the top four that January).
  • Biggest falls include withdrawals: SPY's 72.6% worst is the balance; the market fall alone was 55.2% (plain index at 70/30: 53.5% vs 39.8%).
  • Withdrawals rise a fixed 3% a year, not measured inflation; the T-bill account earns the 3-month Treasury yield.
  • Projections to year 30 assume a constant return from today — they are not data.

G.13. Every retirement that ran out

Every complete retirement of chapters 10 to 12 that ran out, by data set, portfolio, withdrawal rule and length; below the table, the retirements still under way that have already run out. Each start year is followed, in brackets, by the year of the retirement in which it ran out: a retirement begun in 1929 that ran out in its 20th year ran out in 1948. Consecutive start years that ran out in the same year of the retirement are written as one range. The monthly rows of chapter 12 are timed as chapter 12 times them (a month later than chapter 11's), so its fixed mixes can differ from chapter 11's monthly rows. No daily retirement ran out. Chapter 12 groups these retirements by the markets they met.

G.14. Saving instead of spending, month by month and day by day

The tables behind chapter 27 on the monthly data (from 1872) and the daily data (the study's two index funds, from 1987), with the same columns as chapter 27's: for $1M left alone, how many accounts fell below the $1M and how low, and each worst fall named by the years it fell; for the saver, the lowest value as a share of the money deposited so far. The monthly fixed mixes are timed as in chapter 11 and the rule as in chapter 12, a month later (chapter 27 gives what that difference did in chapter 12's retirements); the daily fixed rows are the plain index in each row's proportions.
